By the KING,

A PROCLAMATION,

For DifTolving this present Parliament, and declaring the Calling of another.

GEORGE R.

WH ERE AS we have thought fit, by and with the Advice of our Privy Council, to dissolve this present Parliament, which now Hands prorogued to Tkurf-day the Twenty-fifth Day of this instant April$ wc do for that End publish this our Royal Proclamation j and do hereby dissolve the said Parliament accordingly: And the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, and the Commissioners for Shires and Burghs, of the House of Commons, are discharged from their Meeting and Attendance on

day the said Twenty-fifth Day of this instant April: And we being desirous and resolved, as loon as may be, to meet our People, and have their Advice in Parliament, do hereby make known to all our loving Subjects our Royal Will and Pleasure, to call a new Parliament; and do hereby further declare. That, with the Advice of our Privy Council, we have this Day given Order to our Chancellor of Great Britain, to issue out Writs in due Form for calling a new Parliament; which Writs are to bear Teste on Tuesday the Ninth Day of this Instant April, and to be returnable on the Thirty-first Day of May next.

Given at our Court at S/, the Eighth Day of

April 1754, in the Twenty-seventh Year of our Reign.

And the House being returned;

The Right honourable John Marquis of , Son and Heir apparent of the Mod noble John Duke of Rutland, One of the Knights of the Shire for the County of Cambridge, addressing himself to the Clerk (who, Handing up, pointed to him, and then fat down), spoke to the Effed following; viz.

Mr. Dyson,

As it is necessary, before we proceed in any Business, to make Choice of a proper Person to preside in our future Deliberations and Debates, I rife, if the House will give me Leave, in order to propose one.

That Chair is not a Poll of Ease and Repose, but of great Labour and Activity: It requires a Person of a distinguished Character; whose Authority may the better support the Dignity of this House.

It is of the greatest Consequence, that we chuse the most able Person we can find to supply this important Office; for the Qualifications of a Speaker mud necef-larily have great Weight and Influence in our Proceedings, and the public Business; as the Person we shall fix on may prove ntore or less expert, will accordingly be either facilitated orobftruded, expedited or perplexed.

That honourable Chair, Sir, demands, in the Person who shall be destined to fill it, many Talents and many Virtues: It requires, in general, great Abilities; it requires, in particular, an exact Skill in the Orders, Rules, and Methods, of Parliament; it requires a perfect Knowledge of all the Powers and Privileges of this House, and a consummate Experience in the infinite Variety of Business necessarily to be transaded within thefeWalls: Be-fidcs thefeTalents, the greatest Integrity and Impartiality, an unlhaken Resolution, and Heady Firmness of Mind, are Virtues that ought to be eminently confprcuous irr the Character of the Speaker of this House.

Very difficult indeed, Sir, it is to find so many great Qualifications united in any one Person; yet we have the Happiness of having One Gentleman amongst us, whom Experience'has shewn us, on many Occaliom, to be equal; in every Shape, to this important Office; One whose great Ability and Integrity has appeared, in innumerable In-dances, through the Course of several successive Parliaments; One whose zealous Attachment for our present happy Establishment, and for the whole Constitution of this Nation in general, is well known-; and who has & Heart warm with that Zeal and Affection, which is the proper Character cf a Speaker of this House; a Zeal and Affection for the Rights and Liberties of the Common of Great Britain.

I perceive every Gentleman’s Eyes are already fixed on the Right honourable Mr. Oiijloii); I don’t doubt, therefore, but I shall meet with the unanimous Approbation of this House, when I move, That Mr. Onslow may be desired to accept of this important Trull; and that he will again take Post'elfion of that Chair, which he has filled, in Four successive Parliaments, with the greatest: Ability and Integrity, with so much Honour and Reputation to himself, to the Satisfaction of former Parliaments, and to the Advantage of this Kingdom.

There can but one Doubt occur in the Choice of Mr. Onslow, and that is, how far he himself can be induced to accept of this important and laborious Office; and yet I flatter myself there is one Argument, reful.iagfrom hii own Virtue, and Love of his Country, which will be able to over-rule this Difficulty. There is no Man, whole long and faithful Services give him a juster Title to Re-pufe and Dignity than M r.Onfow:No Man has a strictec or more indisputable Claim to every Argument of Self -defence, that can p iffibly excuse his embarking again in this laborious Office; no Man can ftrtgo the Arguments with greater Grace and Dignity; nO Man so likely to sacrifice every Consideration of personal Eife and Advantage to the Inurcft of the Public, and to the Importunities of this House, than himself.

I therefore move. That the Right honourable Arthur Onfovi, Esquire, be desired to take the Chair as Spealker.

This Acknowledgment is particularly due from me, as the strongest Union and Friendship has ever i'ublifted betwixt his Family and mine, connected by the same Principles, rivetted by the same Views, the Service of their King, and the Good of their Country.

l am particularly happy in being able to dedicate my First Attempt of this Kind to a Person of such high Worth, and in a Cause so highly to be approved of by every one in this House, that it must reflect Honour oa me, though I prove very unequal to the Talk.

It would be extremely utvneeefiary, as well as presump-tuous in me, to aim at a Detail ot nry very honourably Friend’s Excellencies, as every one here must be thorough-

Mr. Speaker,

We have it in Command from the King to acquaint you, that his Majesty is fully persuaded of the Prudence and Temper of this House of Commons, as well as of their Loyally and Duty.

And we do, by virtue of his Majesty’s ConimiCion, and in his Name, declare to you, that the King grants and allows to them all their Privileges, in as full and ample Manner as they have at any Time heretofore been granted" err allowed by his Majesty, or any of his Royal Predecessors.

As to what you, Sir, have detired on your own behalf, the King has never, through a long Course of Years, had any Reason to apprehend, that you can stand in need of Inch an Indulgence; but his Majesty has commanded us to allure you of his gracious Support in the Discharge of your great and arduous Trail; and that be will put the moll favourable Construction both upon your Words and Actions.

The House being returned;

Proceedings Mr. Speaker reported, That the House had been in the in the Peers House of Peers: Where his Majesty, by his Commis-reported. sioners> had been pleased to approve of the Choice the House had made of him to be their Speaker} and that he had, in their Name, and on their behalf, by humble Petition to his Majesty, laid Claim to all their antient Rights and Privileges; particularly that they, their Servants, and Estates, may be free from Arrests, and all other Mo-leftation — That they may enjoy Freedom of Speech in their Debates, and have Accel's to his Royal Person, as Occasion shall require — and that all their Proceedings may receive from his Majesty the moll favourable Construction; which, lie said, his Majesty, by his laid Commissioners, had confirmed to them, by granting and allowing their Privileges in as ample Manner as ever they were granted and allowed by his Majesty, or any of his Royal Predccefiors.

Then Mr. Speaker did again return his humble Thanks to the House for the very great Honour they had now done him; and did allure them of a Continuance of his Fidelity in their Service; humbly requesting the Continuance of their Protection and Assistance to him in the Discharge of this great Trull, and of their Indulgence to him in the Pardon of his Failings and Impeded ions in it} which, he said, he had now much more Reason to desire of them than ever before, as his Age, and the Infirmities attending that, did the more require it.

He then put them in Mind of their Duty, to observe and keep strictly to the Rules and Orders of the House, and particularly to avoid all personal Altercation, and whatever shall lead to that, in their Debates.

He lastly recommended to Gentlemen an earlier Attendance upon the Businessof the House} the Nt-gled of which, he took Notice, had grown to a Degree of late that had rendered the proper Doing of Business almost impracticable; and wifiied therefore that, against the next Session, Gentlemen wotold think of some effectual Methods to prevent the Continuance of so great an Evil.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

A Bill for the more effectual preventing clandestine Outlawries, was read the First Time.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a Second Time.

Mr. Speaker reported to the House, That when the House attended his Majesty Yesterday in the House of Peers, his Majesty was pleased to make a most gracious Speech from the Throne to both Houses of Parliament; of which, Mr. Speaker laid, he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy: Which he read to the House; and is as followeth; viz.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

It is with great Pleasure that I meet you in Parliament, at a Time when the late Elections have afforded my People an Opportunity of giving fresh Proofs of their Duty and Affection to my Person and Government; in the Choice of their Representatives.

The general State of Affairs in Europe has received very little Alteration since your last Meeting: but I have the Satisfaction to acquaint you, that I have lately received the strongest Assurances from my good Brother the King

Vol. 27.

of Spaing of his firm Resolution to cultivate Friendftup and Confidence with me, with reciprocal Acts of Harmony and good Faith; and that he will persevere in these Sentiments. It shallbemy principal View, as well to ft lengthen the Foundations, and secure the Duration, of the general Peace, as to improve the present Advantages ofir, for promoting the Trade of my good Subjects, and protecting those Possessions, which make one great Source of our Commerce and Wealth;

The Plan formed by the last Parliament for appropriating the forfeited Estates in the Highlands to the public Benefit, appears to be of such national Importance, that I am persuaded you will not omit any proper Opportunity of completing it. Let me also recommend it to you to make such further Provisions as may be expedient for perpetuating the due Execution of the Laws, ar.J the just Authority of my Government, in that Part of the united Kingdom.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I have ordered the Estimates for the enduing Year to be prepared and laid before you. The Supplies which I have to ask of you are such as shall be necessary for the ordinary Services, for the Execution of such Treaties as have b.en communicated to you, for consolidating and maintaining that System of Tranquility, which is my great Object, and, at the same time, for securing uurselves against any Incroachments.

The gradual Reduction of the National t)ebt, which has been so wifely and successfully begtm, will, I make no doubt, have your serious and constant Attention.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

It is unnecessary for me to use any Arguments to press upon you, Unanimity and Dispatch in your Proceedings;

I have had such ample Experience of the Fidelity, Zeal, and good Disposition, of my Parliaments, during the course of my Reign, that I trust there is a mutual Confidence established between us; the surest Pledge of my own and my People’s Happiness.

Resolved, Nemine contradicente. Resolved, That no Peer of this Realm hath any Right to give his Vote in the Election of any Member to serve in Parliament,

Resolved, That Where the House shall judge any Petition touching Ele<ftions, to be frivolous and vexatious, the House will order Satisfaction to be made to the Person petitioned against.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath procured himself to be elected or returned a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery, or any xrther corrupt Practices, this House will proceed with the Utmost Severity against such Person.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath teen tampering with any Witness, in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof; or, directly or indirectly, hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence; the same is declared to be a high Crime and Misdemeanour; and this House will proceed with the titmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath given false Evidence in any same before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmdft Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That it is a high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain, for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Members to l'erve for the Commons in Parliament.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from time to time, take into his Custody any Stranger or Strangers, that he shall see, or be informed of to be, in the House or Gallery, while the House, or any Committee of the whole House, is fitting; and that no Person, so taken into Custody, be dill barged out of Custody, without the special Order of the House.

Ordered, That the Back-door of the Speaker's Chamber be locked up every Morning, at the Sitting of the House, and the Key delivered to the Clerk, to be locked up by him: And that he do not presume ro deliver the same to any Person whatsoever, without Order of the House: And that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take care to clear the Speaker’s Chamber every Day, before the Door is locked up.

Ordered, That no Member of this House do presume to bring any Stranger or Strangers into the Haute, or Gallery thereof, while the House is fitting.

Ordered, That the Constables, and other Officers, of Middlesex and Westminster, do take care, that, from Eleven of the Clock in the Morning, to One in the Afternoon, and from Four till Six in the Afternoon, during the Session of Parliament, the Passages through the Streets between Temple-bar and Westminster-hall shall be kept free and open; and that no Obstruction be made by Cars, Drays, Carts, or otherwise, to hinder the Passage of the Members to and from this House: And that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do give Notice of this Order to the Officers aforesaid.

Ordered, That the Constables in waiting do take care that there be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in Westminster-hall, or the Passages leading to the House, during the Sitting of Parliament; and that there be no Annoyance by Chairmen, Footmen, or otherwise, therein, or thereabouts

Ordered, That the said Orders be sent to the High Bailiff of IVefmhfter; and that he do lie the same put in Execution.

Ordered, That no Footman be permitted to be within the Lobby of the House, or upon the Stairs leading thereto.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take care, that there be no Gaming or other Disorders, in the Room appointed for the Footmen, attending the Members of this House, to wait in.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take into his Custody such Footmen as shall presume to disobey the Orders of the House; and that r.o such Footmen be discharged out of Custody, but by the special Order of the House.

Ordered, That, to prevent the Intercepting or Losing cf Letters directed to Members of this House, the Person appointed to bring Letters from the General Post Office to this House, or tome other Person to be appointed by the Post-master G eneral, do, for the future, cvciy L):.v, during the Session of Parliamet t, Sundays excepted, con-Handy attend, from Ten of the Clock in the Morning, till One in the Afternoon, and for Two Hours at the iuut immediately after the Kiting of the House; and also on every Monday, IVedncfJcy, and Friary, trom Five c( the Clock in the Afternoon till Seven, at the Place appointed for the Delivery of the said Letters; and take care, during his Stay there, to deliver the same to the several Members, to whom they shall be directed, or to their known Servant or Servants, or others bringing Notes under the Hands of the Members lending for the lame.

Ordered, That the said Officer do, upon his gffing away, lock up such Letters as shall remain undelivered* and that no Letter be delivered but within the Hours aforesaid.

Ordered, That the said Orders be lent to the Post-master General.

Ordered, That when any Letter, or Packet, directed to this House, shall come to iVIr. Speaker, he do open the lame, and acquaint the House, at their next Sitting, with the Contents thereof, if proper to be communicated to this House.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from time to time, when the House is going to Prayers, give Notice thereof to all Committees; and that all Proceedings of Committees in a Morning, alter such Notice, be declared to be null and void.

Ordered, That the Votes of this House be printed, being first perused by Mr. Speaker* and that he do appoint the Printing thereof; and that no Person, but such as he shall appoint, do presume to print the fame.

Resolved, That this House will receive no Petitions for private Bills, after the Sixteenth Day ol January next.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, and other Freeholders, of the County of Oxford, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was also presented to the House, and read; alleging, That, before and at the last Election for the said County, many corrupt and illegal Practices were made use of by the Lord Parker and Sir Edward , and their Agents, in order to obtain a Majority on the Poll; and that the Lord Wtnman and Sir James Dash-wood, for whom the Petitioners voted, had, at the Close of the Poll, a considerable Majority, notwithstanding the partial Behaviour of the Sheriff, and the Number of illegal Votes admitted for Lord Parker and Sir Edward Turner-, and that a Scrutiny being granted by the Sheriff, at the Request of the said Lord Parker and Sir Edward Turner, the same was proceeded on by the Sheriff in a partial Manner, as it allowed Lord Wenman and Sir James no Opportunity to object to any of the bad Votes on the Side of the other Candidates, nor even Time to answer, by far, the greater Part of the Objections made to those who polled for themselves; and that though the said Scrutiny was not completed, nor any Numbers declared by the Sheriff on the Close of it, yet lie took upon himself arbitrarily and illegally to return Lord Parker and Sir Edward Turner, together with Lord Wenman^.nd Sir James wood, in the same Indenture of Return, contrary to the Majority of Votes received by him upon the Poll, and to his own Declaration of the Numbers at the Close of the Poll, without a subsequent public Examination into the Rights of the Voters on both Sides, previous to such Return; in manifest Violation of the Freedom of Elections, and of the Rights of the Petitioners, and other Freeholders of the said County, who are thereby deprived of having any Representatives to fit in the House: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant the Petitioners such Relief therein, as to the House shall seem just and reasonable.

That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petitions; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petitions,

The Agents for the Petitioners produced to the Committee an Act, passed in the 25th Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for repaiiing the Roads from the Town of Shrewsbury, through in the County of Salop, and Overton, in the County of Flint, to Wrexham, in the county of ; whereby

it appeared, that several Tolls had been granted for repairing the said Roads.

Then the Agent for the Petitioners produced the Account of the Treasurer to the said Turnpike; whereby it appeared, that the Sum of £. 1,000 had been borrowed upon the Credit of the said Act, which ftiil remains due.

And Mr. Corbel Price, Surveyor of the said Roads, being examined, said. That the said Sum of £.1,000, together with the Produce of the said Tolls, had been laid out in repairing the said Roads, eredingToll Houses and Bridges, and other necessary Works in pursuance of the Directions of the said Act; and that a great Progress has been made in repairing the said Roads.

Then a Clause in the said Act being read, which prohibits the Trustees from erecting any Turnpike between the Town of Marc/noiel and the Town of Wrexham, or between the Town of Bangor and the Town of,

or between the To ton of Eliefmere and a Place called Whit mere;

The said Mr. Price further laid, That, by means of the said Restriction, many Persons, though they travel several

Miles

2)° Novembris. A. 1754*

Miles on the said Road, avoid the Payment of the Tolls, to the great Diminution thereof; but that if a Gate was let up at Wrexham, they would all be compelled to pay.

Your Committee then proceeded to examine into the Condition of the several other Roads:

And the said Mr. Price said, That the Road from Marchwiel to Whitchurch, in the County of Salop, which is Thirteen Miles in Length, is extremely bad; and that the Road from the Bottom of Twining Bank, in the Township of Erbistock, to Rhuabon, in the County of Denbigh, is

in the most ruinous Condition that he ever saw a Road in; and that these Roads are the High Roads to several Coal Mines: That the Roads from Orton to Bangor, and from Orton to Hanmer (through both which he has gone very lately), are in so ruinous a Condition, as to be dangerous even to Passengers on Horseback; and that none of the said Roads are capable of being repaired by the ordinary Course of Law.

Mr. John Dawson, being examined, confirmed the whole of the Evidence given by Mr. Price.

Supply. Mr. Charlton, according to Order, reported from the

Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Resolutions, which the Committee had directed him to report to the House j which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Number of Land Forces, including Eighteen hundred and Fifteen Invalids, amounting to Eighteen thousand Eight hundred and Fifty-seven etfedive Men, Commission and Non-commission Officers included, be employed for the Service of the Year 1755.

Refolded, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Six hundred Twenty-eight thousand Three hundred and Fifteen Pounds Seven Shillings and Eleven Pence, be granted to his Majesty, for defraying the Charge of the Eighteen thousand Eight hundred and Fifty-teven effectice Men for Guards, Garrisons, and other his Majesty’s Land Forces in Great Britain, Guernsey, and Jersey, for the Year 1755.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Two hundred Thirty-six thousand Four hundred and Twenty Pounds Eighteen Shillings and Sixpence Halfpenny, be granted to his Majesty, for maintaining his Majesty’s Forces and-Gar-rifons in the Plantations, and Gibraltar, and for

Provisions for the Garrisons in Nova Scotia, Newfoundland, Gibraltar, and Providence, for the Year 1755.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Forty thousand Three hundred and Fifty Pounds Fifteen Shillings, be granted to his Majesty, for defraying the Charge of Two Regiments of Foot, to be raised for his Majesty’s Service in North America, for the Service of the Year 1755.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Seven thousand Three hundred Thirty-eight Pounds Two Shillings and Sixpence, be granted to his Majesty, for defraying the Charge of several Officers appointed by his Majesty to go with the Forces in the Expedition under the Command of Major General Braddock, for the Year 17 55.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding One thousand Seven hundred Seventy-nine Pounds Seven Shillings and Sixpence, be granted to his Majesty, for defraying the Charge of the Officers appointed by his Majesty to attend the Hospital established for the Service of the Expedition under the Command of Major General Braddock, for the Year *755-

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding One hundred and Nineteen thousand Three hundred and Sixteen Pounds Ten Shillings, be granted to his Majesty, for the Charge of the Office of Ordnance, for Land Service, for the Year 17 55-

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Thirty-two thousand Two hundred and Fifty Pounds Eight Shillings and Eight Pence, be granted to his Majesty, for defraying the extraordinary Expence of the Office of Ordnance, for Land Service, not provided for by Parliament.

A Petition of the Trustees appointed to put in Execu- Darlington-tion an Act of Parliament, passed in the 24th Year of his Road*, present Majesty’s Reign, for repairing the High Road leading front Darlington, ill the County of Durham, and several other Roads in the said County, therein mentioned, was presented to the House, and read; reciting some

Provisions in the said Act for amending the several Roads therein mentioned; and fetiing forth, That the Trustees, appointed to put the said Act in Execution, have made a considerable Progress in repairing the said Road; and that several Sumsof Money, to the Amount of £.3,200, have been borrowed by the said Trustees, and are now due, upon the Credit of the said Act; and alleging, that, notwithstanding the Tolls collected, and the Money so borrowed, has been duly applied in amending the Road aforesaid, yet by reason of the many heavy Carriages passing and repairing on the said Road (several of which Carriages, laden with Lime, are, by the said Act, exempt from paying the Tolls thereby granted, and others returning laden with Coals, which come into the Road at a Place called Tree Lane, pay but Half Tolls), the said Tolls, annually received upon the said Road, do not raise a sufficient Sum ot Money to pay the Interest of the Money borrowed, and to amend and keep in Repair the said Road; but the fame, in many Parts thereof, is yet in a ruinous Condition, and cannot be effectually repaired, and so kept, without a very great and extraordinary Expence (the Materials for repairing the said Road lying at a great Distance upon many Parts thereof); and that it will be impossible to complete the Repair of the said Road, and keep the same in Repair, and pay off the Money borrowed, and now due, as atorc-feid, unless the Tolls and Duties by the said Act granted be augmented, and the said Lime Carriages be charged, and the said Coal Carriages returning by the said Lane, called Bur Tree Lane, be charged full Toll; and further setting forth. That the Powers, granted by the said Act, are, in many Instances, found ir.sufficient; and that several Difficulties have arisenin putting the said Act in Execution, whereby the good Purposes by the said Act: intended are greatly obstructed: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for explaining, amending, and making more effectual, the above-mentioned Act of Parliament; and f©r augmenting the Tolls of the said Road, and charging the said Coal and Lime Carriages, for the Purpose aforesaid, in such Manner, and by such Means as to the House shall seem meet.

Eleven Years, from the Feast of St.Michael then next cn-suing; and alleging, that the Passage over the said Ferry is frequently very inconvenient, and sometimes dangerous; and that if a Bridge was built crols the said Haven at or near the said Ferry, a much more safe and convenient Communication would be thereby opened between the Isle of Tka net and the said Town and Port, and also the Towns of Deal, Dover, and several other Places in the Eastern Parts of the County of Kent: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for building a Bridge cross the said Haven, and for supporting and maintaining the fame, and for Performance of all such other Matters as shall be necessary to be done in relation thereto, upon such Compensation to be made to the said Hospital, for the Loss of the Profits of the said Ferry and to the said Lcfiee, as this House shall think proper.

the City of Glasgow, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it i nr at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

The Agent for the Petitioners produced to your Committee, an A (St, passed in the Parliament of Scotland, in the 4th Year of the Reign of King William and Queen Mary, whereby a Duty of id. Scots, or One Sixth Part of a Peny Sterling, was granted to the said City upon each Pint of Ale and Beer to be brewed in, brought, vended, tapped, or fold, within the said City, and other Places therein mentioned, for the Term of Sixteen Years: And also,

An Act, passed in the Parliament of Scotland, in the Third Year of the Reign of Queen whereby the former Act was further continued for the Term of Sixteen Years, from the Expiration of the said former Act: And also,

An Act, passed in the First Year of his late Majesty’s Reign, whereby the said Act was further continued till the lfto (November 1738.

Which said several Acts were read.

He then produced to your Committee, an Act of the 9th Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, whereby it appears that the said Act was further continued for 25 Years, from tft November 1738; and was likewise extended to the Villages oiGorbells and Fort Glasgow, and Privileges thereof.

Then Andrew Cockran Esquire, being examined, said. He had been Four Years Provost of the said City, and had been many Years One of the Baillies:

That many B/ewers, in order to evade the Duties, set up Breweries without the Liberties of Glasgow and the Gorbells, and from thence smuggled the Ale and Beer into the said Liberties.

Then the Witness produced (o your Committee, an Account of the yearly Amount of the said Duties for the last Five Years, which, on an Average, amount to£*1,440 per Annum.

He also produced to your Committee, an Account of the fixed Revenue of the City of Glasgow, amounting to £.1,650 per Annum-, which, with the Amount of the Duty afore-mentioned, makes in the Whole £. 3,050.

The said Witness then produced to your Committee, an Account of . the annual Disbursements of the said City, amounting to£.3,212. in 7 whereby it appeared, that the Expence of the City exceeded their Income yearly £.162.

That though the City Revenues have been managed with the utmost Frugality, the Magistrates have been obliged to increase their Debt to the Amount of£ 2,000, since the patfing of the last Act; Part of which additional Debt was contrafted, in order to pay the Fine laid upon the said City by the Rebels, in the last unnatural Rebellion, the Sum granted by the Legislature to make good the same being insufficient for. that Put^ofe; and that it will be impossible to discharge the said Debt, and defray the current Expences of the Government of the said City, without a further Continuation of the said Duty.

the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by his Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That his Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Conf.deration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; alleging, That the Petitioners have invested the whole Sum, granted for 1754, in Stores and Necessaries for the several Forts, and in Materials for rebuilding the Fort at vialoe-, which Sum is greatly insufficient for carrying on that necessary Work, and supporting the other Forts and Settlements on the Coast c& Afrand that the Fort at Annamaboe, when completed, will be of the greatest Importance for the Protection of the Trade of that Place, and, in Consequence thereof, the Trade of the whole Cold

Coefl, which the French have attempted at different times to encroach upon, and take from the and that the

Petitioners have already expended a much larger Sumthan has been granted for that Service: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant such Supplies for the Year 1755, as to the House shall seem meet.

Whale A Petition of the Merchants, and others, concerned in PUbciy. the Whale Fishery, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That by an Act, made in the 6th Year of His present Majesty, a Bounty was granted of Twenty Shillings a Ton upon all Ships employed in catching of Whales in the Greenland and other Seas; but that few or no Ships being fitted out upon that Encouragement, a further Bounty of Ten Shillings per Ton was

Vol. 17.

granted by an Act, passed in the Thirteenth Year of his present Majesty; and that this Addition to the Bounty being also found insufficient to a.nfwer the Purposes intended by the granting thereof, the same was, by an Act passed in the22d Year of His present Majesty, increased to 40^. per Ton, and was to have Continuance until the 25th Day of December 1757, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and alleging, that, since the granting of this Bounty, a great many Ships have been fitted out from both Parts of the united Kingdom, and employed upon this Fishery with greater Success than could have been rcalonably expected in an Undertaking of so hazardous and difficult a Nature, and which was in a manner new to the Subjects of this Kingdom; and that many Ships have been fitted out for, and a great Number of BritiskSailors have been trained up in, this

Service, and several of our Manufacturers have been in-strufted, and are now constantly employed, in making the proper Utensils and Inllrunvents; and that if the Bounty is not further continued, many Persons will be deterred from engaging in this Trade, and those now concerned therein cannot possibly continue to carry it on against the superior Skill and Dexterity of the Dutch, acquired by their long Experience in.and almost foie Enjoyment of, this valuable and important Branch of Commerce ;but that if Provision was made to continue the Bounty for a further Term, under the present or such other Regulations as the House Avail think fit, it would give great Power to the Efforts of the Persons concerned, and greatly increase the Number of Adventurers; and that if a further Duty was Lidonall foreign Whaleboneimportcdinto this Kingdom, and no Drawback allowed upon the Exportation of the fame, it would be a great Benefit to this Trade, and prevent several Frauds, which otherwise may hereafter be committed: And therefore praying the House to take the Prenvtles into Confident on, and grant the Petitioners such Relief therein as to the House Avail leem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine, and state to the House, the Matter of Fuct contained in the said Petition.

Vol. 27.

Customs, and Bonds executed by the Owners and Matter of each Ship for Treble the Bounty; and Oath was also made by the Petitioners, that the said Ships were to proceed directly for those Seas, for the Bufinets of the Whale Fishery only, arid on no other Account whatsoever; and that thereupon a Licence was granted by the said Commissioners for that Purpose; and the said Three Ships were cleared out of his Majesty’s Custom-house in London the Beginning of April last, and proceeded directly for the Greenland Seas, and arrived there the Beginning of May following; and that the said Ships, in endeavouring to kill Whales in those Seas, and execute the Purport of their Voyages, were unfortunately and unavoidably loft, with Three large Whales on Board, and the Crews of the said Ships with much Difficulty taved their Lives; and that as the Bounty granted by the said Acts, to enable his Majesty’s Subjects to fit out Ships for this Fishery, is directed to be paid at the Return of the Ships, the Petitioners are by this Misfortune, wholly deprived of the said Bounty, without the Aid and Assistance of the House; and expressing the Hope of the Petitioners, that the Owners of Ships, which were sent to Sea in the Manner required by the said Acts, but unavoidably perished, to the great Lois of such Owners, in attempting to carry into Execution the Intention of the Legislature, will be deemed equally defending of the Encouragement given by the said Acts, with the Owners of Ships which have made prolperous and successful Voyages: And therefore praying the House to take the unhappy same of the Petitioners into Consideration, and to grant them such Relief, and in such Manner, as to the House shall seem meet.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; letting forth, That, by his Majesty’s royal Proclamation* dated 5th May 1748, declaring the Cessation of A-ms as Well by Sea as Land, agreed upon between his Majesty, the most Christian King, and the States General of the United Provinces, and enjoining the Observance thereof

and reciting, inter alia. That, to prevent all Occasions of

Complaints and Disputes which mightarife upon Account of Ships, Merchandizes, and other Effects, taken at Sea, it had been mutually agreed, that suchShips, Merchandizes, and other Effects as should be taken in the Channel and in the North Seas, after the Space of Twelve Days, to be computed from the 19th of April then last, being the Day the Preliminaries were signed by the Ministers of the said Three com rad ing Powers, and which should be taken, after Six Weeks from the said 19th of April, beyond the Channel, the British Seas and the North Seas, as tar as Cape Saint Vincent, and for the Space of Six Weeks more beyond the Cape to the Equinoctial Line, whether in the

Ocean or Mediterranean, and for the Space of Six Months from the said 19th of April, beyond the said Equinodial

Line or Equator, and in all other Places of the World, without any Exception, or other more particular Distine* tion of Time or Place, should be restored on both Sides) his Majesty, by the Advice of his Privy Council, notified the same to all his loving Subjects, and strictly commanded that all Acts of Hostilities should cease against France, from and after the respective Times above-mentioned; and that the Commissi.mers of the Admiralty, on the nth May 1748, sent their Order or Notice of thtf above Preliminaries, with feveraf of the said Proclamations, to Rear Admiral Knowles at Jamaica, where he was then Rationed with a Squadron of his Majesty’s Ships of War, directing him to comply with the Terms of the said Proclamation, but to continue Hostilities against Spain, uniil further Orders; and that, pursuant to thefb Orders of the Lords of the Admiralty, Rear Admiral' Knowles having received Information that the Galleons were expected to fail soon from La VeraCruz for the Ha-vannah, failed from Port Royal in Jamaica with his Majesty’s Ships Cornwall, Tilbury, Canterbury, and ’/

Admiral Knowles received a.Second Letter from the Lords of the Admiralty, dated ift July 1748, informing him, that the Crown of Spain had acceded to the said Preliminaries on the 7th of June 1748, and requiring him to cease Hostilities against the Subjects of his Catholic Majesty and Republic of Genoa; and that, on the 16th of February 1748, the Money and Effects were condemned by the Judge of the Court of Vice Admiralty in Jamaica; And that, upon the said Condemnation, and no Claim being made by the Captain of the said Polacra, or on behalf of the Owners of the said Prize, and the said Squadron being on the Point of separating, the said Prize and Effects were duly distributed by Admiral Knowles to and amongst the Officers, Sailors, and Soldiers; and that James Tierny, of London, Merchant, on behalf of Francis Molla Master of the said Polacra, and of Don Libino Fernando Fandenbrouke, of Cadiz, Merchant, and other

Subjects of his most Catholic Majesty, on the 18th of July 1749, entered his Claim and Appeal before the Commissioners of Appeals in Prize Causes, claiming the said Polacra, and her Cargo, and appealing from the said Sentence, condemning the said Money and Effects; and that, upon hearing this Appeal before the said Commissioners of Appeals, on the 26th of March 1752, their Lord ships were pleased to reverse the said Sentence, and decreed the said Money and Effects, or the Value thereof, to be restored; and, on the nth June 1752, their Lordships referred it to Daniel Esquire,

and Two other Merchants of London, to ascertain the Value of the said Money and Effects; and who, by their Report, of the 13th of February 1753, ascertained the Value thereof at £. 13,869. "s.to which Report their

Lordships, by their Order of the 15th of last,

> confirmed, and decreed a Monition for Payment of the Money; and alleging, that, at the time their Lordships pronounced this Decree of Restitution, it was, as the Petitioner apprehends, upon political Principles, and considering it as aQuestion between Nation and Nation, and not from any Opinion that Rear Admiral Knowles ought to pay the said Sum out of his own Pocket, which was he to do, it mud involve him in inevitable Ruin, as the Consequence of his having pursued his Instructions, and discharged his Duty to his King and Country; but that the said Commissioners pronounced the above Decree of Restitution, as the Petitioner apprehended, on an Opinion that the said Sum ought to be paid by the Public to the Spanish Claimants; and that Admiral Knowles should like-wife be repaid the Costs he had been put to in defending tire laid Appeal; and further setting forth, that Admiral Knowles'S Costs in defending this Appeal amount to the Sum ofjf.498. which being added to the said Sum of jC-13,869. 7 s. 10 d.make together the Sum of ^.14,367. 7 s. 10 d.; and that the said Capture was made not only

before Admiral Knowles either had, or possibly could have, any Notice of the Cessation of Hostilities with Spain; but when he was informed of the Cessation of Hostilities with the French, he had express Orders from the Lords of the Admiralty to continue Hostilities against the Spaniards till further Order; and that the present Capture was made, and the Spanish Fleet afterwards engaged, agreeable to those Orders; and representing to the House, that, should Admiral Knowles be left liable to the Payment «f this Money, he must be reduced to the most calami-tousSituation imaginable, as he was bound by the strongest Ties to obey his Superiors, and will now tie undone by that Obedience, that he would have been subject to the bigheft Punishment if he had not done what having done

must be his inevitable Ruin, unless relieved by the justice of the House: And therefore, on behalf of the said Admiral Knowles, submitting the Premises to the Consideration of the House, to give the said Admiral Knowles such Relief therein as the Nature.and Circumstance of the same shall require.

Ordered, That the said’Petitiort do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the several and respective Merchants, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and others, concerned in the Effects and Jewels on board the Prince Frederick Pacquet Boat, taken by Algerine Cruizers, and carried into Algiers, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by his Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, that his Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House, to do therein as they shall think, fit.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; setting forth, That, in the Month of March 174^, the said Pacquet Boat, commanded by Captain Robert,

in her Passage from Lisbon to , having the

Lifoon Mail on board, and Effects and Jewels to the Amount of£. 25,000. (the Property of the Petitioners, and others), was attacked, taken, and carried into by Algerine Cruizers, where her said Effects were plun-

dered and divided amongst the Owners, Captain, Officers, and Crew, of the said Cruizers, and others; and further setting forth, That the Pacquet Boats employed between Lisbon and Falmouth do carry the King’s Commission and Colours, and are respected by the King of Portugal and his Subjects as Ships of the King of Great , and

have never been visited by any Officer of the Revenue in Portugal, nor are liable to any of the Laws which in that Country affect private Merchant Ships; and that the British Merchants trading to and from Portugal, at all timesdepending on an absolute Security against Captures, Seizures, and Searchers, of ail States in Amity with the King of Great Britain, have constantly transported Effects in these Vessels to England, being the Produce of that beneficial Trade which is carried on between the Two Kingdoms; and that the said Ship Prince Frederick, having his Majesty’s Commission on board at the time (he was taken, very soon after her Arrival at Algiers, was released, together with the Officers and Crew, and the Letters were delivered to the Captain; an Acknowledgement, in some degree, from the Algerines, of the Offence committed by them against the English-, and that the Petitioners apprehending that such Capture was a Breach of the Treaty then subsisting between the King of Great Britain and the Dey of Algiers, humbly applied to his Majesty for such Belief, as to his Majesty in his great Wisdom should feetn meet; and that, in consequence of such Application, the Petitioners have been informed, that his Majesty was graciously pleased to direct the honourable Augustus

Keppell Esquire, then Commander of his Majesty’s Squadron in the Mediterranean Seas, to demand Restitution of the said Effects, lo plundered as aforesaid; and that the said Mr. Keppell, in Obedience to such Order, demanded Restitution accordingly, but has not been able to obtain the fame; the Algerines pretending, as the Petitioners have been informed, the Impossibility of their being able to make such Restitution, in regard the said Effects had been long before, as aforesaid, divided amongst many Individuals; and that under these Circumstances, as the Petitioners have been informed, in order to prevent the great Detriment and Prejudice which might accrue to the Trade of this Nation by a Rupture with the Algerines, besides the great Charge such Rupture would occasion before they could be forced to make such Restitution, it was thought more prudent to wave the said Demand, and, by a subsequent Treaty, prevent the like Accident for the future; and thereupon Mr. Keppell, in his Majesty’s Name, concluded an additional Treaty with the Dey of Algiers, whereby it is stipulated. That, for the future, all Pacquets, or Express Boats, bearing his Britannic Majesty’s Commission, should be treated with the same Rel'peCi as his Majesty’s Ships of War, and all - VOL. 27.

dueRefpeCl should be paid to his Majesty’s Commission} and further setting forth, that the Petitioners, being unwilling to give the House any unnecessary Trouble, applied to the Post-master General to be relieved in the Premises; and that the Post-masters did, upon such Application, declare that they were sensible of the Misfortune of the Petitioners; but as they did not think the same any ways owing to, or occasioned by, any Neglectc or Rcmiffness of them in their Duty as Post-master General, they could not make the Petitioners Satisfaction, nor even solicit in their behalf, left it should be inferred from thence, that they the said Post-masters had not done their Duty in the Execution of their Office; and that the Petitioners have no Right to examine the Post-master General touching their Duty, nor any Hopes of obtaining Satisfaction from the Algerines, by reason of the said additional Treaty; and that no Part of the Misfortune of the Petitioners hath been incurred by their Misconduct; and expressing the Hope of the Petitioners, that although it has been thought prudent, on the Conclusion of the said Treaty, to wave their Right as aforesaid, yet they shall not suffer by their Confidence in his Majesty’s Protection, under whole Sanction they traded so much of their Properties on board the said Ship; and that the Advantage obtained to the Nation by the (aidTreaty, in consequence of the Misfortunes of the Petitioners, will render their Sufferings worthy of the Consideration of a British Parliament, which frequently hath had Regard to the Losses of private People, when occasioned by public unavoidable Misfortunes, as the said Petitioners apprehend their same to be: And praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant the Petitioners such Relief and Redress as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

The Lord Dozcne reported from the Committee, to

whom the Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and principal Inhabitants, of the Town of Leeds, in the West Riding of the County of York, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the Lid Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered ir in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Sir Henry Ibbetson Baronet, being examined, informed your Committee, That the Town of Leeds is very large and populous, consisting of many Streets and Lanes, and is inhabited byTradefmen, Manufacturers, and Aitificers, who are obliged to go late and early with great Burthens; and that Burglaries and Robberies are frequently committed in the said Town, which might be prevented, if the said Streets and Lanes were properly enlightened.

He further added, that the Pavements in the said Town are in bad Condition; but that if the same were properly regulated, it would be of general Advantage.

Mr. William Wadfaccrlh, being examined, confirmed the above Evidence in every Particular.

Sand, or any kind of Matter, from any Port, River, Harbour, Creek, or Inlet; and alleging, that the said Richard Lyddell, for several Months past, hath employed his said Machines and Vessels in taking great Quantities of Ballast out of Ships in the River and dropping the same at Sea; and that before the Time of employing the said Machintsand Vessels in manner aforesaid, the Petitioners used to have very good Fishing Ground, in about 14 Fathom Depth of Water, off of Shields and Cullercoats -, but that the Petitioners are now obliged to go Four or Five Miles to the North and South of their usual Fishing Places, in order to catch any Fills; and that, since the using of the said Machines, great Quantities of Ballast and Sand have been driven upon the Rocks and Stones to the North of Cullercoats -, and that thereby many Places, which uled to be good Fishing Places for Lobsters, are now totally destroyed; and that the Fishery upon the Coast will be in great Danger of being totally destroyed, in case such Quantities of Ballast, as of late have been call at Sea upon the said Coast, are permitted to be call there for the future; and that the employing of the said Machines or Vessels in dropping Ballast at Sea, may be of dangerous Consequence to the Port and Harbour of Tyne: And therefore praying, That the Petitioners may be heard, by their Counsel.against giving any Encouragement to the said Richard Lyddell,\wufing his said Machines

and Vessels for the Purpose of taking Ballast out of Ships in the River Tyne, and carrying such Ballast out to Sea.

To prove- the Allegations of the first-mentioned Petition,

Doctor Robert Taylor, being examined, said, That he knows the Road from Ottley to Prejon; That the Road from Otiley, through Burnley, Ilkley, and Addingham, to Skipton, is in a very ruinous Condition; and that it is frequently veiy much overflowed by the River Wharfe: That the Road from Skipton to Carlelon, being Two Miles, is, in many Places, too narrow, and much torn up by the River Air: That the Road from Carleton over the South Side of Pinna, is wide enough; and that there are Plenty of good Materials there: That from Carleton to Coin is Eightmeasured Miles: That the Road from Coin, through Burnley and Blackburn, to Prejon, is in a very ruinous Condition, and, in many Places, too narrow: That the said Road is, in some Parts thereof, much torn up, and, in other Places (eljxccially near Walton Church), in great Danger of being ivalhcd away by the Waters of the River Ribble; and that, upon a Computation he has made, the Expence of repairing the Road from Skipton to Coin, will amount to the Sum of^. 1,030. 4a. 1 which he calculates at the Rate of not quite £.100 per Mile over Pinna, but more from Skipton to Carleton; and that all Carriages, which go from Otiley to Coin, are obliged to go by Skip-ton: That the Inundations of the Rivers and

Ribble, are very considerable: That Carlton Bridge is not always capable of taking the Waters, occassioned by the Negligence of the Bridge Masters, by not making l'uffi-cient Ramparts to it; and that he believed the said Bridge is a County Bridge, is very much out of Repair; and that he believes it has not been repaired lately: That the River Wharfe washes the Road chiefly between Burnley and Addingham: That Skipton is the Centre of Seven great Towns: That the Road is intended to go within Two Furlongs of the Top of which rises on a very

easy A (cent; and that from Carleton to Coin there is about Four Miles of Lanes.

He further gave Evidence, That there are Four or Five Coal Pits in the Nighbourhood of from whence

the Town of Skipton is supplied: That there are near as

many Pits at Holding, which is about the same Distance; but that the Coals are not so good: That the Read over Rowley's Moore, as it now is, is very steep; and that from Skipton to Coin, over Pinna, measures Ten Miles and Three Furlongs:

That an Estimate has been made of the Tolls that will be collected on the said Roads; and that there are People enough ready to advance Money upon the Credit thereof.

Mr. Thomas Whitcock, being examined, said, That he had measured the Road from Cocking End, through Skipton to Coin; and that he found it to be x5 Miles and Two Furlongs.

Mr. Joseph Smith, being examined, said, That he had also measured the said Road; and that, from Cocking End, through Skipton to Shire Lane End, is 12 Miles and Seven Chains; and from Shire Lane End to Coin is Three Miles One Furlong and Three Chains; making together Fifteen Miles One Furlong d en Chains.

Then Mr. Thomas Whitcockbeing again examined, confirmed the Evidence of Dcdtor Taylor, in regard to the Road from Ottley to Coin; and further added, that the Inundations of the River extend a Quarter of a Mile betwixt Carleton and Skipand that it is much alike on both Sides ot Carleton Bridge; but that the same might be prevented, by building Ramparts Two Yards high clear from the Water, and Seven Yards broad, for the Length of a Quarter of a Mile, on each Side the said Bridge: That Skipton is supplied with Coals from the Pits near Coin, where the Coals are cheapest and best, and are likely to Lift, the Vein being newly begun: That the Coals are chiefly carried on Horses; but that if the Roads were made fit for Carriages, the Price of Coals would be much reduced:

That the Inhabitants o( Skipton exchange Lime at Denham for Coals; but that the Coals carried from Denham to Skipton are made use of for all other Uses, as well as burning Lime: That the Pits at are Three Miles

nearer to Skipton that those at Denham; but there being Lime Pits so near the Coal Pits at Lanjhey, there is no Probability of having Occasion to exchange; and that receiving Coals, by way of Exchange for Lime, is more than equivalent.

Mr. Henry Alcock gave the same Evidence in regard to the Distance of the Coal Pits, and to the exchanging Lime for Coals; but said, that there are not 500 Horse Loads exchanged in a Year.

Mr, John Bar croft, concerned sometimes for the Lcftee of the Coal Pits near Coin, being examined, said, That the Town of Skipton has always been supplied with Coals from thence; and that the common Report is, that the said Pits are likely to last.

Mr. John Steere, Churchwarden of the said Parish, produced to your Committee, an Extract of the Will of the said William Hammond, dated the 4th of March 1574, and proved in the Prerogative Court of Canterbury the 7 th Day of May 1575; whereby he bequeathed unto the Churchwardens of the Parish of the Holy Trinity in Guldeford his House next adjoining to the said Parish Church, after the Decease of Elizabeth his Wife, with one other House next adjoining; the Profits thereof to be applied in the repairing the said Church, and particularly in the Repair of St. Nicholas Chancel, which was Part of the said Church, where he directed his Body should be buried.

And Mr. Steeresaid, That a Monument has been erected in the said Chancel to the Memory of the said Mr. Hammond', of which it is proposed proper Care shall be taken.

And, by the Books of the said Parish, it appeared, that, ever finee the Year 1581, the Churchwardens have been in Possession of the said Estates, amounting to £. 53. js. 10 d. per Annum; out of which Sum, Mr. Steere, informed your Committee, the Churchwardens had, from time to time, repaired the said Church and Chancel.

John Garton, a Builder, said, That, in the Year 1740, the said Church fell down; although, a few Years before that Period, there had been applied, towards thesupporting t!:e fame, between £.700 and £.800.

That the said Church is now rebuilding upon the same Ground where it formerly flood; and in which Work the Sum of £.467. collected by a Brief for that Purpose, has been expended; and that there still remains owing to the several Workmen who have been employed therein a considerable Sum of Money.

Mr. Steere further said, That, if the Church is once completed, no Repairs will be wanting for many Years; but that the Inhabitants are not in a Capacity to finish the fame, and to pay off the Money now owing to the Workmen, as aforesaid.

In Support of the Allegations of the said Petition,

Samuel Cox Esquire, said. That many young Noblemen and Gentlemen at Westminfte School are obliged to

l7

lodge at a considerable Distance from the said School, for want of convenient Houses contiguous thereto; which is a great Disadvantage to such Scholars; and it has been made an Objection to the fending of Boys to Westminster School, that they are dispersed at so great a Distance from the School, where they cannot be under the Eye of the Master.

The reverend Mr. Lloyd, Under Master of the School, said, That it is very inconvenient that the Boys should be at so great a Distance from the Mailers out of School Hours; and that several Persons of Distinction had made Objection to the School upon that Account.

And being asked, if the Scholars in the College are more regular than the other Boys, he laid, they are confined in the Chamber; that they are locked up sooner; and that he himsell visits them every Evening.

And being further examined to the same Purpde, he said, that many Persons of Distinction had procured their Sons to be elected into College, for the fake of their Education merely, who did not want the pecuniary Advantages.

Several Members present confirmed what had been said by the Witnesses upon this Head; and one Gentleman added, that the Boarding Houses, being so distant from the School, has been the only Reaibn why he has not sent his Children to Westmin

And both the Witnesses further said, it would greatly contribute to the Safety and Conveniency of the Scholars, if a sufficient Number of Boarding Houses, under proper Regulations, were built in Dean's Yard.

Mr. Cox laid. That, in consequence of a Conversion with Doctor Markham, about Six Months ago, he had applied to Mr. Hoare, a Builder and Surveyor, who, together with the Witness, took a Survey of Dean's , and of the Ground adjoining, and Buildings thereupon and that the Houses in Dean's Yard are chiefly old and ruinous, particularly that Part next the Almonry and Smith Street; and that those in Stable Yard and College Court are also ruinous; but that there are Two new Houses in Dean's Yard.

Mr. George Hoare, Surveyor, said, That, by the Di-redlion of Mr. Cox, he surveygd Dean's Yard, and the Houses and Buildings adjoining: That there are few good Houses, but many bad Houses, and much waste Ground: That there are only Two good Houses, which are in Yard, and One on the South Side, which is l'omething better than the general Run of the Houses; and that it will not be necessary to take down any ether good Houses than those he has mentioned, to form a Square of 500 Feet by 400, and Room left sufficient whereon to build Houses.

Mr. Daniel Gellsaid, That the Buildings in Stable Yard and College Court are old; and that the Houses in general in Deans Yard are in bad Repair, except the Bounty Office, and Two Houses adjoining, and the House wherein Doctor I Vi If on lives.

A Petition of the Churchwardens, Overseers, and other principal Inhabitants, of the Parish of in

the Borough of Southwark, in the County of whole

Names are thereunto subscribed., in behalf of themselves, and several others of the Inhabitants of the said Parish, was presented to the House, and read; reciting the Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of London, in Common Council assembled, presented to the House upon Thursday the 16 th Day of Januarylaft, fora Bill to impower them to remove the Market held within the Lordship and Manor of Southwark; and alleging, that the greatest Partof theNuilances and Dangers complained of in the said last mentioned Petition, are not to be imputed to the Situation of the said Market, but arise from marry other Causes; particularly from the very narrow, incommodious, and dangerous, Passage over London Bridge, the Mischiefs proceeding from which are not to be otherwise remedied than by greatly widening the Pafiiige over the said Bridge; and that the Stops and Impediments, which happen in the high Street on Market Days, are principally occasioned by filling up great Part of the said Street with Sheds, Stalls, Stands, and other illegal Encroachments; and the Stoppages on the Days whereon no Market are held, arise from the said Street’s being made a common Stand for empty Waggons, Carts, DTays, and other Lumber; and that the said Nufances can be imputed to no other Cause than the total Neglect of putting in Execution the Laws now in being for regulating and keeping the said Market within its proper Boundaries, which the Petitioners have long Imce duly remonstrated to the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Common Council, of the City of London, without Succefi; and which the Petitioners would fee effectually performed, were they impowered so to do; but as the Property, Management, and Jurikiiftion thereof, is claimed and exercised by the City of London, as an exclusive Right veiled Iblely in themselves; the Petitioners are deprived of the proper Authorities for that Purpose; and further alleging, that the Removal of the said Market from the said Parish would be detrimental to the Public, and greatly prejudicial to the Landholders, and to the Petitioners; and that if the said Market be removed, without clearing and widening the Passage over the said Bridge, the Nuisance and Danger will still remain: And therefore praying. That, if it shall be the Opinion of the House that the Market ought to be removed, the same may be lodone to Ibme convenient Place within the Parish of St. Saviours, and no other Part of the Borough, conformable to the Privilege granted them by Parliament; and that the Petitioners may have such other Relief and Assistancein the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of London, in Common Council assembled, is referred: And that they do examine the Matter of this Petition; and report the lame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

Tnen Two other Acts were produced to your Committee; one of the 8th of her late Majesty, Queen Anne, the other of the 15th Year of his present Majesty’s Reign; by which it appeared, that the said Corporation were impowered to assess further Sums of Money for the Purposes of the first-mentioned Act.

And Mr. Monfton, Town Clerk of being examined, said, That the Number of Inhabitants of the said Town isgready increased since the passing of the said Acts, and the Poor thereof become much more numerous; and that the yearly Sums, which the said C irporarion are ini-powered to raise, together with their other Revenues, arc not Sufficient to provide for them: That Two Shillings in the Pound is now rallied for that Purpose, but not at a rack Rent; and that the Corporation is become greatly in Debt.

And he produced to your Committee, An Account of the Debt of the said Corporation, Rated the aid of January 1755; by which it appeared, that the said Debt amounted at that time to the Sum of £. 76 5 145. 8 And he laid, that several Powers are wanting to enable the Commissioners to carry the said Acts cll'edually into Execution:

Tuat it has been the Custom for the Corporation of the said Town to buy Materials for paving the Streets, and the Inhabitants to pay the Workmens Wages; but that many of the Inhabitants now refuse it:

That, by real'on of the many heavy Carriages upon narrow Wheels, (hod with Iron, used in the Streets and Squares of the said Town, the Pavements thereof are become very uinous, and are, in many Places, very silt> y and dirty; and that proper Powers are wanting to enforce the paving and cleansing thereof:

That no Part of the said Town is properly lighted in the Night-time, there being no Lamps, except lbme ca-iual ones at Alehouses; and that it would be a great Advantage, if proper Provision was made for lighting the Streets, and securing the Lamps from being destroyed and broken.

Mr. Joseph Sill, being examined, confirmed the whole Evidence given by Mr. McnStcn.

Encouragement as the House shall think proper.

And it appeared by the Evidence of Thomas Moor Matter, and William Scott Boat Steerer, of the Elizabeth and Mary, and John Giffton Captain of t he Argus (who was within Sight of tint Elizabeth and Mary, when Ihe was loft), Irhat the said Ship failed from the 5th Day of

April last, on her Voyage to the Greenland Seas, with no other View but to sith for Whales, where they arrived: Some few Days before the Loss of the Ship, they were laying hooked to a Field of Ice, fithing, where they had taken One large Fish, and (truck Three more, finding the Ice come on violently by the Current, they sawed a Dock in the Field, to prclerve their Ship, and lay there tolerably well that Day; the next Day, being the 17 th of June last, the Ice came on with such Force, that a Point linking the Elizabeth and Mary in the Midship, funk her so suddenly, that the Crew had not time even to save either their Provisions or Clothes, but saved their Lives by getting upon the Ice, and were taken up by the Happy Nuptials of London, and the Resolution of:

That the Company used their utmost Efforts to save the Ship; but it was impossible; and that a new Dutch Ship was loft close to them at the same time, and the Argus a few Hours afterwards.

And it appeared by the Evidence of John Gelfion Captain, and Jacob Woolsbury Line Coiler, of the Argus, and

Francis Moor Matter of the Elizabeth and Mary (who was aboard the Argus, when Ihe was loft), that the Argus failed from Gravesend the 5th Day of April last, and proceeded to the Greenland Seas; and that Ihe was employed in no other Business but Whale Fishing:

That Ihe took a Whale on the 25th Day of May, and, on the 16th of June, was made salt to a Field of Ice, in order to fish, and taken One Fish that Day; soon after the Fish was got aboard, a large Piece of Ice let the Ship l'o hard down on the Larboard Side, that (he lay on the Careen Five Feet and a half: She continued thus a few Minutes, when the Ice went away, and Ihe right.*d; they then founded the Pump, and found (he had received no Damage: Fro in this time they lay well till the 18th (the Resolution of Newcastle lying then about Half a Cable’s Lengfh ahead of them), when the Point of the Field of Ice, to which the Resolution was fattened, broke, and ihe

drove upon the Argus, and greatly damaged her Rigging: This exposed her to the loose Ice, which soon after run into her Waist on the Larboard Side; the Water then came in with great Force; the Carpenter attempted to rig the Pump; but, before that could be done, he saw the Water up to the Cuntlings of the Calks, and, in a Few Minutes after, it came up to the main Hatchway; flie did not go down immediately, having no Ballast; they cut away the Matt, to keep her above Water, and saved what they could; but it was impossible to save the Ship.

And it appeared by the Evidence of Jasper berg Matter, Thomas Hodfhorn Mate, and Carpenter, of the Mary, and James Boddy Matter, and Thomas Harman Carpenter, of the Young Eagle (who were within Sight when the Mary was loft), That the* Mary failed from Gravesend on the 3d of April last, and was employed in no other Business but Whale Fishing: That Ihe arrived in the Greenland Seas, but met with no Success; (he got amongst the Ice on the 9th of , going Hill further Northward, to get into a proper Place for Fishing: On the 12th of May last, they met wiih hard Gales of Wind and Drifts of Snow, when a Piece of Ice, that they could not fee, (truck the Ship on the Larboard Bow, and made such a Hole in her Bottom, that, in Ten Minutes time, Ihe filled with Water, and overset so suddenly, that the Crew had lcarce time to get their Boats clear of the Ship, and lave their Lives: As they were getting into their B »ats, they saw the Young Eagle of London, which took them up in about Half an Hour: All possible Endeavours were used to lave the Ship, but to no Purpose.

Mr. Oswald reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Merchants, and others, concerned in the Whale Fishery, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of Fact contained in the said Petition; and had directed him to report a State thereof to the House; and he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

By an Act of the 6th Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, for the further Encouragement of the Whale Fishery, after a Recital of the Provision made by Two former Acts, passed in the nth Year of his late Majesty’s Reign, and the Fifth Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, that the Whale Fins, Oil, and Blubber, taken in the Greenland Seas, or Davis's Straits, and the adjaccvt Seas, in British Ships, and imported by Subjects,

should be free of Customs, on the Conditions therein mentioned; and after a Recital* tint the said Encouragements had been, by many Years Experience, f <und insufficient for the regaining of this beneficial Trade, which was then in gteat Danger of being utterly loft; and that large Quantities of Oil and Whale Fins were, at a great Expence, bought of Foreigners and annually imp rted into this Kingdom, it is enacted, That, on the Conditions in the said Act mentioned, the Commission_n> of the Customs in England or Scotland, respectively, Ih mid* on Demand, cause Payment to be made to the M. ft.r or Owners of every Ship employed in the said Fishery, according to the Directions of the said Act, or to Ins or their Assigns, by the Receiver General of the Customs f r that Part of Great Britain, from wienc.* the S ip departed, the Sum of 10s. per Ton, acc >rding to the Au-naeafurement of such Ship, duly certified, as in the said Act is directe I: and by an Act, made in t.ie 13th Year of his present Majesty, a further Bounty of Ten S filings per Ton was granted for all Ships employed in the Whale Fishery, during the then present War.

And by an Act* made in the Year of his present Majesty’s ileign, for the further Encouragement and Enlargement of the Whale Fishery, reciting, That the Enlargement of the said Fishery would be a grenr Advantage to the Trade and Navigation of this K ngd >m» the said Acts* made in the 5th, 6th and 13th, Years of his present Majesty’s Reign, were further continued untb the 25th Day of December 1757, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and by the same Act, over and above the Allowance ot 2 a Ton, according to the Afimeasurement of the Snip, by the said last mentioned Act granted, an additional Bounty wa*> granted upon every Snip, payable in like manner as in the said Act is directed.

In Support of the Allegations of the first-mentioned Petition,

An Inspeximus of a Charter, 15 Char. 2. reciting a Charter of 4th of Edward the 6th, which grants to the Mnyurand Commonalty, Citizens of the City of London, and their Successors for ever, a Market or Market, and

all things thereunto appertaining, to be hnlden within the Borough and Town of Southwark, in the County of Surrey, was read; and an Act of the 29th Year of the Reign of his laid late Mijeily King Charles the Second was ulfo read; which directs the said Market to be kept in the same Place where it had then antiently been, and was at the time of making the said Act, kept; and that it should not be kept in any other Place whatsoever.

And by an Account, laid before your Committee by Mr. Green, it appears that the Produce adding from’tJu* laid Market to the City of London, far Yen Years hit pall:, amounted, upon an Average, to /\ 145 4 s. $ d. per Annum.

To shew that the Market, in its prefer.t Situation, is inconvenient and dangerous to Passengers and Carriages, and is also a public Xuifmcc,

John Grand laid. That the Market is held in the hiofi Street in the Borough: That he has frequently met with Obstructions, in that Part of the Street, from Carts/ Drays, and other Carriages, which he attributed to the Market being kept there.

Piobert Potts said, That he has been frequently flopped in the said Market, occasional by Stalls and Carts (landing in the Street; and, in Summer time, when the Carts with Peas and Beans are placed across in the Street, they make such Stops that Carriages cannot get along; and that he thinks in general the Market is a Xuitance:

That persons coming from the Counties of Surrey, Suffix, and Kent, are obliged to pais through this Marker; and it is with Dimcuhy Carriages can go Two a-bread in iome Places; but, if the Market was removed, there would be a more cpen and tree Passage.
