Upon the Petition of the Churchwardens, Overseers, and other principal Inhabitants, of the Parish of Saint Saviours, in the Borough of Southwark, in the County of Surrey, whole Names arc thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and several others of the Inhabitants of the said Parish;

Mr. Samuel Day laid. That he has known the Market in the high Street in the Borough many Years: 1 halt there are now more Stalls in it than there used to be formerly.

Being asked, to what he attributed the frequent Stops of Carriages in the Market, the said, to the NairowmeR of London Bridge: That, from the Narrowness of the Bridge, frequent Stoppagesarife, and arc continued into the Market; and that if the Market Ihouui remain where it now does, and the Bridge was to be widened, there would not be a Twentieth Part- so many Stops as there would bo it the Bridge remains in its present Condition, though the Market should be removed; and that the Bridge is much more dangerous at pretent than the Market, and ought to be widened before the Market is removed, if both ;tie pro-poled to be done:

28 Geo. II. 14° Februam. . 159

Thar the widening the Bridge would prevent many Stops in the Market, as the Scops in the Market generally begin upon the Bridge:

That there is a Constable upon the Bridge, to keep the Passage clear, and whole Business likewiicic is to keep the Passage in the Market clear; hut he is not so often in the Borough as upon the Bridge.

That he thinks the greatest part of the Commerce, betwixt the Counties of Kent, Sussex, and the City of London, carried on through Toolcy Street.

Mr. Peter Co/ljon, who had lived in Gracechurch Street, near 50 Years, said, that the Narr- wnels of the Bridge, as well as the Market, are both Nu nances, and do frequentlyoccalionStopsof Carriages; but that the Bridge is a much more dangerous Passage than the Market, and the Country People are so afraid of passing over ir, that they would go two Miles about to avoid it:

That the widening the Bridge would be attended with a very great Expence, but not equal to the Benefits that would arile therefrom:

And that if the Bridge is proposed to be widened, and the Market to be removed, the Widening the Bridge ought to have the Preference.

Mr. James Collijon and Mr. Thomas Browne confirmed the aforegoing Evidence, with respecttotbelnconvenicncy and Dangers ct the present Passage over the Bridge, and the Necessity of making the Passage more commodious: And Mr. Collijon added, That there are a greater Number of Scops on the Bridge than in the Marker, which isoving, in some measure, to Persons loading and unloading Carrs at their Shop Doors; but that, if the Stalls in the Market were removed, there would be fewer Stops on the Bridge than at present, as many Stops on the Bridge are whokv owing to the Market.

Mr. — Shadwell laid, He has lived at the Corner of Thames Street, upwards of 50 Years, and has frequently fecn Slops upon the Bridge; That Two Thirds of the Carts which come into the City, come from the Wharfs at the other Side of the Water, and turn along Thames Street to the right or left Hand:

And from the befl: Observation lie has been able to make, more Carriages come from Toolcy Street and the WaterSide, than come out of the Country through the Market:

That the Parish of Saint Magnus have, for several Years pad, contracted annually with Persons to maintain their Poor; but, ot late, the Contractors have complained that they could not maintain them upon the 'Terms they had formerly done, upon Account of the many Casualties which happen upon the Bridge; and, for that Reafcn, the Parish have nude them a further Allowance of £.20 or /.joper Annum.

And being elked, if all the Poor’sRatesin the Cityhave not increased within these 14 Years, he laid he did not know but they might.

Mr Stephen Cooper said, he was born on the Bridge, and lived there till he was above 20 Years old, and since that time has lived in Gracechurch Street:

That he was once run over on the Bridge by a Chaise; but if the Bridge had been wider, and there had been a Foot Parii, he believes that Accident would not have happened to him.

That he has also been in great Danger of having his Chaise overturned in the Market, by the Stalls standing too far into the Street; and that it is very dangerous going through the Market any Day in a Carriage.

And, being asked the Question, he said, that he never heard of any Accident happening in the Market; but has heard of Accidents on the Bridge.

That he should be glad to have both the Market removed, and the Bridge made wider; but the widening the Bridge is of more Consequence than removing the Market/

Then to shew that, if the said Market was put under proper Regulations, there would be lulhcient Room for Carriages and Fallen go rs;

Mr. Hardinge, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of the Report from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Merchants, and others, concerned in the Wale Fishery, was referred, the Resolutions, which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Twenry-second Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, for the further Encouragement and Enlargement of the Whale Fishery, which was to be in Farce unto the 25th of December 1757, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, be further continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Bounty of Forty Shillings per Ton on all Ships employed in the Whale Fishery, according to the Directions of the Acts relating thereto, and which is payable by the Receivers General of the Customs in England and Scotland, respectively, be paid by the said Receivers out of any Monies remaining in their Hands.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

The House was moved, That an Act, made in the 22d Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act for thefurlherEncouragement and Enlargement of the Whale Fishery, and for continuing suchLaws as are therein mentioned, relating thereto; and for the Naturalization of such foreign Protestants as shall serve, for the Time therein mentioned, on board such Ships as shall be fitted out for the said Fishery; might be read.

And the same being read accordingly;

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill pursuant to the said Resolutions; and to explain and amend the said Act: And that Mr. Hardinge and Mr. Oswald do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of several Freeholders, Farmers, Graziers, and Breeders of Cattle, in the County of Norfolk, in behalf of themselves, and others, the Farmers, Graziers, and Breeders of Cattle, in this Kingdom, was presented to the House, and read; alleging, That the g;eat Number' of Dogs now kept, and suffered to go at large, in this Kingdom, is a great Nuisance to the Public, and very injurious to the Petitioners in particular; and that the Bites of mad Dogs are now become more frequent than ever; and that there is great Reason to apprehend, that the In-section and pestilential Diseases, now raging amongst the horned Cattle, are extended by means of the said Animals: And therefore praying the House, That Provision may be made to remedy a Grievance so prejudical to all the Occupiers of Land in this Kingdom, so dangerous to the Public, and so frequently fatal to Individuals.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill to avoid and prevent Inconveniencies, Damages, and Mischiefs, occasioned by the Multiplicity of ulclels and unnecessary Dogs, is committed.

THE Order of the Day being read;

The House proceeded to the further Hearing of Cy the Matters of the several Petitions, complaining of an n* undue Election and double Return for the County of Oxford, and of the said double Return.

And the Counsel were called in.

And the Counsel for the Lord Parker and Sir Edward turner Baronet, examined several Witnesses, in order to disqualify Nineteen other Persons, who voted for the Lord Wenman and Sir James Dashwood Baronet; One as not having a Freehold in the said County of the Value of 40 j. per Annum, and as not being assessed to the Land Tax; Three as not being assessed to the Land Tax, and as not having any Freehold at all In the said County; Four as not having been, for the Space of Twelve Calendar Months before the said Eieftion, in Possession of the Freeholds for which they voted; Four as not being assessed to the Land Tax for a Freehold of the Value of 40 per num; Two as being Leaseholders; Two as not having any Freeholds at all in the said County; and the other Three as net having Freeholds in the said County of the Value of 40 s. per Annum.

And a Witness having been examined, in order to disqualify One other Person, who voted for the said Lord Wenman and Sir James Dashwood, as not having a Freehold in the said County of the V alue of 40 s. per Annum; The Counsel on both Sides were directed to withdraw. They were again called in.

And another Witness was examined, in order to prove, that the Freehold, for which the said last mentioned Person voted at the said Eieftion, was not of the Value of 40;. per Annum.

Then the Counsel for the said Lord Parker and Sir Edward turner examined several Witnesses, in order to disqualify Four other Persons, who voted for the said Lord Wenman and Sir James Dashwood; One as not being assessed to the Land Tax, and as not having any Freehold in the Place where, at the time of the said Eieftion, he swore his Freehold did lie; Two as not being assessed to the Land Tax, and as not having any Freeholds at all in the said County; and the other as not being assessed to the Land Tax for a Freehold of the Value of 40 Atmum.

They also examined a Witness, and produced Evidence, in order to disqualify One other Person, who voted for the said Lord Wenman and Sir James Dashwood, as not having a Freehold in the said County of the Value of 40 s. per Annum.

They also examined several Witnesses, in order to disqualify Three other Persons, who voted for the said Lord Wenman and Sir James; One as not having

been, for the Space of Twelve Calendar Months before

the said Eieftion, in Possession of the Freehold for which he voted; One as not being assessed to the Land Tax, and as not having any Freehold at all in the said County; and the other as not being in Possession of the Freehold for which he voted.

They also produced Evidence, and examined a Witness, in order to disqualify another Person, who voted for the said Lord Wenman and Sir James Dashwood, as not having any Freehold at all in the said County.

They also examined several Witnesses, in order to disqualify Nine other Persons, who voted for the said Lord Wenman and Sir James Dashwood \ One as not having a Freehold in the said County of the Value of 40 s. per Annum; Three as not being assessed to the Land Tax; One as not being in Possession of the Freehold for which he voted; Two as not having been, for the Space of Twelve Calendar Months before the said Eieftion, in Possession of the Freeholds for which they voted; One as not having any Freehold at all in the said County; and the other as not being assessed to the Land Tax for a Freehold of the Value of 40 s. per Annum.

And then the Counsel on both Sides were again di-rested to withdraw.

By whose Evidence it appeared, that, in the Year 1728, there was a general Complaint amongst the free Burgesses, of the Admission of Foreigners:

That about Michaelmas a Rumour having prevailed, -that Freedoms were to be given or fold, Two hundred free Burgesses, or more, went upon a Monday to the Moot Hall, and remonstrated against making any free Burgesses, but such as had Right:

That there was no Poll; and that there was a great Noise and Confusion in the Hall:

That the free Burgdfes t hen complained, tha t they were not summoned to that Court:

Thomas Hales added, That he had been a Serjeant the Year before: That, when the free Burgesses were to be summoned, the Four Serjeants uf'ed to go to their Houses in different Parts of the Town; and that he has often summoned the Burgesses by going from House to House: That Burgesses paying Scotland Lot are usually summoned to the Choice of a Mayor, and when there is to he voting for Officers; and that the Court he went to was such a Court as the Scotland Lot Men ought to be summoned to.

In Answer to the last: Head of Objection,

The Cuiiiiicl for the fitting Member called a Wit-

r O

refs, to prove that the honorary Freemen, made by Purcliaie in 1728, have constantly, since that time, enjoyed ali the Privileges of Freemen, and that they voted at the Election in 1734.

And they argued, that the Order, under which those free Burgesses purehaied their Freedoms, was made in Conformity to the lall Kesolution of the House at the Court held upon Thursday the Thirty-first Day of October 1728, when all the free Burgesses were present, as appears by the Entry in the Book:

That the Witnesses produced to prove the Dissent of the tree Burgesses, though their Evidence was very imperfect, and they recollected very few Circumstances, all agreed, that the Court, to which they went, was held on a Monday, so that their Evidence was plainly applied to the subsequent Court held on a Monday by the (elect Body:

That these free Burgesses objected to have constantly exercised their Franchises since 1728 unimpeached, and voted at all Elections:

That they are not to be looked upon as honorary Freemen, but as bona fide Purchasers of their Right:

That though Blatckwas found to be no Alderman in 1740, it does not follow that lie was no Alderman in

1727 — That suppoling he was only a Mayor de in

1728 — those who had purchased their Freedoms for a valuable Consuleration, notwithlbuuhng tiiey were admitted in pursuance of the Order of an Assembly where h" presided-, will not lose their Right; for, though a voluntary Act, done by an Officer de may not he valid, yet the Act of a Corporation (which afilfts a Stranger who has paid a valuable Consideration) shall not be set aside, although the presiding Officer was only an Officer de facto, especially if such Officer does not come into his Office by Usurpation, but under a colourable Right.

But the Counsel for the Petitioner, in Support of their Objection, indited, that the Afilmbly held cm the 31st of October 1728 being called for filling up Vacancies, the

lice Burgesses then present must be prelumed to be such as have a Vote in filling up Vacancies, those only who pay Scotland Lot; but all the free Burgesses have, in contccjuencfc of the Refclution of the House, a Right to be present at the making Foreigners free:

That, at an Assembly held for a particular Purpose, they could not proceed to do another Act, for which Notice to all the free Burgesses was neceflhry:

That if all the free Burgesses had been duly summoned to that Court, they could not (according to the Resolution of the House,) delegate their Power toaCom- mittee:

That the said Order for felling Freedoms made on the Thirty-first of October 1728 was general, and no Person was nominated that Day.

And that at the Assembly held on Monday the Twenty-fifth Day of November 1728, when the Order was made stor admitting 56 Persons therein named, with whom the Committee had agreed, and that the same Committee should agree with Two hundred more, it is not pretended that the Free Burgesses were present.

That the Witncfiesipokeof that Assembly; and proved, that the free Burgesses then opposed the Admission of any but such as had a Right:

That the felling Freedoms was an extraordinary not a necessary Act, and therefore could not properly be done by a Mayor de facto:

That Purchasers should fee with whom they contra ft:

And that the Mayor, in making Foreigners (whether Purchasers, or honorary free Burgesses!, is not Considered as presiding at an Assembly of the Corporation, but as associated for that Purpose with a particular Part of the Body; and that his own Consent is neccltaryto make that Act valid, and therefore he ought to l^e a legal Mayor. Sir Peter 7'hompfon, being examined, said. He was One of the Trusteees, and present at the Meeting when the said Plan was produced; and that he objected to its being totally confirmed, and would not have agreed to it, without the qualifying Words in the Resolution.

And, being asked his Reason, said, Because he thought the Entrance dangerous and bad; and that Ships, forced from their Anchors by a Storm in the Downs, could not have Room to turn their I leads to the West, as they necessarily mull, without running against the West Side, and (laving the Ship:

And that the Opening was at S. S. W.; but it was of no Consequence to what Point of the Compass the Harbour opened.

And, being asked the Question, he said, That Ships, when driven from their Anchors, would venture in, if the Entrance was fffe; but if there was not Room to turn their Heads to the West, there would be Danger.

That he thought the Flood Head, which is the West Head, ought to be further out than the Ebb Head; and that the Tide runs near Three Miles an Hour, upon a Spring Tide, at the Mouth of the Harbour:

That when there is Water enough for a Vessel to come into the Harbour, the Tide runs E. N.E.

John Beta Icy Esquire, a Commander in his Majesty’s Navy, being examined, said. That he was at Ramsgate last Summer, when they were beginning to contract the Harbour; and that he saw, by the Stakes and Scaffolding, where the Curve was intended; which, if carried into Execution, will ruin the Harbour;

That, in his Opinion, the most proper Time for Ship? to come into this Harbour is at hack Water upon the Flood Tide: When live enters the Harbour, (he mult bring up with her Head to the Westward, and, upon a Gale of Wind, will run some Way before Hie stops; and if the Curve is no more than 200 Foot, (he will run against the Wall; but if the Curve was 5 or 600 Foot, that would be the most useful Part of the Harbour; for, jf the Curve is smaller, Ships will be in the Way of one another upon coming into the Harbour.

Being shewn Plan, N° 4. with the larger Curve, he said, That was much better than the other Plans, and would not alter the Entrance into the Harbour:

That a Harbour at Ramsgate will give an Opportunity to outward-bound Ships to lay there, which would clear the Downs:

That it is very possible to fix upon a proper Plan to make a good Harbour there; but ’tis hardly possible to make a worse than that which is now executing:

That, from the parallel Lines carried out, the Curve might be larger, without altering the Point of the Com-pafsat the Entrance; but that Half a Point Variation is of no great Consequence:

That, upon a Ship’s coming into the Plarbour before Wind and Tide, (he will shoot to the Westward about 300 Foot; and that if they let go an Anchor, before the Ship has loft her Way, (he would run a Risque of bulging on her own Anchor.

Mr. Stephen Reed, being examined, said, He lives at Ramsgate, is now and has been Matter of a Ship 29 Years, and a Pilot above 30.

Being aiked his Opinion of the Plans, said. The larger Curve to the Westward would make the most commodious Harbour; and that it would be impossible to come safely into the Harbour with the smaller:

That he has seen Ships this Year come into the Harbour, which, with the utmoftDifficulty, have avoided running on the Wall now carrying on at the West Head; of which there is about 300 Foot of the contracting Curve already built:

That formerly he had carried Two Ships into Ramsgate Harbour without their Rudders; but, had the new Harbour been built according to the contracting Plan, he durst not have attempted it; because, as loon as they had come in, they would have canted to the Westward, and run foul of the Pier.

Mr. George Haynes, being examined, said. He had been a Sailor from 10 Years of Age, was Matter of a Ship in 1731, and a Pilot in 1737.

Being shewn the Plan with the larger Curve and contracted Curve on the West Side, he said. That the larger would make the more commodious Harbour: That the Pier Heads might be placed at the same Point; and that both Curves would have the same Effect on the Current of the Tide:

That he did not think the contracted Plan would be intirely useless; but that Ships would be in great Danger of running against the West Side; which they would not be, if the Curve was larger:

That if one Ship should run against the Pier coming in, and others were following her, they would be all wrecked, by running against each other; but if the Curve was larger, they might get out of the Way,

Then Mr. Ockenden'sReport, in pursuance of the last mentioned Survey to the Trustees, dated the iftof May *753. was read; Part whereof is as follows:

" Gentlemen,

" Agreeable to your Request, I have been at Ramsgate, and gone through all the Particulars you did me " the Honour to rest rto my Examination. — The uncommon Lownest of the Ebb Tides, and the extreme Calmnels of the Weather, gave us a moll favourable Opportunity to measure the Depth of the Water where the " Pier is intended to be run: Your Surveyor began by

" drawing a Base Linealong the Bottom of the Harbour, " and from thence geometrically determined the Point " where the Middleoi the Entrancemuft be placed, if the " Piers are carried out too Feet beyond the original " Plan. We then went on Board a Boat, rowed ofi from " Shore, and fixed a final 1 Pile in that very Point between " the Two intended Oftagons which are to form the Mouth of the Harbour: After this, your Surveyor, " in the same manner, drove a Imall Pile in the Middle " Point between the other Tw'O' OCtagons, more to the " East; and, by Means of these Maiks, was enabled to " trace out at Sea the whole Line of the Piers. We fathomed it very carefully in every Point from Octagon " to Octagon, at lowed; Ebb Tide, for Three Days succesfively, and took tire various Depth of Water with " greater Correctness than has been attempted at any " other Measurement; all which are wrote down in the Plan your Surveyor has drawn for the Approbation of the Trust, and to which we have both let our " Names.

" As the Waterwhere the Western Pier is to be carried " out proves much (hallower than what was expected, " so I cannot but regret our having placed the Harbour " so much that Way, since it now lays us under an absolute Necessity of extending the whole Work into " the Sea 100 Feet beyond the original Design, and " even then we shall not gain that Depth of Water " which might have been otherwise obtained.

" I was always taught, that the Depth of the Harbour’s Mouth would measure Five Foot, though built " according to the First Scheme; whereas it now appears " upon Trial, that, when carried out 100 Feet further, " the Entrance, at the lowed Ebb ot a Spring Tide, will " have no more than Three Foot and a Halt of Watery ‘‘ but your Surveyor proposes to deepen it a Foot and a " Half after the Octagons are erected."

Being raked, Which would decay soonest. Piles always tinder Whiter, or Piles only washed by the Spring Tide ? He laid. That the Timber, which was wet and dry alternately, would alvvavs decay loonest.

You. 27.

Being examined as to the Hxpences of taking up the 340 Feet of Stone Work done upon the contracted Plan, he laid, He would contract to take up that and the cr>f$ Walls, and deliver the Materials into the old Pier, for /. 1500. provided he could have his Craft delivered as loon as they came into the old Pier; and that he was sensible he could get Money by the Bargain; and that he would deliver it into any Carriage or Craft that should lie along side his, or on the old Pier under Shore, or dole up to the Wall, any where within the Harbour, for ft.500 more.

Being cross examined, he was asked, Whether he had a better Plan than the present working Plan ? To which he answered. He had not.

Being asked, if he could take upon him to say, that the Weeds out of the Slower did not come to Ramsgate ? he said, He never law any of these Weeds there; and that the old Farmers told him they never saw any of the Stower Weeds among the Sullage at Ramsgate.

Being asked. If there was not Suilage lying at the Back of the West Pier? he said. There was a Collection of Weeds, such as came to the old Pier, which now lie at the Back of the West Pier; but that he does not know whether there is any Sand or Sullage there; for he never dug down.

Being asked, he said, He had never undertaken such a Work as taking up this Stone Work; but that he had i n* dertaken to remove Hills of Ballast, and had taken up a Ship and Cargo Seven Fathom under Water:

That he never weighed the Stones in this Work; but thinks few of ’em exceed Three Tons, and some not above One Ton; and that some arc laid in Terras, and some not.

Being asked. Which would make the most useful Harbour, the large or the contracted Plan ? he said, He was of Opinion, upon the Whole, that the large Plan would be much the best, because, when ships came from the Downs with the Wind at S. S. W. or S. S. E. they can’t alw'ays steer to Haifa Point; the Tide and the Wind will take her Stern, and there will be some little Eddy, and flie will come with her Head to the Wind; and he thinks she can’t avoid running against the Wall, if the Ship is 60 Feet long, and conies above Three Miles an Hour; for that no Man can stop a Ship in her Length; and that when a Ship comes within a Foot of the Ground, file loles her Steerage, and, in smooth Water, she must drive against the Pier.

Being asked, What Depth of Water there was in the larger Curve ? he said. There was about a Foot and

ft

Half, or Two Feet, less in the West Curve than in the rest of the Harbour.

'Being asked then. Whether a Ship would not run a-ground before she came to the West Pier in the larger Curve? he laid, That was in proportion to the Sail they had to stop her} which could not be done in less than 3 or times her Length; but he would rather chuse to run his Ship aground than against the Pier.

Being asked. Whether 16 Ships lying in a Tier can lie in the Harbour in the Space of 400 Feet ? he said, They could not be piled up close to the Walls; and that every Ship would require 30 or 35 Feet between each Ship, to keep them from knocking each other to Pieces, as ’tis a dry Harbour.

Captain George "Hooper, being examined, said. He had lived at Ramsgate 64 Years; and that he had observed the Timber Work in the new Pier, which looks as well as when first built:

That the Piles are about Five Inches thick, and are likely to last as long as Oak will endure, which is for Lives, under Water; and that the Piers are not liable to be worm-eaten, ii they are kept clean, and tarred:

That lie had observed the Timber Work in the old Pier, which had flood ever since his Memory, and some of it some Generations before; but that a great deal of it, which was lappy, was decayed:

Mr. Cooke reported from the Committee, to whom Lvddeil’s the Report was re-committed, which was made from the jvilfchines Committee, to whom the Petition of Richard and also the several other Petitions relating to the Ma-cliines or Vessels invented by the said Richard Lyddell, for the Removal of Earth, Ballast, Sand, or any other Kind ot Matter, from any Port, River, Harbour, Creek, or Inlet, were referred, That the Committee had reconsidered some of the Matters mentioned in the said Petitions; and had directed him to report the fame, as they appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the iame was read; and is as followeth; v/z.

To prove the Allegations of the Petition of Richard Lyddell,

Mr. John Major, an elder Brother of the Trinity House, being examined, informed your Committee, That he has seen the Machine or Vessel invented by Mr. Lyddell for the Removal of, or carrying away. Earth, Ballast, Sand,

Rubbish, Rocks, Stones, or any other Kind of Matter, from Ports, Rivers, Harbours, Creeks, or Inlets:

That he has never seen any thing of the like Kind in England: That the Use of it is to take Ballast out of Ships in Harbour, and carry it out to Sea at less Expence than landing it on the Wharfs — And that it is of genera.

Utility to remove Shoals, or any other Obstructions, from Rivers in shoal Water — That when the Ports of the Machines are Unit, it is impossible they should lose any of their Ballast in going to Sea.

And being asked if he apprehends that carrying Ballast to Sea into Fourteen Fathom Whiter is later than carrying it by Land the same Difiance off ? he said, If it is call in Fourteen Fathom Distance from the Shore, it will make some Difference.

And being atked the Question, he said, He could not tell whetherBallaft dropped into Fourteen Fathom Water can be drove into Thirteen; but that, if he was to have the Direction, it should be thrown Two Miles off Land.

He then said, Thar there is more Danger by unloading the Ballast on Shore than by unloading ir into 14 Fathom Water — That the Mailers of these Machines or Vessels may be obliged, by St re Is of Weather, to open their Hatches, and let the Ballast out in less than 14 Fathom Water: That Keels or Lighters having no Decks are more likely to be funk than the Machines — That Lightermen have more Inducement to throw' the Ballast out of the Lighters than the Masterof this Machine has, because the Machine gives no Trouble to unload.

Being asked the Question, he said, That the Machine* may, in the Day-time, drop their Ballast in less than 14 Fathom imperceptibly; though, he said, where the Ballast is let out, it makes a Froth in the Sea which may be seen At some Distance.

And

1 Adder's Ballad Machines.

2x6 17° Martit. A. 17^5.

And being asked the Question; he said, It would he lor Mr. Lyddell's, Interest to keep the Matches of the Ma-

chine open whilst loading, to let the Ballast keep running out, and so it would to drop the Ballad: before they come to Fourteen Fathom — That it would be of Service to the Public to limit the Distance of carrying the Ballad out from Shore, as well as into what Depth — That Two Miles from Shore would be a sufficient Didance.

Mr. Thomas Bennett, likewise an cider Brother of the Trinity House, confirmed Mr. Major's, Evidence as to the Utility of the Machine; and added, that it is equally as safe to carry the Ballad to Sea as to lay it on Shore, if it is carried into 14 Fathom, or to a proper Didance.

Mr. Henry Bird senior, a Shipbuilder, being examined, informed your Committee, That Mr. Richard Lyddell was the Inventor of the Machines, and has been at great F.xpence in building them — That Four oft hem have been built, which, with their Furniture, cod £, 3C0 apiece; and that there are Two more in Hand now, bigger than the others, and will cod more: And he likewise added. That the Ports arc so contrived, that, when they are shut, no Ballad can go out or in.

Captain James fVi/foninformed your Committee, That

he has loaded and failed in One of the Machines — That his Opinion is, that it will be of great Service to Navigation — That it has been worked at , and no where else, and that it answers the Intent: That the Expence is heavy, Four Men being required to fail it — That Ballad is removed Sixpence per Ton cheaper by the Machine than by landing it on Quays by Keels cr Lighters, and that it is farer for the River to have it thrown into Fourteen Fathom Water: That Ships frequently throw Ballad into Ten Fathom Water in eroding a Mile and an Half without Timnouth Harbour, without meeting with any Interruption from the Corporation of — That he has

known Ballad thrown into Ten Fathom Water, but that he never heard of any one’s being punished for it, nor ever heard that there was any Law to punish for doing it: That it is Two Miles and an Half from Tinmouth Bar to Fourteen Fathom Water at high Water, and that he has not been at Shields since lad September was Twelve-month: That making use of the Machine is a Dispatch to Shipping, as w'cll as a Saving, because it unloads sooner than other Vessels — He further added. That there is Seventeen Feet Water at the Bar at high Water on a Neap Tide, and Twenty-two on a Spring Tide: That theie is Seven Feet Water there at lew Water on a Neap Tide, and Six on a Spring Tide; and that Ballad thrown into Fourteen Fathom Water cannot drop into Shore.

Mr. Thomas Curtis, who is concerned in Shipping, gave the same Evidence with Mr. Major and Mr. Bennett, as to the general Utility of the Machine.

Mr. Robert Clayton, aShipmaster, informed your Committee, That he has employed the Machines, by which he has found a Saving of Sixpence Ton — That a

Ship has been overset by unlading Ballad on Quays; and that it is a greater Security to Shipping to dispose of Ballad to these Vessels, than by going alongside the Quays — That the Bank has so great a Descent, that it cannot hurt the Harbour: That there is Twenty-four Feet Water close to the Bar at Spring Tides — That the Machine has taken Forty Tons of Ballad at once — That he has observed, that a Land Flood has been on the Top of Burdens Ballad Quay, when there has been Ballad on

it: That this happened Ten Years ago, and that be then rowed a Boat over it — That if Forty thousand Tons of Ballad yearly were to be thrown into Fourteen Fathom Water, he thinks the Current or Tide would drive it cither Northward or Southward, and that it would not be washed into Thirteen Fathom.

Then a Patent granted by his Majesty to the said Richard Lyddell, dated 12th of 1752, for the foie

Use and Exercise of his said Invention, was produced, and read to your Committee.

Mr. Bird senior further informed your Committee, That Mr. Lyddell has employed a great deal of Time, and

been at great F.xpence, in trying Experiments, and in bringing the said Invention to Perfection: And,

That your Committee might be the better infotmed of the Utility of the said Machine, the Agent for the Petitioner Air. Lyddell, produced to your Committee a Model thereof: And,

Captain Bronell,a Surveyor of Sloops and i' effcls to the Cudom House in London, being called to explain to your Committee the Method of working the said Machine, laid. That he has fcen One of them on the Stocks — That he took particular Notice of it; and allured your Committee, that it is built exactly correspondent with the Model:

That the Ports of the said Machine draw close up with a Chain that goes with a Span or circular Iron, anil takes both Sides of the Ports, from whence the Chain comes through the Beam in the Middle of the Vessel; by which means the Pons are so ft cured, that ihe Vessel cannot, in failing, drop any of the Bailad, unkfs unavoidable Accidents happen: And also.

That a Two Inch Rabbit is fixed all round the Port; which makes it shut as close as a Box; and, of course, impossible, while the Forelock is in, that any thing can go out — That he thinks it very useful both lor Security and Convenience: That it may go to Sea as fafclv as other Vessels of the same Burthen; and that if he was in One of them in a hard Gale, and Sea Room enough, he should not think himself in any Danger.

And being asked, if there was any Contrivance on board for removing Rocks, Shoal?, or other Obstructions, from the Bottoms of Rivers? he said. That there is no such Contrivance at present, but that it may be made fit for those Purposes: and that if it was to be furnished with Engines anil Nets, it might serve as well as the Ballad Lighters in the River Thames.

And being asked the Question, he said, He could not tell to what Degree the Sand at the Bottom of the Sea rolls in tempeltuous Weather; but that he has seen the Water break, in Thirty Fathom W ater, by meeting with contrary Weather and a counter Tide — And being asked, he said. That carrying Ballast out in these Vessels will not hurt the Road-Head, nor injure Ships Cables — That he should chuse to anchor in Fourteen Fathom, and not fulpeit any Danger — That Ballast dropt into Fourteen Fathom Water will be dispersed by the Motion of the Tide, and go to a Level; but that in time it will vvalh towards the Shore — That it is naturally Four times still Water in Twenty-four Hours.

And being asked it Two hundred thousand Tons of Ballast dropped in Thirteen or Fourteen Fathom Water will fall into a Flat, or in Heaps ? he laid. He is nor certain, but believes it will fp read, for that aGale of Wind will spread any thing above the Level of the Surface--That he apprehends the Intention of this Machine is only to take the Ballast from Ships, and not out of Rivers, and never heard it was tiled for other Purposes — That nobody, except those on board, can tell when the Ballast is dropped — That if it is frequently dropped in one Place, it will make a Hill — That dropping Ballast makes the Water rife in Bubbles — That the Ballast ought to be carried into the Sea, to keep the Haven clear; for that it would beaPrejudiceto the River to haveitdroppedthere: That there is a Possibility of these Vessels committing Frauds, as they may drop their Ballast in what Depth they please, without being discovered.

Captain Peter Vardell, a Mailer of a Ship, and likewise Agent or Manager for these Vessels, being asked what Interest he bad in them ? said, He shall be neither Gainer or Loser by the Patent, and that he lus no fixed Salary; but, as he is obliged to put another Muller into his own Vessel whilst he is ailing for these, he expects something; and that he has made a verbal Agreement only to have a Halfpenny a Ton from all Ballast removed by the Machines: That he has been on board, and thinks them well adapted for the Purpose of removing Ballast: That they do not lose their Ballast in working; for, after

Then in order to shew what Penalty has been inflicted upon Mailers ot Vessels for calling Ballast in the River Tyne into Ids than Fourteen Fath-m Water, An Order of Council, made in the Year 1616, was read whereby it appeared, that all Matters of Slops, who should be detected in calling Ballast between the Places ca'led Souter and Hartley, or within Four.een Fathom of the Haven of Netxcafile, should be brought into the Town Chamber, and be there constrained, in the Presence of the People, to cut a Purle with Money in it, as a Mark, of Infamy; it being as much as to say he had offended against the River in as high a Degree as if he had cut a Purle from the Person of a Man.

And being asked if the Bar is not liable to vary much ? he said, That with the Wind at the East, or Ealt-North-East, the Sand breaks up from the Sea, and flops up the Bar — That the Sea rolls from Jutland 100 or 150 Leagues, and sets directly into the Harbour, and fills up the Mouth of it; but that a strong West Wind and Land Flood sometimes will redress it:

That he compared a Sounding of the River Tyne in 1752 with one in 1650, and found very little Variation as to Depth, but that the Channel has grown a little narrower within these few Years, which he attributes to the Land Floods bringing down DirtandSand, and also from Ballast blown from the Ballast Quays into the River:

That he never saw the Water waih any great Quantities of Ballast off the Quays — That the Keelmen may throw Ballast into the River, but he does not know that they have; but that he does not doubt but some Abuses have been committed — That at high Water there is sometimes Eighteen Feet Water on the Bar; but, if the WindisSouthcrly.it is not so good by Two or Three Feet; and if the Wind is at North-West there isabout Twenty-two Feet Water — That from the Bar to Fourteen Fathom is a Descent; but he finds it altered, and grown more into a Flat — That the Bar is about a Mile wide, and, when he founded in 1754, and found only Five Feet Water, he means in the bell Passage, which was the only Place he founded in them — That from the Top of the Bar to Fourteen Fathom Water, at low Water, is more than a Mile and an Half — That at low Water, and good Tides, it flows Twenty-one Feet:

That it is safer to the Navigation to land the Ballast: on Quays than to carry it to Sea; for, if it is dropped in the Sea, when the Wind is at East-North-East, it will fill the Bar.

That, in 1752, as he was going from Newcastle to Shields in the Night, he (aw Two Keels at anchor between the lower Part of Jatrczv Quay and Whitehill Point, cading their Ballad over-board.

And being asked. If he spoke of his own Knowledge with regard to the Observations at Jarrow Quay, since 1737? he laid, He had not been at that Quay since that time.

Mr. Michael Newton, being examined, informed your Committee, That he is Conveyor of Ballad from the face of IVillington Quay — That he has seen many Thoufaod Tons landed, some from Ships, and some from Keels — That when Ballad is landed from Keels, they set up the Huddick Board, and Two Men are employed in heaving the Ballad — That that Method of landing Ballad is not f> safe as from Ships; some of it drops into the River, and there is generally a Loss for want of Care:

That between 20 and 30 Years ago, when Keels lay to the Quay they generally laid their Yard upon the Quay*' and hung their Sail down the whole Breadth, and set up their Huddick Board against it — Wiiilft that was the Practice very little Damage was done by the Keels; but that Method has been left off above 20 Years:

That the Keels bring a Certificate to the Quays front the Water Bailiff, specitying the Quantity of Ballad they took on board; and that he has sometimes found them deficient of Half the Quantity so specified:

That having asked the Keeimcn the reason of it, they have told him, the Wind and Weather obliged them to throw their Ballad out rather than lose the Keel and their Lives; and that he has seen them heaving Ballad overboard in the Night, in moderate Weather -.

That he has known 40 out of 42 Tons of Ballad wash ed from the Quays in one Night by a high Tide:

That Ballad being washed from the Quays had happened often, long ago, as well as lately, at Quay in particular:

That there is not so much Ballad cad there now' as v/as formerly; but that some small Damage may have been done there within these few Months:

That, at the North, and South Road, there used to be good lying; but there is no Road-dead now, occasioned, as he believes, by the Ballad being washed from the Quays:

That he has been put in Danger of his Life for speaking to the Keeimen for cading their Ballad into the River:

That the Corporation has given Rewards for Informations; but he never heard that any one had been punished.

Being asked. If he thought the Corporation lndbcsa negligent? he said, He could not tell.

Mr. Humphrey Coward, Mailer of a Ship at

coates, being examined, informed your Committee, That he has belonged to the Coal Trade Thirty-five Years — That the River Tyne was deeper when he fii ft knew it than it is now — That there were several Road-steads where. Ships, drawing Twelve Feet Water, could swing in low . Water; but now there is no Road at all to do Business in — That they load their Ships now at Shields in the Chanel — That they can’t load at the Quays at low Water; which he apprehends isowing to the bad Usage of the River by the Keels; for, if the greatest Care imaginable is taken, there will be feme Waste — That he has seen it blow off the Quays in great Quantities, and has had 3,4, or 5 Bushels blown in 24 Hours from Quay,

which is a Quarter of a Mile long, upon Ships between 70 and 80 Feet long.

And being again asked, How long Quay is

he said, He had never measured it; but it might be a Mile and a Half; and that he observed the Ballast to blow from all Parts of the Quay at the same time; and that a high Tide will come on some Parts of that Quay — ' That loading Ballast on the Quays from the Keels has already hurt the River and Harbour very much; and if that Practice is continued, the Harbour will be quite dc-. stroyed.

And being asked, what Condition the Baris in now ? he said, He founded it Eleven Days ago, and found near 19 Feet Water within an Hour or less of high Water and Half-Spring Tide; and he said, that he founded only in the belt of the Channel — That it was as good then as it has been these Two or Three Years:

That he has known Ballast being thrown out of Ships into Fourteen and Seven Fathom Water; but that it is not the Custom now:

That heaving Ballast into 14 Fathom Water can never hurt the Bar:

That he knows nothing to the contrary, but Fish have been as plenty this Year as formerly; and that he never heard any Complaint that calling Ballast into Fourteen Fathom will hurt the Fish:

That conveying Ballast from Ships by the Machines is more expeditious, and less expensive, than using Keels — That Ballast dropped into 14 Fathom will mend the Road-stead:

That the North East Wind has no Effect upon Ballast call into 14 Fathom Water; there being so great a De-feent from the Harbour to that Depth, that it is impartible Ballast can be washed in.

And being asked the Question, he said. The last time lie saw the Bar the Flat was not so broad as it had been by several Fathom:

That only the People on board the Machines can tell when they drop their Ballast — That a number of the Machines would discharge all the Ballast from the Ships in the River Tyne-,but they cannot get out when the Wind blows hard from the Sea — That it flows 15 or 16 Feet on the Bar at a Spring Tide; and that it must be a very good Spring to make 22 Feet.

And being again asked the Question, he said, That Keels are as expeditious for removing Ballast as the Machines.

Mr. William Clarke, being examined, confirmed Mr. Cowards Evidence with regard to the Goodness of the Bar, and the River’s being grown worse than it was formerly, occasioned by the Ballast being washed off the Quays, and likewise with regard to the Impossibility of Ballast being washed from 14 Fathom Water on to the Bar; and he said, his Reason for thinking it impossible that B.-.haft, dropped into Fourteen Fathom at Sea, can

hurt (he Bar, is, that the Tide out of the ! larbour goes nofuither than 5 or 6 Fathom — That 14 Fathom Water is about $ of a Mile from the Bar, and is in the North and South Tide, (lie Coast Tide — That the liar, at low Water and Neap Tide, has about 6 or 7 Feet Water on it ;and that he thinks it morally impossible that the Bsl-last (liould raile io steep a Hill so as to affect the Bar: And he furtheradded, that a small Number of Machines would dispatch the Shipping, allowing for bad Weather.

Upon the whole Matter, your Committee came to the following Resolutions: viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Richard Lyddell hath not made good the Allegations of his Petition, so as to entitle him to the Encouragement deli red by his laid Petition.

Rejoived, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That employing the Machines, mentioned in the Petition of Richard Lyddell, in taking Ballast from Ships in the River Tyne, and carrying the same to Sen, may be of dangerous Consequence to die Harbour of,

and the Navigation of the River

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,' That discharging Ballast from Ships or other Vessels rifling and being within any Haven, Port, or navigable River, otherwise than by conveying and laying the same upon Land above high Water Mark, is liable to great Frauds, and may be prejudicial to such Havens, Port:, dr navigable Rivers.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That further Provision ought to be made to prevent any Damage which may happen to Havens, Channels, and navigable Rivers, by the unlading or calling of Ballast from Ships or other Vefll-ls.

MR. Alderman Baker reported from the Committee, Whale to whom the Petition of several Merchants, and Lihery. Owners of Shipping, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of Fast contained in the said Petition; and had directed him to report a State thereof to the House; and he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

By several Acts of Parliament, passed in the 6th, 13th, and 22d Years of his present Majesty’s Reign, it appeared, that the several Bounties granted by those Acts to Ships employed in the Whale Fishery are confined to Ships of the Burthen of 200 Tons, and upwards.

To prove that Ships of a lets Burthen than 200 Tons are as proper to be used in the Whale Fishery as larger ones,

Mr. William Moody said, That he had been employed in the Greenland Fishery for the last Three Years; and that last Year he was on board a Ship of 328 Tons, in Company with Two Snows employed in the said Fishery, of about 140 Tons Burthen each: That he observed them, and wished he had been in One of them, for he was obliged to keep out to Sea, when these small Ships could go in amongst the Ice, where there was not Room to turn the large ones; and that they were built as strong in proportion as larger Ships:

That if the large Ships could have got first into the Ice, they would have had the best Chance; but that he thinks a Vessel of 15c Tons would be as serviceable as a large one, and he should chuse to go in a Ship of that size*.

That these small Vessels were capable of carrying home as many Whales as have been carried home, on an Average, by each Vessel, of late Years; for that they would bring over 100 Tons of Blubber, besides Fins:

That these Two Snows had each of them Five Roatr, and his Ship had Six; but that their Boats were not quite so large as his, but that they might be as useful:

And that they caught One Whale apiece, and made upwards of Twenty-one Ton of clean Oil between them.

Being asked the Question, he laid, He had been employed in the Dutch Whale Fishery, and they gem rally employ Ships between 5 and 600 Ions Burthen; but he would as soon go on the Whale Fishery in a White J ftr-ring Buss, which is but 80 Tons, as any Vessel That they could carry Four Boats, but they uuid be Ids:

That

Fishery*

252 22* — 14? Martii. -^.1755.

That the final! Vessels are able to cant a Fish, i. e. to turn her upside down, to cut off the Blubber as well as the large ones, and are sufficient to carry Six Months Provisions and 100 Tons of Oil,

Mr. Ralph Grey laid, He was on board the Charming Jenny Snow (One of the Snows mentioned by the lull Witness) lad Year, on the Greenland Fishery: That lhe was about 14.0 Tons, and went in Company with the other Snow: That they killed Two Whales, which were both struck by the Crew aboard their Ship, and the First of them canted by them alone; but that the Crew in the other Snow assisted them in canting the last Whale, though they could have done it very well without any Assistance, for that Four Hands at the Windlass are sufficient to cant a Whale; but in canting the latter Whale, they broke their Capftern, and went down to the other Snip for Assistance; but the Two Ships were not lalhed together, only tied with a Rope; and that the Snows did not assist each other in getting out of the Ice, only they waited for one another:

That the Two Whales produced 21 Ton and an Half of Oil:

That their Ship received a great deal of Damage by breaking her Timbers between the Ice, but that they repaired her there; and, if it had not been for that Miffortune, they should have fiflied much longer; and he thought, if a large Ship had been there, fhc would not have recovered the Damage; and that they went into Places where the large Ships could not go; and that he would as soon go upon the Greenland Fishery in such a Ship as theirs was, as in any Ship whatsoever.

Mr. Thomas Davis, Mariner, had been Nine Voyages to Greenland, informed your Committee, That he was on board the last mentioned Snow on the GreenlandFishery last Year, with Five or Six Sail in Company: That they parted Company with the large Ships at the Skirts of the Ice, when the Two small Vessels went in, and the large Ships could not follow them: That they caught Two Whales, which produced about a Ton of Bone; and that the Oil was as good as any boiled in the Dock: That the Dutch usually employ Ships of 500 Tons in the Whale Fishery; but that he saw a Dutch Ship of about ico Tons which caught Two Whales; and that ’tis customary for One Ship to assist another in case of Damage:

That a small Ship will force through the Ice as well as a large one, if lhe is strong enough, and she can get through a narrower Passage; but that the heavier a Ship is, the better she will force through the Ice:

That they had 27 Hands on board, Four Harpooners, and Provisions for Six Months; and that he never saw a Whale that a Ship of 140 Tons could not cant.

Mr. Geo. Spurrel said, He had beenMasterof a Ship 35 Years in the Hudson's Bay Service, and that they use Ships from 120 to 190 Tons, and find small Ships much handier than great ones: That the Ice in Bay is

more subject to lie in Islands, and is reckoned more dangerous, than that in the Greenland Seas:

That he never was in Greenland, but had often seen Ice driving from Davis's Straits, which he was told was much the fame; and that the Hudson's Bay Ships are much stronger built than those employed in the er)’, and that small Ships might be built as strong as large ones; and that he had received several Squeezes between the Ice in Hudson's Bay, in a Ship of 190 Tons, which no Ship that now trades to Greenland would have borne.

Mr. Jonathan Fowler, being examined, confirmed the Evidence given by the last Witness in every Particular.

Ordered, That the said Report be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Monday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the said Report.

That in no one Year, before the last, above Three new Inhabitants have come into the Borough hnce he has known it.

To shew the Custom of making Rates for the said Parishes.

Charles Roberts said, That in both the Parishes of New-lyn and 6A Enoder, the Rates are usually made about a Fortnight before Easier for the Year preceding; but that in the Year 1744 there was an Half Year’s Hate made at Michaelmas, because the Poor a e very burthensome; and that before the Eledhon in the Year 1741 there was a Rate made in the Beginning of the Year, and some small Sum collected within the Borough, but not in the rest of the Parish:

That, on the Sunday after the Rates are made, they are ufugilly brought to the Vestry, where the Parishioners peruse them, and, if they think proper, allow them; and that they are afterwards signed by the Justices: That the Rate made for the Parish of Newlyn before last Easier, being brought into the Vestry, was objected to.

Robert Clemoes, who has known Newlyn Parish all his Life-time, and served the Office of Overseer and Churchwarden Three or Four times, confirmed what had been said by Roberts as to the Method of making Rates; and added, That if Tenements are divided intoieveral Parts, the Rates are collected from all the Occupiers; and that if the Occupier of a Tenement quits it in the Middle of the Year, and another iuccecds, each pays in proportion to the Time of his Occupancy:

That the Officers endeavour to recover the Rates due from those who leave the Parish; but if they cannot get the Money, the Parish in general bears the Loss:

That the Officers make the Rates as near as they can to reimburse themselves, and no more; but that some-times there may be a Surplus of Three, Four, or Ten Pounds, which is paid over to the succeeding Officers.

Anthony Cock, Richard Woon, and Nicholas Francis, who had been Overseers of the Parish of Saint Enoder, all laid, That it was the Custom of that Parish to make the Rates a Week or a Fortnight before Easier for the Year preceeding; but that in the Year 1741 there was an Half Year's Rate made at Michaelmas.

As to the Behaviour of the Returning Officer;

Mr. Joseph Hawkey said. That, before the Poll began, it was debated by what Rule the Portreve should govern himself:

That the Friends to the Petitioners, imagining that new Persons were put upon some of the Rates, infilled, that the Rates ought not to be the Rule; but that the real Occupiers of Tenements only ought to vote: But when the Portreve delared he would govern himself by the Rates, they proposed to him the Rates of 1752, as the best Rule, because the Borough was then quiet, and no Opposition thought of; but the Returning Officer was of the contrary Opinion: That then the Yol. 27.

Friends to the Petitioners alleged, that the Rates made before Eafer 1754, for the Year 1753, were more proper than those made after the Election was proclaimed, especially as the Officers, who signed the last mentioned Rate, were not legally nominated, upon Account of a prior Nomination for both Parishes; for Mr. Justice Gregor allowed that he signed the Nomination of the Officers for Nezu/ynon the Sunday in the Evening, and the other Nomination for the same Parish was signed in the Morning; but the Portreve gave it as his Opinion, that, as there was no Fraction in a Day, the Officers nominated by the Two Justices Gregors had as good a Right as the others; and as they had entered into their Office, by making a Rate, they were at least Officers de faPio; and then declared, that he would poll by the Rate they had made:

That, during the Poll, the Portreve paid no Regard to any Rate but the last — That he suffered no Argument to prevail against that Rate; and, in all Cases where Objections were made, he only inquired whether the Person objected to was or was not upon that Rate, and determined to receive or reject the Vote accordingly; except in the following Instances:

1 ft, In the Caie of John Martin, who offered his Vote for a Tenement, for which the Earl of Sandwich was rated; and it was received.

2d, In the same of Richard who was disallow-

ed by the Portreve, because he owned that he came into the Tenement, for which he offered his Vote, alter the Teste of the YVrit.

That Martin and Bampfield voted for the Petitioners — Benney and Edmonds offered their Votes for the Sitting Members:

Stephen’s He was called in; and, at the Bar, presented to the Mamnafiure Jjoufej purhunt to their Order, a Declaration of several Pot Ash. Merchants, Planters and others, concerning the Manufacture of Pot and Pearl Ash in his Majesty’s Plantations in America, dated 26th November 1753.

And then he withdrew.

And the said Declaration was read; and is as follow* eth; viz.

Whereas it has beenrequested of us to declare our Opinion concerning the Manufactory of Pot and Pearl Ash in the American Colonies belonging to this Crown, we the underwritten Merchants, Planters, and others, trading to, and interested in, his Majesty’s Plantations in America, do hereby declare. That it doth not appear to us, that either Pot or Pearl Ash are made there since the late Indulgence granted by Parliament, in greater Quantities than before.

Further That we know not of any Importation made here of those Commodities from America except small Quantities, as Trials, which have always proved deficient in some respect or other.

We are of Opinion that the ill Success of this Manufacture in the Plantations is owing to the Want of Know-lege in the Method of making the same; and that all due Encouragement should be given £>r the Removal of this Impediment; inasmuch as the Interest of his Majesty’s Subjects, and particularly our own, is concerned in the Cultivation of lo necessary a Commodity; by means of which a new Article of Returns may be made to us from North America for the Goods we lend there, for want of which our Trade is oftentimes very much circumlcribed.

London, 26th November 1753.

Mr. Secretary Robinfonacquainted the House, That he

had a Message from his Majesty to this House, ligned by his Majesty: And he presented the same to the House; and it was read by Mr. Speaker (all the Members being uncovered); and is as followeth viz.

GEORGE R.

His Majesty, having, at the Beginning of this Session declared, that his principal Object was to preserve the publick Tranquility, and at the same time to protest those Possessions which make one great Source of the Commerce and Wealth of his Kingdoms, now finds it necessary to acquaint the House of Commons, That the present Situation of Affairs makes it requisite to augment his Forces by Sea and Land, and to take such other Measures as may best tend to preserve the general Peace of Vol. 27,

Europe, and to secure the just Rights and Possessions of his Crown in America, as well as to repell any Attempts whatsoever that may be made to support or countenance any Dftigns which may be formed against his Majesty and his Kingdoms; and his Majesty doubts not but his faithful Commons, on whole Affection and Zeal he entirely relies, will enable him to make such Augmentations, and to take such Measures for the Support of the Honour of his Crown, and the true Interests of his People, and for the Security of his Dominions in the present critical Conjuncture, as the Exigency of Affairs may require; in doing which, his Majesty will have as much Regard to the Eale of his good Subjects as shall be confident with their Safety and Welfare. G. R.

Resolved, neminecontradicenie. That an humble Ad-

drels be prelenied to his Majesty, to return him the Thanks of this House for his most gracious Message; and to express the entire Confidence this House has in his Majesty’s constant Attention to preserve the publicTranquillity, to maintain the Commerce and true Interests of his People, and to secure the just Rights and Possessions of his Crown against all Attempts whatlocver; to assure his Majesty, that his faithful Commons will, with the utmost Zealand Affection for his Royal Person, Family, and Government, effect ually enable his Majesty to make such Augmentation of his Forces by Sea and Land, and to take such Measures for the Security of his Dominions, the Trade and Commerce of his People, and the just Rights and Possessions of his Crown, as shall be found necessary in the present Conjuncture; and that they will, with the greatest Vigour and Kesolution, (land by and support his Majesty in repelling every Attempt that may be made to countenance or support any Designs which may be formed against his Majesty and his Kingdoms.

Resolved, That the said Address be presented to his Majesty by the whole House.

Resolved, I'liat it is the Opinion of this Committee, That towards raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, a Sum of Money, nor exceeding One million, be raised by way of Lottery, One hundred thousand Pounds thereof to be deducted for the Benefit of the Public, and the rema'ning Nine hundred thousand Pounds to be charged on the Pioduceof the Sinking Fund, at the Rate of Three Pounds per Centum per , to commence from the:5th Day of January 1756; the Tickets to be Ten Pounds each, Two Pounds whereof to be paid down at the time of subscribing, by way of Deposit, such Subscription to be finally closed at Five of the Clock in the Afternoon of the 15th Day of this instant April; and that every Person be at Liberty to subscribe for any Number of Tickets; and in case a larger Sum than the said Million shall be subscribed within the said Term, a proportionable Reduction upon such Excess shall, as near as possible, be made out of each Subscriber's Share.

After which, his Majesty was plealed to make a most gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, as followeth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen.

The many eminent Proofs which you have given of your Duty and Affection to my Person and Government, during the course of this Session of Parliament, have afforded me the greatest Satisfaction; and the Zeal you have shewn for supporting the Honour, Rights, and Possessions, of rny Crown, has been no Ids agreeable to me.

My Desire to preserve the public Tranquillity has been sincere and uniform: I have religiously adhered to the Stipulations of the Treaty of Aix la Chapelle, and made it my Care not to injure or give just Cause of Offence to any Power whatsoever; but I never could entertain a Thought of purchasing the Name of Peace at the Expence of suffering Encroachments upon, or of yielding up, what is justly belonging to Great Britain, either by ancient Possession or by solemn Treaties: Your Vigour and Firmness on this important Occasion have enabled me to be prepared for such Contingencies as may happen. If reasonable and honourable Terms of Accommodation can be agreed upon, 1 shall be satisfied. In all Events, I shall rely on the Justice of our Cause, the effectual Support of my People, and the Protection of the Divine Providence.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I return you my Thanks for the necessary Provisions you have made for the Service of the current Year: The extraordinary Supply which you have granted me towards augmenting my Forces by Sea and Land, is such a Proof of your Confidence in me, and of your constant Attention to the Service of your Country, that I cannot sufficiently express the Satisfaction I take in this feasonable Care of the Safetyofmy Kingdoms and Dominions, or in the Evidence it has produced of the Extent of our public Credit, and of the Zeal of my Subjects in this Conjuncture.

A MESSAGE from his Majesty, by the honourable Sir Henry Bellendtn, Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The King commands this honourable House to attend his Majesty, immediately, in the House of Peers.

Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to attend his Majesty.

And being returned;

Several Members, returned upon new Writs, took the Oaths, and made and subscribed the Declaration, and took and subscribed the Oath of Abjuration, according to the Laws made for those Purposes.

A Bill for the more effectual preventing clandestine Outlawries, was read the Eirft time.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a Second time.

Mr. Speaker acquainted the House, that 'Jeremiah Dyson Esquire, Clerk of the House, desired to be abi'ent, upon Account of the Indisposition of a near Relation;

Ordered, That Mr. Poyntz do attend at the Table, during the Absence of the said Mr. Dyson.

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House had attended his Majesty in the House of Peers: Where his Majesty was pleased to make a most gracious Speech from the Throne to both Houses of Parliament; of which, Mr. Speaker said, he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy; which he read to the House; and is as followed!; viz.

With a sincere Desire to preserve my People from the Calamities of War, as well as to prevent, in the midftof these Troubles, a general Wan from being lighted up in Europe, I have been always ready to accept reasonable and honourable Terms of Accommodation; but none such have hitherto been proposed on the Part of France.

I have also confined my Views and Operations to hinder France from making new Encroachments, or supporting those already made, to exert our Right to a Satisfaction for Hostilities committed in a Time of profound Peace, and to disappoint such Designs, as from various Appearances and Preparations, there is Reason to think have been formed against my Kingdoms and Dominions.

By these Methods, I have pursued the Plan which I formerly pointed out to you, and for which I had the Satisfaction to receive the strongest Assurances of your vigorous Support.

What other Power can object to Proceedings so absolutely necessary to our own Defence and Security ? My good Brother the King of Spain fees, with Concern, thele Differences; and the Part which he generously takes in the common Welfare of Europe, makes him earnestly wifti the Preservation of the public Tranquility. He has / also given Assurances, that he will continue in the same pacific Sentiments.

In pursuing these great Ends, I make no doubt of the vigorous and chearful Support of my Parliament; and that, whilst I am engaged in this just and national Cause, the affectionate Assurances, which they gave me the last Session, will be effectually made good: In consequence thereof, I have greatly increased my naval Armaments, augumented my Land Forces in such manner as might be the least burthenlbme, and have concluded a Treaty with the Empress of Russia, and another with the Landgrave of Hejfe CaffeI; which shall be laid before you.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The present critical Conjuncture of Affairs, and my constant Inclination to have the Advice and Assistance of my Parliament on all important Occasions, have made me desirous to meet you here as early as possible.

Since your last Session, I have taken such Measures as might be most conducive to the Protection of our Possessions in America, and to the regaining of such Parts there-

of as had been encroached upon, or invaded, in Violation of the Peace, and contrary to the Faith of the most (b-lemn Treaties.

For this Purpose, the maritime Force of this Kingdom has been got ready with the utmost Application and Expedition, and been principally employed. Some Land Forces have been lent from hence to North America, and all proper Encouragement has been given to the several Colonies there, to exert themselves in their own Defence, and in the Maintenance of the Rights and Posses-lions of Great Britain.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I have ordered the proper Officers to lay before you Estimates for the Service of the ensuing Year; and likewise Accounts of the extraordinary Expences which have been made this Year, in pursuance of the Power given me by Parliament. I fee, with great Concern, that the necessary Services before-mentioned will require large Supplies: I alk only such as shall be requisitetbr the effectual carrying on of those Measures, which shall be necessary to support what has been begun according to your Inclination, for the Security of my Kingdoms and Dominions, and for the Purposes which have been a! ready mentioned to you. Whatever you grant shall, with the strictest Economy, be applied to those Uses only for which it shall be given.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I rely upon your Duty and good Affections, which I have so often experienced. There never was a Situation,

Resolved, That if it shall appear that any Person that been tampering with any Witness, in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof, or directly or indirectly hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing or giving Evidence, the same is declared to be a high Cnme and Misdemeanor, and this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any Person hath given false Evidence in any same before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the ut-tnoft Severity against such Offender.

You may be allured, although I wish for nothing more than a safe and honourable Accommodation, I am determined to protedf and maintain the valuable and urn doubted Rights and Poflfessions of my Crown.

Your Assurances that you will aflish mein the Defence of my foreign Dominions, if they should be attacked on Account of the Measures I am pursuing for the true In>-t ere ft of these Kingdoms, are such Proofs of your Affection to me, and of your Regard to my Honour, as give me the greatest Satisfaction.

A PETITION of the Trustees, whole Names arc thereunto subscribed, appointed to put in Execution Two Acts of Parliament, one made in the 1 ith and the other in the 26th Year of his Majesty's Reign, for repairing the Roads from Shoreditch , through Hack*

ney, to Stanford Hill, and cross Cambridge Heath, over Bethnal Green, to the Turnpike at Mile End, in the County of Middlesex, as also of several Gentlemen, and other Persons, frequently travelling through the said Roads, was presented to the House, and read; alleging, That the Petitioners the said Trustees have cauled the said Roads from Shoreditch Church, through Hackney, to Stanford Hill, and by the South Side of Cambridge , over Bethnal Green, to be repaired} but have been prevented

from repairing the Road leading from Hackney, by the East Side of Cambridge Htath, to Bethnal Green, a Doubt having arisen, whether the said last mentioned Road be comprehended in either of the said Acts, or ought to be repaired by the Authority thereof; and that it is therefore necessary, in order to the effectual Amendment and Preservation of the said Road, that Provision should be made by Parliament for removing the said Doubt: And further alleging, that, by the said Act of the 26th Year of his Majesty’s Reign, the said Trustees are impowered to purchase Lands for widening, turning, or altering, any Part of the Roads in the said Act mentioned, and to cause such Lands to be taken into, and made Part of, the said Roads, or to turn the same through any such Lands; and are also impowered, after any such new Road shall be made, or any Lands shall be taken into, and made Part of, the said first-mentioned Roads, to sell and convey the Lands constituting the former Road, as also such Part of the Lands purchased by the said Trustees as shall not be made use of for the Purposes aforesaid; but that a Doubt hath arisen, whether the said Trustees, not being a Corporation or Body Politic, can convey the Fee-simple of any Landsfo by them to be sold; and that it may there- fore be very difficult for the said Trustees, under those Circumstances, to find Persons willing to purchase such Lands: And letting forth, that the said Roads, by reason of their Contiguity to the Suburbs of the City of London, are frequently infefted in the Night-time with Robbers, and other wicked and evil-disposed Persons, upon which account many ol his Majesty’s Subjects coming from the Northern and Eastern Parts of this Kingdom to the said City, as also many others residing in, or resorting to, the said City, and Places adjacent, being often obliged to travel upon the said Roads during that time, are exposed to great Dangers and frequent Outrages and Violences; and that iftbelaid Roadswereenlightened, anda proper Guard was kept thereon (the Expence of both which Services, it is apprehended, maybe defrayed out of the Tolls to be collected upon the said Roads) such Outrages and Offences might in a great measure be prevented: And there-foreprayingthe House, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for removing the said Doubts, and for impowering the said Trustees to erect Lamps, and keep a Guard, upon the said several Roads in the Night-time.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fathe, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

Translation of the Treaty, and of the Two separate and secret Art ides belonging thereto, between his Majesty and the Empress of Russia, signed at St. Petersburg,
