In the Name of the Holy and Undivided Trinity.

Whereas the sincere and intimate Friendship which unites his Britannic Majesty and her Imperial Majesty of all the Ruffias, as well as the Engagements which they contrafted by the Treaty of Defend vc Alliance of the Year 174a, oblige them at all times to be watchful of the public Tranquillity and their reciprocal Security: And whereas, in the present Conjuncture of Affairs, the Preservation of the General Peace, and the Defence of their respective Dominions, Rights, and Subjects, have appeared to them necessarily to require that they should be guarded against the Attacks with which they may be threatened on the Part of any Power whatever, by (ccuring a Body of Troops capable of making a powerful Diver-fion in case of such Attacks: And whereas, considering

the

26° Novembri

29 Geo. II#

the present Situation, the Contingents of the Succours stipulatedby the above-mentioned Treaty, would not be iuificient for all the aforesaid Objects, his Britannic Majesty and her Imperial Majesty of all the have

thought proper to concert, before-hand, the farther Mea-furcs of Precaution which the general Tranquillity* and their common Interests and Security seem to demand:

' and, for this Purpose, they, have authorized their respective Ministers; that is to say. His Majesty the King of Great Britain, Sir Charles Williams Knight of

the most honourable Order of the Bath, One of the Members of the Parliament at Great , and his Ambaffadour at the Court of the Emprefsof all the and

her Imperial Majesty of all the Raffias, her Chancellor, actual Privy Counsellor, Senator, and Knight of the Orders of Saint Andrew, of the White , and of Saint Alexander Newjhy, Alexis Count dt Beftouckeff Rumin, and her Vice Chancellor, actual Privy Counsellor, Lieutenant of the Company of the Body Guards, actual Chamberlain, and Knight Of the Orders of Saint Andrew, of the White Eagle, of the Black E,of St. Alexander Newjky, and of St. Anne, Michael Count dt who having

communicated their respective full Powers, and having conferred together, have agreed on the following Articles.

Article I.

The High Contrafting Parties renew expressly, by this Convention# the Treaty of defensive Alliance concluded between them, the 11 th December 1742, at in

all its Articles, and confirm the Stipulations of the Succours to be given reciprocally, as they are contained in the 4th Article of the said Treaty, which Succours shall be furnished on each Side in the Manner and on the Conditions therein expressed.

Article a.

Whereas it is declared by the 17th Article of the before-mentioned Alliance,." That if the Succours therein stipulated should not be sufficient, the Contrafting Parties shall then agree, without Delay, on the farther Suc-" cour&to be given and as that would not answer the Ends proposed, and there may happen Cales which may hot allow them Time to agree thereupon:

In order to obviate the Incohveniencies which would necessarily result from such a Delay, they have agreed to settle, from henceforth, and at all Events, the Means of their Defence; With this View, her Imperial Majesty of all the Ruffias has not only caused to march towards the Frontiers of Livonia, adjoining to Lithuania, but engages

also to hold there as long as this Convention shall subsist, as near to those Frontiers as the Quarters will permit, a Body of her Troops, amounting to 55,000 Men t that is to say, 40,000 Infantry of her regular Troops, furnished with the.necessary Artillery, and 15,000 Cavalry, >'composed of Tfree Regiments of Cuirafiiers, of Twenty Companies of Horse Grenadiers, of Two Regiments of Hussars, and the Remainder of light Troops, to wit, of Cossacks and of Calmucks, each with Two Horses, as many as shall be wanting to complete these 15,000 Cavalry; lo that the whole Infantry and Cavalry shall form a complete Body of 55,000 Men.

Article 3.

Her Imperial Majesty engages, moreover, to cause to be held in Readiness, during the time above specified, on the Coasts of the above-mentioned Province, Forty or Fifty Galleys, with the necessary Crews, in Condition to act on the First Order.

/ Article 4.

I The Body of Troops and the Galleys, mentioned in the Two preceding Articles, shall not be put in Activity, but in case his Britannic Majesty, or any of his Allies, should be attacked; and, in that Cafe* the General Commander in Chief of the said Corps, who, for this Purpose, shall be furnished before-hand with the Orders of her Imperial Majesty of all the Ruffias, shall march, as soon as he shall receive the Requisition on the Part of his Britannic Majestr, and shall make, as loon as possible, a Diversion with a Body of 30,000 Infantry, provided with the necef-Vci. 2 7.

l°9

fary Artillery, and with all the 15,600 Cavalry above Treaty mentioned, atld shall embark at the same time the other with

10,boo Infantry on board the 40 or 50 Galleys, in order Russia.

to make a Delcent, according to the Exigence of the Cafe* and the Utility of the Service.

Article 5.

In case the Dominions of his Britannic Majesty in Germany should be invaded* on account of Interests which regard his Kingdoms, her Imperial Majesty declares, that (he will look upon such an invasion as a same of the above-said Alliance of 1742 and that the said Dominions shall be therein comprised in this respect*

Article 6.

In Consideration of so important an Augmentation of the Succour ftipul&ted by the Treaty of defensive Alliance above mentioned, as also of all the other extraordinary Expences which the March and Maintenance of Troops in Livonia, with the Artillery and its Appurtenances, as well as the Preparations of the Galleys, may have cost, or shall still cost, his Britannic Majesty promises and engages to cause to be paid to her Imperial Majesty of all the Ruf-Jifis the Sum of 500,000 Pounds Sterling to

be reckoned from the Day when the Body of her Troops shall have passed the Frontiers of her Dominions, in Con-' sequenceof the Requisition made by his Majesty the King of Great Britain. This Sum shall be paid by Baron Resident of Great Britain, in the Place where it shall be demanded, at the Rate of Ten Florins and Fifteen Stivers, current Money of Holland, for every Pound Sterling, and always Four Months ih Advance and the First Payment thereof shall be made the Day that this Body shall go out of the Dominions of her Imperial Majesty.

Article 7.

Whereas her Imperial Majesty of all the Ruffias is particularly interested in the Preservation of the Tranquillity of the North, and that no Innovation iliould happen in the Neighbourhood of her Dominions; considering also the Proximity of the Countries wherein the Diversion irt question will probably be made, and the Facility her Troops will have of subsisting immediately in an Enemy’s Country, (he takes upon herself alone, during such a Diversion, the Subsistence and Treatment of the said Troops by Sea and Land; as also the heavy Artillery which they may have Occasion for, and of the Requisites thereto be* longing.

Article 8.

Her Imperial Majesty engages to continue the Diversion to be made, and not to recall her Troops, even though (he should be attacked by any other Power. On the other hand, his Britannic Majesty promises, that, in case her Majesty the Empress should be disturbed in the said Diversion, or should be attacked herself, hh Britannic Majesty wilifurnish immediately the Succour stipulated by the Treaty of 1742.

Article 9.

In case that, contrary to all Expectation, a War should break out, his Britannic Majesty engages to fend into the Baltic Sea a Squadron of his Ships of Force, suitable to the Circumstances; and the Admiral Of this Squadron shall act in Concert with the Imperial Russian Army, as long as they shall be within Reach of each other;

Article IO;

For the ConVeniency and Readiness of Corresponderice, his Britannic Majesty shall keep with the auxiliary Body (which shall be commanded solely by the General whom her Majesty the Empress shall put at their Head, to whom also the Person who shall command the Galleys is to be subject)* a Cohimiflary, who, as well as the Admiral of the British Squadron, in case there should be one, shall always be invited and admitted tb the General Councilsof War; and shall have, moreover, Communication of every thing which may concern the common Service.

Article ti.

All the Plunder Which the Ruffiait Ttoops shall gain from the Enemy, of what Nature and Quality soever, shall be for the Advantage of those same Troops.

This Convention shall subsist for the Space of Four Years, to be reckoned from the Day when the Ratifications of it Hull be exchanged.

In case Peace should be made, or the Object of the Dr-; verlion to be made should cease to exist, before the Expiration of the Four Years, above mentioned, the abovesaid auxiliary Body shall return also before that time into the Dominions of her Imperial Majesty; and his Britannic, Majesty consents, that after the Return, the said Body; shall enjoy Three Months of the Succour agreed on; but in case Peace should not be made before- that Term, then the contracting Parties shall agree farther upon the Prolongation of this Convention. .

First separate and secret Article.

Whereas her Imperial Majesty of all the Russias has caul’ed to be represented to his Britannic Majesty, that the March of the Troops, as well Infantry as Cavalry, stipulated in the Treaty signed this Day, towards the Frontiers of Livonia, as also the Artillery, with what belongs thereto,. with which her Imperial Majesty has charged herself, and the Expence required to maintain them there during Four Years, as well as the necessary Preparations for keeping in lleadiness the Galleys during the said Term, have already cost, and must dill cost, great Sums of Money, over and above what would otherwise have been necessary for the ordinary Service of these Troops; in Consideration of what is above, and of the great Utility which the remaining of such a Body of Troops in the above-mentioned Province, during the 1 Term of Four Yeats, will be of, and the better to enable her Imperial Majesty to supply the Expence thereof, h is Britannic Majesty has been pleated to engage himself,' and engages himself by this Article, tofurniih a Succour, at the Rate of 100,000 Pounds Sterling per Annum, payable each Year before-hand, to be reckoned from the Day of the Exchange of the Ratifications to the Day that, on the Requisition of his Britannic Majesty, this Body of Rup pan T loops shall go* out of her Imperial Majesty’s Dominions; for, from that Day, the abovesaid Succour of

100,000 Pounds Sterling is intirely to cease; because the Payment of the Sum of 500,000 Pounds Sterling

num, which has been agreed upon by the 6th Article of the Treaty, must commence and besubstituted in the room of it; so that whatever shall then be found paidih Advance at the Rate of the abovesaid 100,coo Pounds Ster-. ling pir Annum, shall bedilcounted and deducted from the Payment of the ;oo, oco Pounds Sterling; it being to be understood that his Britannic Majesty shall be at Liberty to fend once every Year into the said Province of Livonia a Commissary, to fee and examine the Number and Condition of the (aidTroops: Moreover, what is stipulated in the 6th Article of the Treaty signed this Dav, with regard to the Manner of paying the Succour in Money, is exprefe.lv confirmed by this present Article.

Article 2.

For this Purpose it is agreed, That if in Times to come/ their said Majesties, or either of them, Ihoulc) be attacked by Sea or Land, by whomsoever it be, they shall lend each other, immediately after Requisition, the necessary Succours, which shall be determined as well with regard to the Nature as to the Quantity, according to what is hereafter ftipuluted in the following Articles of this Treaty.

Article 3.

His Britannic Majesty and her Imperial Majesty from henceforth declare, that they do not mean, by making this Alliance, to offend or injure any one Dover; but that it is, on the contrary, their only Aim and Design to provide, by thele Engagements, for their reciprocal Advantage and Security, and to contribute, as much as it shall depend upon their Care, to the Preservation of the general Peace of Europe, and ot that of the North in particular; for which Ends, they shall employ themselves in the most effectual mannerpofT:Me, and shall mutually communicate to eaclt other their Ideas and Cuunfels for that Purpose.

Article 4.

As the principal Design and End of this Alliance is rmr tually to secure one another from all Invasion, Injury, and Damage, and as each of the High Contracting Parties desires nothing moreearnefl.lv than to be able always to fulfil this reciprocal Engagement in the Manner which shall be most advantageous to their Ally, according to the Means which God has put into their Hands respectively; and as the natural Strength of Great Britain principally consists in Ships of War, and that of Rvjjia in Land Forces, it is agreed, that, in case his Britannic Majesty should be attacked or disturbed in his Kingdoms, Provinces, States, or Possessions whatever, so as to find it necessary to require his Ally’s Assistance, her Imperial Majesty of all the Raffias will fend him forthwith Ten shoulmd Infantry and Two thousand Cavalry; which Succour shall be continued to him, on the Part of her Imperial Majesty, during the whole time that the said Attack or Disturbance shall last; and on the other -hand, in case her Imperial Majesty of all the should be attacked

on disturbed in her Kingdoms, Provinces, States, or Pof-sessions whatever, liras to find it necessary to require her Ally’s Assistance, his Britannic Majesty will lend her forthwith a Squadron ol Twelve Men of War of the Line, carrying Seven hundred Guns, according to the following Lift: Two Si tips of Seventy Guns, making together 140 Guns and 960 Men; Six Ships of 60 Guns, making 360 Guns anti 2400 Men; Four Ships of 50 Guns, making 100 Guns and 1200 Men; in the Whole, Twelve Ships, 700 'Guns and 4560 Men; That Squadron shall be duly fitted cut and armed for War; which Succour shall be in like planner continued to her during the whole time the said Attack or Disturbance shall last.

Article 5.

Hut if the Nature of the Attack or Invasion was such> tint the Patty attacked or invaded should not find it suitable to demand the spedfic Succoursstipulated in the preceding Article, as not being proper for their Defence, the Aid High Com nutting Panic , in order togive each other, in every i hing. Article 6.

In case the Party required, after having furnished the Assistance stipulated by the 4th Article of this Treaty, should be attacked themselves, so that it should be neccl-lary for thera torccall their Forces for their own Security, they shall be at Liberty to do it Two Months after they shall have duly apprised the Party requiring thereof; and it is likewise stipulated, that, in case the Party required should, at the time of the Requisition, find themselves involved in a War, so that it should be absolutely necessary to keep at Home, for their own Security and Defence, such Forces as they ought to furnish to their Ally by virtue of this ^Treaty; when this same happens, the Party required shall bedispensed with, for the time the said Ne-cdlity shall last, from furnishing the above-mentioned Succour.

Article 7.

The auxiliary Troops of RuJ/ia shall be provided with a Field Artillery of Two Three Pounders lor each Batta- 9 lion, and with warlike Stores; and shall likewise be paid, replaced, and recruited^by herlmperial Majesty of all the RuJJias; but his Britannic Majesty shall furnish them the Portions, to wit, a Pound of Flesh per Diem, Bread, or, instead of it, 60 Pounds of Rye Flour Month, a Pound of Salt and Four Pounds of Grots per Month; tho Weight reckoned upon the Foot of Holland, and the Rations of Forage, Oats, Hay, according to the Russian military Establishment, and in Holland Weight, as well as the necessary Quarters; the Whole upon the same Foot as those Troops are used to be subsisted by her Imperial Majesty of all the RuJJias.

Article 8.

In calc the said Russianauxiliary Troops, being demanded by his Britannic Majesty, were to march by Land, as it might be indispensable for the said Troops to pal's through the Dominions of same other Powers, his Britannic Majesty shall take care to procure a free Passage for them, furnishing them with Bread and Forage in the same manner as is stipulated in the preceding Article of this Treaty; and when they shall have the Sea to pass, his Britannic Majesty shall take upon himself either to transport them in his own Ships, or to furnish the Expences of this Transportation; which is likewise to be understood as well with regard to the Recruits which her Imperial Majesty shall be obliged to send to the said Troops, according to the preceding Article, as with regard to the Return of those Troops, upon their

being either sent back by his Britannic Majesty, or recalled by her Imperial Majesty of all the or her own De-

fence, according to the Sixth Article of this Treaty: It is moreover stipulated, that when the aforesaid Troops shall be either recalled or Lent back, a sufficient Convoy of Men of War shall escort them for their Security.

Article 10.

And that there may be no Difficulty or Mistake with regard to Rank and Character, the Party requiring shall notify ih Time what Commander is tb be employed for the Command in Chief, either of the Fleet or of the Land Forces; to the end that the Party required may settle and proportion the Rank, and Character of the Person who shall have the Command of the auxiliary Troops or Ships.

Article ix.

The auxiliary Forces Hull have their own Ministers or Preachers, and the free Exercise of Religion; and shall not be tried upon whatever relates to the military Service, but according to the Laws, Articles of War, and Ordinances of their own Country: But if any Disputes should arise between the Officers or Soldiers of the combined Forces, they shall be examined and debated by Commifla-ries, in equal Number, of both Parties, and the Offenders shall be puifished according to the Articles of War of their Sovereign. In likesmanner, the General, as well as the rest of the auxiliary Forces, shall be allowed to carry on a free Correspondence with their Country, whether by Letters or by Expresses.

Article 12.

The auxiliary Forces on the one Side and on the other shall be kept together, as far as that can be done; and, in order that the said respective auxiliary Forces may not be exposed to greater Fatigues than the others, and that there may be an exact Equality in all Expeditions and Operations, the General in Chief shall be obliged to observe a just Proportion in all the Commands, according to the Strength of the whole Fleet or Army.

Article 13.

The Squadron of Ships which his Britannic Majesty is to furnish by virtue of this Alliance, shall be admitted in all the Ports of her Imperial Majesty of all the , where it shall be treated in the most friendly Manner, and provided with every thing it may (land in need of, upon paying the same Price as is paid by the Men of War of her Imperial Majesty of all the; and the said Squa-

dron shall be allowed to return each Year of the War to the Ports of Great Britain, as soon as the Season will not

permit them any longer to keep at Sea; provided it be expressly stipulated, that whenever the same of this Treaty shall exist, the Squadron his Britannic Majesty is to fur-nifti shall arive every Year in the Baltic about the Beginning of the Month of May, and shall not leave that Sea before the Beginning of the Month of October.

Article 14.

The Party requiring, upon making the Demand of the Succour stipulated by thisTreaty, shall, at the same time, acquaint the Party required with the Place where it is intended the said Succour should forthwith repair; and the said Party requiring shall be at Liberty to employ the aforesaid Succour during the whole time it shall be continued to them, in such Manner and such Places as they shall judge most convenient for their Service against the Aggressor.

Article if.

It is agreed, that the same of this Treaty of Alliance shall not be extended to the Wars which may happen to arise between her Imperial Majesty of all the and the Ottoman Porte, or the Tartars, or other

Eastern Nations; his Britannic Majesty being to be dispensed with, in any one of theft Cafes, from furnishing the Succours stipulated by this Treaty; as in like manner, on the other Side, her Imperial Majesty of all the Rufsias shall not be obliged to furnish the Succours stipulated by this Treaty for the Defence of his Britannic Majesty’s l’oflessions in America, or in any Part whatsoever out of Europe.

Article 16.

It is also agreed, that, on account of the great Distance of Places, the Troops which her Imperial Majesty of all the Rufsias shall be to furnish by virtue of this Alliance,

Article 17.

If the Succours stipulated in the 4th Article of this Treaty are not sufficient, then the Contrafling Parties shall agree, without Delay, about the further Succours which they shall give each other.

Article 18.

If it should happen that they should be obliged to have Recourl'e to Force of Arms, neither Peace nor Truce shall be made without including therein such of the Contrafling Parties as shall not have been attacked, that they may suffer no Damage in Relentment for the Succours they shall have given to their Ally.

Article 19.

The present Defensive Alliance shall be no Obstacle to, nor in anywise derogate from, the Treaties and Alliances which may have been entered into by the contrasting Parties with other Kings, Princes, or States, in lb far as the said Treaties shall not be contrary to the present Treaty, or to the Friendftnp and good Understanding which shall always be ftriflly observed between them.

Article 20.

Their said Majesties have moreover agreed, that they shall concert together about the Admission of l'uch other Powers as might be disposed to enter into this Alliance.

Article 21.

The Peace, Friendship, and good Understanding, shall lad for ever between the High Contrafling Parties; but as it is usual to fix a certain Time for Treaties of formal Alliance, the said High Contrafling Parties have agreed that this One shall continue in Force for the Space of Fifteen Years, to be reckoned from the Day of the Signing of this Treaty.

Article 22.

This present Treaty of defenfiVe Alliance shall be approved and ratified by his Britannic Majesty and by her Imperial Majesty of all the R; and the Letters of Ratification in due Form shall be exchanged at St. kurgh, within the Space of Two Months, or sooner, if possible.

In Testimony whereof, the aforesaid Plenipotentiary Ministers on both Sides have ligned the present Treaty of Alliance, and have put the Seals of their Arms thereto. Done at Moscow the 1 ith of December 1742.

Be it known to all whom it may concern, That- his Majesty the King of Great , and liismost Serene Highness the Landgrave of having called to

mind the drift Ties which unite the Interests ot their respective Houses, anil having judged that, in 1 he present Situation of Affairs, it would, contribute to the reciprocal Benefit of Great Britain and the States of to

strengthen and confirm, by a new Treaty of defensive Alliance, the Union which subsists between them; His Britannic Majesty, and his mofl Serene Highness the said Landgrave, have thought proper to direct, for this Purpose, their respective Ministers; that is to say. His said Majesty, Robert bar! of Holdern One of his principal Secretaries of Si ate, and the most Serene Landgrave, his Major General, General of Artillery, and Governor of the Refulence of Cajjel, Commander of the Teutonic Order, the

S;eur Diederic Diedede Fwjlenjl and the Sieur Jijius

Henry Alt, hi-' Privy Counsellor of Legation, and Minister, charged with his Affairs, to enter into Conference thereupon; who, after the Excnat ge of their respective fail Powers, have agreed upon the Points and Articles following.

Article 1.

There shall be, betw'een his Majesty the King of Great Britain and his most Serene Highness the Landgrave of Hejfe Cajjel, their Successors and Heirs, a drift Fiiend-ship, and a sincere, firm, and lading Union; insomuch that the one shall consider the Interefb of the other as his own, and shall apply himself sincerely to advance them to the ut most, and to prevent and avert mutually all Trouble and Damage.

Article 2.

To this end it is agreed, that all former Treaties, principally of Guaranty, be deemed to be renewed and confirmed by the present Treaty, in all their Points, Articles, and Clauses, and shall be of the same Force as if they were inserted in this. Word for Word, lo far as is not derogated from them by the present Treaty. '

Article 3.

His Majesty the King of Great Britain having desired to secure, for his Service, a Body of the Troops of the most Serene Landgrave, in case the Good of his Kingdoms and States should require this Succour, his most Serene Highness has willingly complied with these Views; promising and engaging, by virtue of this Article, to hold in Readiness for this Service, during the Space of Four successive Years, to be reckoned from the Day of the Signing of the present Treaty, a Body of 8,000 Men; to wit, Eight Battalions of Infantry, ea’ch of 800 Men, including the Officers, and Three Regiments of Dragoons, or Cavalry, making in all 1,400 Horse; which Corps shall be provided with the necessary General and Subaltern Officers: The Infantry shall be held in a Condition to march, for the Service of his Britannic Majesty, Two Months after the Requisition shall have been made for that Purpose, or sooner, if possible, elpccialiy if it should be for the immediate Defence of the Kingdoms or Electoral Dominions of his Majesty, or of the Low Countries , in which Cafe, the said lntantry shall march immediately

Article 5.

Towards defraying the Expences to which the most Serene Jundgrave will be engaged to remount and equip the said Corps of 8,000 Men, his Majesty the King of Great Britain promises to pay to his most Serene Highness, for every Trooper or Dragoon duly armed and mounted, 80 Crowns, and, for every Foot Soldier, 30 Crowns , in manner following; that is to say, the Moiety of the Levy-money for the Infantry and Artillery, amounting to 99,000 Crowns Banco, shall be paid at the Exchange of the Ratifications, and the Remainder for the Infantry and Artillery, when they shall march; and, with regard to the Cavalry, One Moiety of the Remount-money shall be paid when the Requisition shall be made to put the said Corps of 8,000 Men in a Condition to march, and the bther Moiety when the said Cavalry shall actually march.

Article 6.

Besides what is stipulated in the preceding Article, his Majesty the King of Great Britain engages to pay the most Serene Landgrave, during the time that this Treaty shall last, an annual Subsidy, in the Manner and Proportion following; that is to (ay, this Subsidy shall commence from the Day of the Signing of this Treaty, and for the Time which shall elaple from that Day to the Time of the Requisition to pot them in a Condition to march, shall be paid at the Rate of 150,000 Crowns Banco per Annum, the Crown reckoned at 53 Sols of Holland, or at and 9%d. English Money, from the said Time of making the Requisition to the Day when the whole Body, as well Cavalry as Infantry, shall be in the Pay of the Crown of Great Britain, the Subsidy shall be augmented and paid at the Rate of 300,000 Crowns aforesaid; and, during the whole time that the said Corps shall be actually in the Pay of his Majesty, the most Serene Landgrave shall enjoy aa annual Subsidy of 150,000 Crowns aforesaid. When the said Troops shall be sent back by his Britannic Majesty, from the Day of their Return into the Territories of his most Serene Highness, until the Expiration of the Treaty, the Subsidy shall be again raised and continued on the Foot of 300,000 Crowns aforesaid per Antitm; and the Payment of this respective Subsidy shall be made regularly, without Diminution, and quarterly, in the City of Cajjtl, into the military Chestof the most Selene Landgrave, authorized for the Receipt thereof.

Article 7.

With regard to the Pay and Treatment, as well ordinary as extraordinary, of the said Troops, whilst they shall be actually in the Pay of Great Britain, it is agreed, that, as long as they serve in the Empire, they shall enjoy the same Advantages and Emoluments in every thing as his Majesty allows to his German Troops, according to the

Article 8.

If itlhoufd happen unfortunately, that any Regiments or Companies of the above-mentioned Corps Ihwuld be ruined or destroyed, in the Whole or in Part, or that the Pieces of Cannon, with which they shall be furnished, should be taken by the Enemy, his Majesty the King of Great Britain shall cause to be paid the Expences of the necessary recruiting and remounting the m; ns also the Value of the said Field Pieces, in order forthwith to re-instate the Artillery, and the said Regiments or Companies; and the said Recruiting and Remounting, shall be regulated likewise on the Foot of what was furnished to the Htjian Officers by virtue of the Treaty of 1702,

Article 5th; to the end that this Corps may be always preferred, and sent back one Day in as good a State as it was delivered in.

Article 9.

His Britannic Majesty shall be at Liberty to keep this Body of Troops in his Service the whole Time of the Duration of this Treaty, and to employ it whereibver he shall have Occasion for it, provided it be not on board the Fleet or beyond ihe S a, when once it has departed out of the Territories of the most Serene Landgrave, excepting always for the Defence of Great and Ireland-, in w'hich Cafe, these Troops shall eim y fully, and without any Restriction whatevtr, the same Pay and Emoluments as the English Troops enjoy, as has been said above; and when his Majesty the Kngof Great Britain shall think fit to fend back the said Troops, he shall give Notice thereof to his most Serene Highness Three Months before-hand, and shall cause to be paid to them One Month’s Pay for their Return, and iurnish them gratis the necessary Transport Vessels.

Article 10.

In case the most Serene Landgrave should be attacked or disturbed in the Possession of his States, his Britannic Majesty p romifes and engages to fend back to him speedily the said Body of Troops, not only paying them a Month’s Pay, but allb furnishing them gratis the Transport Vessels requisite for their Returnand to give moreover to his most Serene Highness all the Succour of Troops which the same shall require; which Succour shall be continued to him until he mall have obtained an intire Security and just Indemnification; and the most Serene Landgrave promises, in like manner, on his Part, that, in case his Majesty the King of Great Britain is attacked or disturbed in his Dominions, Estates, Lands, Provinces, or Towns, he will also yield him all the Succour that it shall be in his Power to give him; which Succour shall in like manner be continued to him, until he shall have obtained a good and advantageous Peace.

Article 11.

In order to render this Alliance and Union the more perfect, and to leave no Doubt with the Parties about the Certainty of the Succour which they may expect by virtue of this Treaty, it is expressly agreed, that, to judge for the future whether the same of this Alliance and Succour exists or not, it shall suffice that either of the Parties are actually attacked by Force of Arms, without his having fitft used open Force against him who attacks him.

In Support of the Allegations of the first and fetond-mentioned Petitions,

The reverend Mr. Neale said. That the Lands comprised in the said Petitions amount to upwards of 40,000 Acres, the greatest Part of which is overflowed with Water, and in the Summer Season great Part of the said Lands are drowned; and that the whole Lands at present are of very little Benefit to the Proprietors:

That he apprehends they are capable of being drained and thereby greatly improved; but that the necessary Works for draining the fame, and for the Preservation of the said Lands when drained, cannot be carried into Execution without the Assistance of Parliament.

Henry Morley Esquire confirmed Mr. Neale's Evidence; and added, That several Persons, experienced in Works of Draining, have given it as their Opinion, that the said Lands are capable of being drained.

In relation to the Two last mentioned Petitions,

Mr. Benjamin Woodward, Registerto the said Corporation, laid before your Committee a Schedule of Lands vested in the said Corporation, lying within the aforesaid Ddtricts proposed to be drained; and by the said Schedule it appeared, that the Wholeof the said invested Lands amount to 9,405 Acres, and the Produce thereof for the Year 1754 amounted only to the Sum of £. 24. 4J.; and he (did, that it would be for the Benefit of the said Corporation, if the said invested Lands were fold.

And he also produced Articles of Agreement, dated 2:d of May 1755, by which it appeared, that the Corporation had agreed with Matthew Robinf Esquire,

for the Sale of Part of the said invested Lands lying within the said Great Level, between the Rivers of the Hundred Foot and the Ouze.

And by an Entry in the Corporation Book of Order, it appeared, that at a Court held at the Fen Office the xi th Day of this Instant December, the said Court did resolve to accept the Proposals of the Duke of Bedford, and others, for the Purchase of the Rifidue of the said invested Lands lying within the said Distrust.

And several Members present informed your Committee, That moil of the said invested Lands intended to be sold are at present overflowed with Water, and are of little or no Value.

a former Prebendary whereof, in the Reign of Queen Elizabeth, demised the same amongst other Lands, for a long Term of Years (many of which are yet to come), to the Mayor, Commonalty, and Citizens, of the City of London, who, by Lease bearing Date the 6th Day of July 1705, demised the same (among other Things) to one William Jennens, fora Term of Fifty-two Years, from Chrifmas 1712, at the yearly Rent ot£. no; and that the Petitioners Sir Atwill Lake&nd bibye Lake, by virtue of mesne Alignments, are become intitled thereto for the Remainder of the said Term;and that the said private Way being kept in very good Repair at the Expence of the Petitioner John Witton, their Lessee, a 1 mall pecuniary Satisfaction is taken by him for Horses, Carts, and Carriages, parting that Way at tLie Dog House Bar at the End thereof, leading into Old Street aforesaid; and that there are already Two other Roads maintained and kept in good Repair at the Expence of the Parishes in which the same lie, through which, Horses, Carts, and Carriages, conveniently mis from the Center of the City of London, through Moor-gate, into the Old Street, Ntiv Market, and great Northern Roads; and that if the Trustees of the said Turnpike should be enabled to lay open and widen the kid Road leading from the Red Lion, through the Dog Bar, it will greatly a fie ft the Property of the Petitioners, who have been at great Expence in repairing the said Road, and have paid large Sums of Money as a Consideration for the fame: And therefore praying the House, That the Petitioners may be at Liberty to be heard, by themselves, or Counsel, against the said Bill, or such Part thereof as affects the Interest of the Petitioners, and that they may be relieved in the Premises in such manner as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed: And that the Petitioners be heard, by themselves, or their Co unfel, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same rime, in favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the Town of bury, in the County of Salop, whose Names a;e thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and other the Inhabitants of the said Town* was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Streets and Lancs within the said Town are so numerous and extensive, and the Pavements thereof so torn and broken up, that they' cannot, by the Laws now in being, be kept in any tolerable Order and Condition; and that the Mayor and Corporation have usually applied the Sum of Thirty Pounds annually, out of their general Stock or Income, towards the Repair thereof; and are for the future willing to apply the Sum of Forty-five Pounds yearly for the same Purpose; but even that Sum will not be sufficient to put and keep the said Streets and Lanes in such good Order and Repair as they ought to be kept; and that the cleaning and enlightening of the said Streets and Lanes, and keeping of a well-regulated Watch within the said Town, would be of great Use and Importance, and tend to the Suppression of many Disorders therein, and to the Preservation of the Persons and Properties of the Inhabitants thereof, and all others relorting the reto: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to enable and oblige the Mayor and Corporation of the said Town of Shrewsbury to pay and apply the Sum of Forty-five Pounds yearly, out of their general Stock and Revenues, towards the Repair of the Streetsand Lanes within the said Town; and also to enable the Mayor and Justices of the Peace of the Laid Town, and Liberties thereof, in Conjunction with the principal Inhabitants in each Parish within the said Town, to order the further and better repairing of the said Streets and Lanes, and the cleaning and enlightening of the fame, and to appoint a Watch, at such Times, and in such Manner, as the House shall think proper; and that the Money to be raised for the Purposes aforesaid, over and above the said yearly Sum of Forty-five Pounds, may be raised by a Rate to be made upon the Inhabitants of such Part of the said Town, and Suburbs thereof, as shall receive Benefit thereby, or by such other Ways and Means, or in such other Manner, as the House shall think fit.

A Petition of Richard Hughes was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, in the 23d Year of his Majesty’s Reign, an Act was made for erecting a free Market for the Sale of Fish in the City of -

Jter, and a Piece of Ground near Cannon Row was thereby allotted for the said Market; and that the Petitioner did, in April 1753, among many others, deliver to the

Trustees for carrying the Act into Execution a Proposal, in Writing, for taking such Ground, and building Houses and Shops thereon; which Proposal was accepted; pursuant to which, the Petitioner erected on the said Ground Eight good and substantial Brick Houses, according to the Directions of the Surveyor to the Trustees, and got the same covered in by Christmas 1753, at the Expence of upwards of £.i, Soo.; and, reciting a Clause in a Lease granted to the Petitioner by the said Trustees, after the Houses were covered in; by which Clausethe Petitioner is restrained from permitting any Person to inhabit or occupy any House, Shop, or Building, which is or shall be erected upon any Part of the Premises, who shall exercise or carry on therein, or on any Part thereof, any Occupation or Bu-liness other than buying and selling of Fish; in which Clause the Petitioner was obliged to acquiesce, the Trustees being of Opinion, that they were not authorized by the Act to grant a Lease without a Covenant of this Kind; and alleging, that the Petitioner has laid out the greatest Part of his Fortune in erecting these Houses, and fitting Six of them for Fishmongers, with Shops, and other Conveniences requisite for that Trade, according to the Covenants of his Lease; and the same have been completely finished a long time; and that the Petitioner has used all Means in his Power to let the Houses to Fishmongers, or Persons dealing in Fish, and, wtih great Difficulty, has got Two of the Houses let to Fishmongers; but they seem inclined to quit the fame; and that there is not the least: Appearance that ever the said Market will be established; which must prove the utter Ruin of the Petitioner and his Family, unless some Relief is speedily granted: And therefore praying the House to take the same of the Petitioner into Consideration, and to grant him such Relief as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Orders of this House to the Constables of Middlesex and Westminster, to keep the Passages through the Streets between Temple Bar and Westminster Hall free and open, and to prevent Gaming, and other Dilbrders, in Westminster Hall, and the Passages leading to the House, are not duly executed.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the same is chiefly owing to the Want of asufficient Number of Constables in Wthere being but Thirty-leven aAing Constables in the several Parishes thereof; whereas Fifty-four are the usual Complement;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Want of Constables in Westminster is owing to the Rufufal of many Persons to take upon them the said Office, after being appointed thereto; there being some DefeA or Irregularity in the said Appointment which ought to be remedied.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards railing the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Sum of One million Five hundred thousand Pounds be raised by Annuities at Three Pounds Ten Shillings per Centum per Annum, and the Sum of Five hundred thousand Pounds by a Lottery, to be attended with Annuities redeemable by Parliament, after the Rate of Three Pounds per Centum per Annum, the said several Annuities to be transferable at the Bank of England, and charged on the Sinking Fund; and that every Person subscribing for Four hundred Pounds shall be entitled to Three hundred Pounds in Annuities, and to One hundred Pounds in Lottery Tickets, and so in proportion for a greater or lesser Sum; That the said Lottery shall consist of Tickets of the Value of Ten Pounds each, in a Proportion not exceeding Eight Blanks to a Prize, the Blanks to be of the Value of Six Pounds each; the Blanks and Prizes to bear an Interest after the Rate of Three Pounds per Centum per Annum, to commence from the Fifth Day of January 1757; and that the Sum of One million Five hundred thousand Pounds, to be raised by Annuities, bear an ln-terest after the Rate of Three Pounds Ten Shillings per Centum per Annum, from the nth Day of February next; which said Annuities shall be redeemable in the Whole or in Part by Sums not iefs than Five hundred thousand Pounds at one time, after the Expiration of Fifteen Years, and not sooner, Six Months Notice having been given of such Payment or Payments respectively: That any Sub-feriber may, on or before Wednesday the nth Day of February next, at Five of the Clock in the Afternoon, make a Deposit of Ten Pounds per Centum on such Sum as he shall chule to subscribe towards raising the said Sum of Two millions, with the Cashiers of the Bank of England, as a Security for his making the future Payments on the Days herein alter appointed; viz.

On Annuities.

Fifteen PoundsCent. on or before the 30th Day of March next.

Twenty Pounds per Cent, on or before the 15th Day of May next.

Twenty Pounds per Cent. on or before the 16th Day of July next.

Twenty Pounds per Cent. on cr before the x 6th Day of September next.

Fifteen Pounds per Cent. on or before the 30th Day of October next.

On the Lottery.

Twenty Pounds pe> Cent, on or before the ead Day of April next.

Twenty Pounds per Cent, on or before the 161h Day of June next.

Twenty-five Pounds perCent. on or before the 14th Day of August next.

Twenty-five Pounds per Cent. on or before the 20th Day of October next.

Which several Sums, so received, shall be by the said Cashiers paid into the Receipt of the Exchequer, to be applied from time to time to such Services as shall then have been voted by this House in this Session of Parliament, and not otherwise: That any Subscriber paying in the Whole or any Part of his Subscription previous to the Days appointed for the respective Payments, shall be allowed a Discount after the Rate of Three Pounds per Centum per Annum, from the Days of such respective Payment to the respective Times on which such Payments are directed to be made; and that all such Persons, as shall make their full Payments on the said Lottery, shall have their Tickets delivered as soon as they can conveniently be made out: That the Lottery shall be drawn for Five hundred thousand Pounds, or for such lesser Sum as shall be subscribed by the 1 ith Day of February next; and in case there shall be more than Two millions subscribed on or before the Twenty-eighth Day of this inllant January, at Five o’Clock in the Afternoon, the Sum fub-5 K feribed

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Sir Peter ThcmpjonKnight, being examined, said, That

lie has known the Town of Poole Fifty Years: That it carries on a great Trade to Newfoundland, and other Places, and employs Two hundred Sail cf Ships: That he has paid the Duties of Quayage and Wharfage for his own Goods; and that it has been the Custom of Merchants importing and exporting Goods, to pay those Duties, which have always been under the Management of tIre Mayor and Corporation; and that he believed fm all Sums have been paid for Boo mage: That it has been the general Reputation that those Duties had been paid Time immemorial:

That some Persons have lately refused to pay those Duties; and, on a Trial at Law, the Town was non-doited, by the Town's People not being allowed to be Evidence; and that the Payment ot those Duties has been lincc discontinued:

That the little Quay has fallen down into the Harbour, and the great Quay in great Danger of tailing.

Mr. William Milner, being examined, laid, That the Town of Poole is a Place of great Trade; and that it has

Two Quays, one called the , the other the Great Quay: That a contidcrable Part of the Little Quay has fallen into the Harbour, and the Great Quay in a very ruinous Condition, every Pile being almost rotted away: That lie apprehended it would cost near One thousand Pounds to put these Two Quays into Repair:

That he has d'een the Duties paid for Quayage, Wharfage, Boomage, and Ballast, which were paid to, and under the Management of, the Mayor and Corporation:

That the Chanels leading to the Harbour are choaked up: That the Chanel, through which all Ships mull pais to deliver at the d own, is tilled with Mud; and that many Ships have lluck there: That there will be no Landing of Goods at the Town, if these Channels arc not cleansed: That the Mayor always directed the Repair of this Harbour, and defrayed the Charge out of the Money collected by Receipt of these Duties; and that it is the Opinion of every body, that the Town had, Time immemorial, received those Duties for the Repair of the Quays and Harbour:

Sir Peter Phompfon, being further examined, said, That

it has been customary to lcour the Channels leading to the Harbour in a certain Number of Years: That, at present, they want cleansing very much; and that the Charge of scouring (he Channels was defrayed out of the Duties collected for Quayage and Wharfage; and that, as he apprehends the Discontinuance of the Payment of those Duties is the Keaton the Channels are not cleanled.

Then an Inquisition of the 12th of May, in the 15th Year of Edward the Third, was produced to your Committee, directed to the Elchester of the County of Dorset, and other Counties, to inquire into the Right claimed in behaltof the Town of Poole to the Duties ot Careenage, and other Duties arising from Merchandize and other Goods brought into the Town of Poole.

By the Return to which Inquisition, on the 7th of June, in the 15th Year of Edward the Third, it appeared, upon the Oath of the Enquirers, that, for Time immemorial, the Town of Poole was entitled to Two Pence for Anchorage and Two Pence for Careenage, and to particular Sums therein mentioned, for Merchandize and other Goods therein particularly described.

Mr. William Milner, being further examined, said, That it is necessary to have a nightly Watch: That there are many public and private Warehouses, wherein arc contained great Quantities of Goods and Merchandize; and that many Houses have been broke open; and that if a Fire was to happen at low Water, it might destroy most of the Shipping and Craft lying at the Wharf:

Act Mr. Godolphin reported from the Committee, to whom relating to the Petition of the Members of the Council, and other Quarantine. pr|ncjpai Inhabitants, of the Island* of Scilly, whose Names are thereunto subsenbed, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition ;and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, together with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the tame was read; and is as followeth;

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

The Agent for the Petitioners produced an Act, made in the 26th Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, whereby it appeared, that all Vessels being to the Northward of Cape Finisterre, which shall appear to have the Plague on board, shall immediately proceed to the Harbour of New Grimsby, in the Islands of Scilly, and remain there tHl his Majesty’s Pleasure shall be known; and every Commander, who shall not comply with this Regulation, shall suffer Death: And,

Captain Shepherd, being examined, fiid. That he is well acquainted with the Scilly Islands: That the Harbour of NeivGrimsby is not more than Four hundred Yards wide, and lies between the Islands of Trejco and Bryer, which are both well inhabited, and that great Numbers of homeward-bound Ships put in there; and that if an infected Ship should put into this Harbour, it would be extremely dangerous:

That the Harbour of St. Helens Pool lies between Three uninhabited Islands-.That Ships may lie there with great Safety.- That there is Plenty of freth Water in these Islands, and convenient Places for airing any Goods without the least Danger of Infection; and that it is as eafv to give notice of the Arrival of any Vessel from this i I arbour as trom New Grimsby.

Mr. Gilbert Douglas confirmed the Evidence given by Captain Shepherd; and said, that there are about 300 Inhabitants in the Island df Trejco, and above 200 in the Island of Bryer — That he has seen between 50 and 60

Ships at a time in the Harbour of New Grimsby, and at tome times (as he has been informed) there are more:

That there is a good Harbour at St. Helens, and a Baton that will hold Three or Four large Ships.

20

Upon the whole Matter, your Committee came to the following Resolutions;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Harbour of New Grimsby, in the Islands of Scilly, is an improper and dangerous Place for the Reception of Ships and Vessels infected with the Plague, by reason that the same lies between the Islands of Trejco and Bryer, both fully inhabited.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Harbour called St.Helen's Pool, in the Islands of Scilly, is a safe and commodious 1 larbour for the Reception of Ships and Vessels; and being situate between Three uninhabited Islands, is a mere proper Place for the stationing of Ships infected with the Plugue, than the Harbour of New Grimsby.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the House be moved for Leave to bring in a Bill te explain and amend a Clause in an Act made in the 26th Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act to oblige Ships more effectually to perform their Quarantine, and for the better preventing the Plague being brought from foreign Parts into Great Britain ox Ireland, or the Isles of Guernsey, Jersey, Alderney, Sark, or Man, whereby the stationing of Ships infected with the Plague, to the Northward of Cape Finisterre, is confined to the Harbour of New Grimsby, and removeable to no other Place.

The Two First Resolutions of the Committee, being severally read a Second time, wer^, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to explain and amend a Claute in an Act, made in the 26th Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act to oblige Ships more effectually to perform their Quarantine, and for the better preventing the Plague being brought from foreign Parts into Great Britain or Ireland, or the Isles of Guernsey, jersey, Alderney, Sark, or Man And that Mr. Godolphin and Mr. Clevland, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

In Support of the Allegations of the said Petitions,

An Act of Parliament, made in the 5th Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, and also an Act made in the 1 ith Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, and also an Act made in the 18th Year of his present Majesty, were read, by which Acts le-vcral Tolls and Powers were granted and continued, from the Expiration of the Term granted by the said Act of the nth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, for the further Term of 2 1 Years, for the Repairs of the Highways between Sheppards Shord and the Devizes, and between the Top of Ashlington Hill and Rowd Ford\ in the County of Wills.

Mr. Charles Garth, Mr. Edmund Nice, said, That the said Roads cannot be sufficiently amended, and the Money due upon the Credit of the said Acts repaid, unless the said Term and Powers are further continued: And Mr. Nice laid, That the Sum of £. 2,000 has been borrowed by the Trustees towards the Reparation of the said Roads.

In regard to the Method of railing Money for cleansing the Streets,

The Witness said, That the Inhabitants of the high Street meet once a Year in the Vestry, and chuse Two of their own Body to be Scavengers; then they adjourn to a public House, spend £. 7 or £. 8, and make a Rate upon the Inhabitants of 6d. in the Pound, which they collect, but never account for, and at the End of the Year put the Surplus in their own Pockets.

Joseph Bound, Surveyor for the Year 1755, said, That he had found great Difficulty in collecting the Rates: That a great many Gentlemen would not pay a Farthing: That he has not collected^. 50, and ought to have col-ledted above £. 150.

Mr. John Christian informed your Committee, That he is well acquainted with the Harbour, and the Proceedings of the 1 ruftecs in regard to the same:

1 hat/. 2,000 has been borrowedand applied according to the Directions of the said Act, which has been a great Advantage to the I own in the Increase of their Trade: That upwards of/. 1 j,oooo. has been laid out in build-

ing of Houses ih Ellenfoot, within the Six Years last past:

That an Iron Furnace is fiftished in the said Town, where great Quantities oflron are fmeked, and a Glats-house is erected there.

That a common Brewery is begun, and a Paper Mill, Pottery, and Ropery, are set up there, and a considerable Herring Fishery carried on from the said Town, to the Increase of Seamen, the Benefit of the adjacent Country, and the Public:

That the Trade of the said Town and the Harbour Duties have greatly increased:

That the Witness hitnfelfhasa Colliery, which, before the patting of the late Ad, was not worth above /. 200 a Year, and now brings him in /. 800. a Year; and that the Trade and Duties will be still greater when the Waggon Way, which is already begun, shall be finished: That it will be necessary to build Two Stone Quays, which will amount the one to /. 128, and the o'hcr 10 /. 224. in order to make the Harbour commodious: and that Contracts have been made by the Commissioners for that Purpose, as well as for deepening the Harbour, on which Works the Commissioners have already expended Sixty-two Pounds, and are under Contract to pay the further Sum of/. 200. and upwards:

That there is the greatest Reason to believe that the Harbour Duties will still continue to increase, as in the Year 1749 they amounted only to/.22 2 and in the

Year 1754 to/. 189 is. $J.and the Increase will be still larger when tire Waggon Way is complete:

That it will require a much larger Sum to complete the Works already begun, and make the Harbour Lie and commodious, than can be raised within the Term for which the present Duties are granted; and that it will be necessary to restrain Buildings within a certain Space of the Harbour for the Convenience of the Quays and Wharfs, to which Humphrey Esquire, the Pro-

prietor of the Ground, has given his Content, and that several further Regulations and Provisions are necessary for the Convenience of the Trade carried on in the said Harbour.

Sandys reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Mayor, Burgesses, and Commonalty, of the City of Bristol, under their Common Seal, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is ns tolioweth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

The Act made in the last Session, for establ idling, maintaining, and well governing, a nightly Watch within the City of Bristol, was read: And,

Mr. Elton, being examined, laid. That some Doubts have arisen upon the Construction of one of the Claulls in the said Act, whether Power is thereby given to levy Money, for the Purposes of the said Act, upon Meadow and Pasture Lands lying within the Liberties of the said City.

And he observed to your Committee, That some further Provisions may be necessary for the more effectual carrying the said Act: into Execution, and to render the same sufficient for answering the good Purposes intended thereby.

And that some Difficulties have arisen upon the Direction in the said Act: for rating Lands and Persons according to their Abilities:

That it has been thought reasonable that the Watchmen Vol. 27.

Februarii. 425

to be appointed by the said Acc should be limited to a certain Number, except in Cafes of Riots and Tumults:

That the Power given by the said Act, of committing to Prison Coiledors or Constables refuting to account far or pay the Monies in their Hands, without Bail or iM.un-prize, has been thought inconvenient: And,

That the Power of committing Persons, refusing or neglecting to pay the Rates, to the House of Correction, for want of Distreis, hath been found unnecessary.

And it appearing by several Clauses in an Act: made in the 22d Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, " For " making more effectual an Act: passed in the nth and " 12th Years of the Reign of King William the Third, " for the better preserving the Navigation of the Rivers "Avon and Frvome, and for cleansing, paving, and en-

Mr. Elton observed to your Committee, That it hath been thought reasonable that the fimelhouk! be made liable to the Assessinonts made in virtue of the ibid Act of the last Session, or of the Bill, now depending in the House, to explain, amend, and render more effectual, the said Act of the last Session.

And he further observed, that a Power vested in the Justices of the said City, in their Sessions, to hear and determine Appeals, will be sufficient to answer the Purposes of the said Act of last Session.

By an Account of the Receipts and Disbursements of the said Corporation, from the 15th of April 1754 to the 25th of April 1755, produced to your Committee, and properly vouched and authenticated, it appeared, that the said Sum of £. 1,800 had been raised by the Sale of Taxes in the North Level, pumant to the Directions of the said Act; and by Eighteen Bonds for £.100 each, paid off by the said Corporation, and produced likewise to your Committee, it appeared, that the said Sum of £. i,8go had been applied in discharging so much of the remaining Debt.

And it appearing by the said in Part recited Act, that the Reiidueof the said Debt of£.49,153. nr. 9d. (till remaining due, is become a Charge upon the said Middle and South Levels only, the Agent for the Petitioners ob-served, that as the Money so due is secured by Bonds under the Seal of the said Corporation, entered into before the making of the said Act, it is necessary to exchange the said Bonds, and to mention in the new Bonds, to be given in lieu thereof, that the Money secured thereby is due from the said Middle and South Levels only; and it also appearing by the said Act, that the said North Level is not to be chargeable with the Payment of any Money to be hereafter borrowed upon account of the said Middle and South Levels; and that the said Middle and South Levels are not to be chargeable with the Payment of any Money to be hereafter borrowed upon account of the said North Level, the Agent for the Petitioners further observed, that it is become necessary to distinguish in all Bonds, to be entered into for the tuturc by the said Corporation, whether the Money so borrowed be upon ac-

Mr. Benjamin Pujolis and Robert Anflen Esquire, being severally examined, said. That they arc well acquainted with the Bedford Level, and have known Accidents happen frequently by the breaking down of Banks, whereby the Country has been overflowed, and that such Breaches muff occasion great Expences: That the North Level is as much or more liable to Accidents as the South and Middle Levels, and they particularly mentioned, that the Banks of Mortem'sLeant: are frequently walked down, which have occasioned great extraordinary Expences.

Mr. Mantling, Deputy Regitrer to the Corporation, said, That he, having inspeifted the Books of the Corporation, apprehend', that the Revenues are not sufficient to answer any extraordinary Expences which have happened, or which may happen, for the future, without some further Provision is made to enable them to borrow such further Sums as may be necessary for extraordinary Expences: And also laid, That he has heard it objected by everal of the Creditors, that the funds for securing the Debts of the Corporation are not sufficiently ascertained.

L;ncn Ma- The House, according to Order, proceeded to take into nuMurei. Considerationthe Report from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to considerof the State of the Linen Manufactures of Great Britain and Ireland.

And the Ref dutions of the said Committee were read j and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it is proper, for the Encouragement of the and

Irish Linen Manufactures, that a Bounty be allowed upon the Export at ion of British and Irish coarle Linens from this Kingdom, of One Halfpenny for every Yard of such Linens as shall be under the Value of Five Pence per Yard, and of One Penny for every Yard of such Linens of the Value of Five Pence per Yard, and under the Value of Six

Pence per Yard; and of One Penny Halfpcny for every Yard of such Linem ul the Value of S;x Pence Yard, and not exceeding the Value of One Shilling and Six Pence per Yard.

Resolved, That is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Bounty be paid out of any Monies arising from any of the Duties and Revenues under the Management of the Commissioners of the Customs in England and Scotland.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it is proper, in order to enable the Linen Manufacturers of Great Britain and Ireland to work up their Manufactures with more Advantage, that the Duties, now payable upon the Importation of foreign raw or brown Linen Yarns, and Ipruce or MtfcYarns, be taken off.

To prove the Allegations contained in the said Petitions,

John Quinehant Esquire, informed your Committee,

That he knows the Town of Shrewsbury: That it is large and populous, and considerable Business is carried on therein: That the Assizes, and many Fairs are yearly kept and held there: That many Coal Carriages pass and re-pass through the said Town: That many Gentry reside there in the Winter Season: That the Streets and Lanes are very numerous, and the Pavements very bad, and cannot be repaired by the ordinary Course of Law:

That the Corporation of the said Town have hitherto annually expended £.$o per Annum, towards the Repair thereof; and are now willing to allow 45 for the same Purpose; but that will not be sufficient to put and keep the said Streets in proper Repair.

And he further added, that cleaning and enlightening the said Streets and Lanes, and keeping a well-regulated Watch within the said Town of Shrewsbury, would be of great Use and Importance, and tend to the Suppression of many Disorders therein, and to the Preservation of the Pe rfons and Properties of the Inhabitants thereof, and of all others resorting thereto.

Mr. John Roberts being examined, confirmed the foregoing Evidence.

Blackfriare A Petition of the Rulers, Auditors, and Assistants, of Bridge, the Company of Watermen, Wherrymen, and Lightermen, of the River Thames, was presented to the House, and read; alleging. That if a Bridge is built cross the River Thames, from Black Fryars, in the City of London, to the opposite Shore in the County of Surety, the Navigation of the said River will be greatly obstructed, and rendered very inconvenient, and inlome Cafes dangerous, and will highly prejudice the Members of the said Company, by totally destroying the several Sunday Ferries between Westminster Bridge and London Brwhich were

established by an Act made in the 1 ithand 12th Years of the Reign of King William the Third; and the Profits thereof were, by the same Act, appropriated to the Relief of the poor, aged, and decayedWatermen, and Lightermen, and their Widows and Children, who, for want of such Relief, mud become burthensome to their respective Parishes; and that many Hundreds of Watermen, who are able and willing to work, will be also deprived of their daily Support, by conveying Passengers and Goods upon the said River, and may be reduced by Necessity to seek their Bread in foreign Parts; and a veryconsiderable Nursery for Seamen will be greatly prejudiced: And therefore praying the House to take this same into their Consideration, and to do therein as they shall think proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of London, in Common Council assembled, is referred; And that they do examine the Matter of this Petition; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

The said Report is as followeth; viz.

The Copy 01 the preliminary Articles between Great Britain, France, and Holland, ligned at Aix la referred to your Committee, were read, which appear to be dated the 30 th of April 1748, which was the 19th of April

1748,0 S. by the 16th Article whereof it appeared, that the Cessation of Hostilities between all the Parties at War was to take place by Land within Six Weeks, to be reckoned from the Day of signing of the said Articles; and that the Terms and Spaces of Time fixed in the Act of Suspension of Arms between England and France, ligned at Paris the 19th of August 171a, should be followed by Sea.

And it appeared by the Declaration ligned the 8th of July 1748, at Aix la Chapelle, by the Plenipotentiaries of his Britannic Majesty, his most Christian Majesty, and of the Lords the States General of the United Provinces, that the Cessation of the Hostilities was to take place as far as Cape St. Vincent, and beyond the said Cape to the Equinoctial Line, whether in the Ocean or Mediterranean, within Six Weeks from the Date of the said preliminary Articles, and consequently that Hostilities were to cease on the 31st of May 1748, O. S. or the nth of June,

Captain Nicholas Newton informed your Committee, That he commanded the Land Forces under Admiral Knowles in September 1748: That he was on board the Tilbury: That he remembers the taking of the Polacra about the 3d of September: That the Money was put in Proportions on board the several Ships-: That he received his Share, amounting to about 40 Piflolcs, from the Hands of Captain Pow/elt, before the taking the Conquesta-dere: That he never had any further Payment, though he returned with the Squadron to Jamaica, and that lie cannot remember that he made any further Demand.

David Brodie Esquire, being examined, said, That he was Captain of the Strafford, and failed under the Command of Vice Admiral Knozvles from Jamaica, about the 16th of August 1748, in consequenceof Orders from the Admiralty to continue Hostilities with Spain: That the 3d of September following the y took the Polacra Anna Maria y 67. Felix: That the Day following it was agreed by a General Council of the Officers of the Squadron, that it was for the Good of the Service todeltroy her, as they found by the Chace that Hie was a heavy sailer, and were apprehensive that she might fall into the Hands of the Enemy, and give Information of their Strength, which was judged at that time inferior to the Enemy, as the Warwick had not yet joined the vSquadron: Accordingly it was ordered, that the Money and other Effects should be taken out of the Prize, and divided according to the Rates of the different Ships, as near as might be calculated, that some Part of the Treasure might be preserved in case of an Accident happening to any of the Ships: That accordingly the Money was counted, and nailed up in different Boxes, and delivered to the Captains, who were to be accountable for their own, their Officers, and Companies, Shares:

That in cruising off the Havannah, the 5th or 6th of OElcber, they took an Advice Boat, which had failed from Cadiz Six Weeks before, who had a Pals on board from the Regency of England, by which they were informed of the Cessation of Arms: Afterwards some Letters passed between the Spanifk Governor, the Spanish Admiral, and Admiral Knowles: The next Da) r it was agreed that there should be a Restitution of Prisoners on both Sides: That the Day following all the Prisoners were font on Shore: That he was by when Admiral Knowles gave Directions that the Mailer, and Two others belonging to the Polacra, ftiouid be detained onboard, and carried to Jamaica: That thereupon the said Mailer carnally begged to be let on Shore at the Havannah, as he might more readily get to Old Spain from thence; whereas it he was carried to Jamaicay lie might not perhaps get home in less than a Year: That he wFas well informed by the People belonging to the Advice Sleep, that Prizes taken antecedent to September the 2Sth were just and legal Captures and there-

fore, as he had no claim to make for Restitution of his Refotutioa Efle&s, it would be cruel to carry him so far out of his s ° Way: That accordingly he and the other Two were permitted to go on Shore:

That about the Middle of November authentic Orders came from the Admiralty for a Cessation of Hostilities with Spain: That no Proclamation was delivered to him, nor did he know of any being delivered to the other Captains: That he never saw any Proclamation pofled up in any public Place, though he continued there till the Middle of April: That the EITefls were begun tobedif-tributed by the Witness, on board the Strafford, to those Persons of the Ship’s Complement who were ordered to be reduced, and lent home, by Orders from the Admiralty to reduce the Complements of the Ships of their Squadron to the Peace Establishment: That those Sailors who were to go away became clamorous for their Prize Money, and that this Distribution was made alter tliQ Monition, but before Condemnation:

That he did not receive any Orders from Admiral Knowles for that Distribution, who,'he apprehended, had no right to give Orders concerning the Money.

Mr. reported from the Committee, to whom the

Petition of those whole Names are thereunto subscribed, being several of the principal Inhabitants of the Parish of Clirow, and other Parishes lying. near, thereto, in the VoL.

County of Radnor, and also of the Town of , and other Parishes lying near thereto, in the County of Brecon; and also the Petition of those whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being several of the principal Inhabitants of the Town of Hay, and other Parishes lying near thereto, in the County of Brecon; and allb of the Parjlh of Clirow, and of other Parishes lying near thereto, in the County of Radnor; were referted, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petitions; and had directed him to report the lame, as it appeared to them, to the House , and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s 'Fable: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petitions,

Mr. James Price, being examined, said, That he knows the Fold through the River Wye, betwixt the Town of Hay, in the County of Brecon, and the high Road on the opposite Shore, in the County of That the Passage of the said Ford is very dangerous; and he knows that many People have been drowned in attempting to pals,; ancf that there is no Bridge between Glasbury and Hereford, which is above Twenty Miles:

That, about Eight Years ago, a Subscriotion was raised for building a Bridge across the said River, just above the said Ford; which, if carried into Execution, would be of great public Advantage; and that Part of Three Piers, and an Abutment, were raised, at about 300 Expence, which have been since much damaged by the Floods:

That be knows the Pay Boat belonging to Sir William Fozvler, which is about Haifa Mile above the Place where the Bridge is proposed to be built; and that the Lands on both Sides the high Road leading to the Ford on the Rad-norshire Side, are claimed by Sir William Fozvler Baronet; and that the Whole of the Fowlers Estate in Clirow Parish, or Neighbourhood, are about £. 135 per Annum; and, if the Bridge was built, he would, in a few Years, be glad to have those Estates at £. 40 per Annum Advance; and that £. 50 per Annum has been offered for the lame:

That the Town of Hay is a Market and a Poll Town, and is separated from the County of Radnor by the River Wye only; which, when the Water is high, cuts off all Communication for many Miles; at which Time it is dangerous passing the said River in the said Pay Boat: That Carriages do not usuallypafs in such Boat; nor can such Boat pals at any time in Safety, without the Use or a Rope fattened to the Poll on Mils s Land:

And he said, that, about Two Months ago, a Man was drowned in attempting to pass with the Boat:

That there are no Lime Kilns on the Radnorshire Side the River, within Ten Miles; and that he used to carry Lime from the Kilns near die River on the Brecknockshire Side, to his Lands at Clirow, through the Ford, till about Two Years ago, when the Ford became so dangerous, he avas obliged to desist; and that it is Eight Miles round to go over Glasbury Bridge, which is the nearest Passage.

Mr. John Pugh, being examined, said. That he has rented the Ferry Boat of Sir William Fowler 20 Years j and confirmed Mr. Price's Evidence of the Bridge being begun: And he added, that Sir William's Steward seemed to countenance the Work for the First Three Months; but then began to obstruift the Works; and the Witness went with the Steward, Mr. Richard Morgan, when he destroyed Part of the said Works, and forbid going on with the fame.

Mr. Thomas Lewis said, That when the Boat croflcs the said River to the Brecknockshire Side, Passengers are obliged to land upon, and go over, about 200 Yards of Mils Vaughan's Land: That the Sum of Two Guineas a Year has always been demanded, and paid, till very Jately, for putting up Polls on Mils s Lands, and suffer-

ing Passengers going over the said Land; but that the present Occupier of the Boat having refused to pay the said Two Guineas, the Polls necessary for fastening the Rope to navigate the Boat are taken away, without which it is very dangerous passing:

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

The Petitioners produced an Act made in the 22d Year of his present Majesty's Reign, for repairing the Read from H ansford to Stamford: And,

Mr. William Smith, Surveyor of the fuel Road, laid. The Tolls collected, and £. 1,500 which hath been borrowed on the Credit thereof, have been expended in repairing the said Roads: That the Money borrowed remains unpaid, and that Two Years Interest is due upon the same:

Mr. Stephen West (Engineer, and who has lately surveyed the Works of the said Harbour) laid before your Committfee an Account of the necessary Works, with an Estimate of the Expence thereof, to complete the said Harbour, in making it navigable to the Town of Rye, amounting to£.26,009. 3*. t and said, that he thinks the Harbour may be made to be of great Uie to Trade and Navigation, and that it may prevent many Accidents, as it will hold 150 Ships of 300 Tons Burthen each, and as many small ones as ever will come in at a time.

Mr. ‘Thomas Cooke, Treasurer to Rye Harbour, produced an Account of Money which he had received from the Receiver General of the Customs, towards the Repair of Rye Harbour, from ift May 1738 to the 12th of May last, which, communibut annis, during that Period, amounted to about £. 1,600 per Annum; and he said the Money which had been borrowed to carry on the Works of the said Harbour, amounting to about £. 11,000, was all paid off: That the Money belonging to the Harbour had not been diverted to any other Uses; and that the Accounts had been annually settled and pafl'ed pursuant to the Directions of the Acts of Parliament; but that the Works are now flopped for want of Money.
