Then a Report, which was made to the House upon the 12th Day of February 1699, relating to the Harbour of Dover: And also.

An Act made in the 1 rth and 1 zth Year of King William the Third, for the Repair of Dover Harbour, were !ea<i; whereby it appeared, that the said Harbour had been found to be of very great Benefit to Vessels passing

through the narrow Seas, to avoid the Dangers of Tempers and Enemies, and likewise convenient for small Ships of War to refit and clean in; but that the same was very much gone to Decay, and in great Danger of becoming totally useless; and therefore the said Act directed, that a Duty should be laid upon certain Ships and Vessels therein described, for raising a Sum of Money for repairing the said Harbour; and it appeared to your Committee, that the Terms and Powers by the said Act granted have been, by several subsequent Acts, further continued till the ift Day of May 1765: And,

Mr. William Packham, being examined, laid, That he has known Dover Harbour many Years, and that great Progress has been made in the Works there; and by an Estimate, which he laid before your Committee, it appears, that the further necessary Expences for putting the said Harbour into proper Repair will amount to £.24,077.

Captain ’John Baze/y, being called, said. That, upon examining the Haven Books, he finds, that, besides the Vessels and Pacquets belonging to Dover, 16,125 Strips have, by Slrefs of Weather, been driven into Dover Harbour within these Thirty Years last pad, several of them without Anchors or Cables; and he particularly mentioned, that in 1752 a Ship drawing 18 Foot Water came in therewith Eight Fool of Water in her Hold.

Mr. Davidson Flint, Master of the Pilots at Dover, confirmed the Evidence given by Captain Baze/y ;and added, that he has known Ships of 5 or 600 Tons Burthen come into the said Harbour, and that the same is capable of great Improvements: And Captain Baze/y, being again called, said, That the Bason in the said Haris 400 Feet from East to West, and 500 Feet from North to South, and that it would make a fine wet Dock for small Men of War — That there were about 300 Sail of Prize Ships in the Harbour at a time in the late War, and that there are near 60 Sail French Vessels there now.

And being asked the Question, he said, That if the new Road is made, it will be a Convenience to the Public, but he could give no Reason for it: That he did not know any Convenience it would be to the Proprietors of Lands; but that it would be the better for Cattle to be drove that Way to Smithfield, and that it will prejudice the Duke of Bedford’s Estate several Hundreds per Annum.

And being asked how far a House of £. too per Annum will be damaged ? he said, He could not (ay, it isimpoffible to guess; but that he believed a House of£. 100. per Annum would be reduced to Ninety Pounds., on account of the Dust from the new Road, and the Buijding thereon, and that it would be equally convenient to the Public to go round by Fig Lane: That the Mu-feum at Montagu House will beaflected with the Dust from the new Road, throughit is not so near as is: That Montagu House is nearer the Road which leads from St. Giles’s Pound that it will be to the new Road: It is about Two hundred Yards distant from tire old Road but that there are Houses built, which prevent in a great measure the Dust flying from that Road to Montagu House, but that it will be more affected by Two Roads than One: That the Dust from the new intended Road will not affect Mr. Lee’s or Mr. NoePs Houses in Bloomsbury Square; and that he has not heard any Complaints of the Mufeunn being prejudiced by the Dust from the old Road.

My Lord,

TAM informed of a Road intended to be made at the Back of your Grace’s Estate, which, from the Dull and Number of People, must intirely spoil those Fields, and make them no better than one common Land.

I most humbly intreat your Grace to prevent such an Evil, for it will be impossible for me to hold your Grace’s Estate without a large Abatement of Rent.

I am, with all Submission,

Your Grace’s most dutiful and obedient Servant,

In Support of the Second Petition, the Petitioners called Mr. John Taylor: Who laid, That the Price of Coals had rilen in Coventry of late Years: That those from Bedworth Pits used to be sold, at an Average, from to ${d. the Cwt. in the Winter Season, and loinetimes 6 d. in frofly Weather: That they are now fold for 6d. and have been at 8 d. this Winter: That the Colliers said, they raised them on Account of the Toll, and could fell them at the same Price at the Coal-yards: That, last Year, the Price was from 6 <7. to 7 and the Year before from 5 d. to 6 d.: That he apprehended, an additional Toll would enhance the Price of Coals, and the Burthen would fall chiefly on the poorer Sort of People, who cannot afford to buy them by Waggon Loads.

Beingafked, If the Colliers could not fell their Coals as cheap, if they were obliged to pay a Toll of a Penny a Hone, and the Roads good, as without paying any Toll, if they were to travel through bad Roads? he laid, They might, if they were reasonable People; but they would make the Toll a Pretence to raise the Price; and that it was the general Opinion at Co, that the Toll would advance the Price of Coals:

That he thisks the Road may be repaired, if a Toll-gate was erected between Nuneaton and Bedworth, and a Toll of 9 d.paid for Waggons at that Gate, without any Toll on Horlesj and that this is the general Opinion.

Mr. Dudley, being again examined, said. That the

Gate between Bedworth and Coventry produces /.4 a Week, 0:1 an Average. And,

That the Statute-work would support the Road in every Parish, except Exhall’, if it was properly repaired:

That a Toll would increase the Price of Coal, and the People of Coventry are against it; but that a T.oll on Waggons would not hurt the Poor, because the poor Manufacturers in general buy their Coals off Horl'es; but the Rich supply themselves in Summer by Waggons.

Part of an Act, made in the 5th and 6th Years of the Reign of King William and Queen Mary, was read; whereby it appeared, that, in the Year 1617, the Inhabitants of Wppping, at their Charge, built a Chapel for their own Use, and, by voluntary Contributions, maintained their Minister and Clerk, and had been at great Charge in the Repairs, Ornaments, and Conveniences, of the said Chapel.

Mr. George Dance, Surveyor to the City of London being examined, said, That, by the Form of the Church, it seemed to be built only for a Chapel: That the Walls are only Two Bricks and a Half thick: That there is no Steeple; and that it is not built in that substantial manner that Parish Churches usually are: That the Walls of Churches ought to be Four Bricks thick at the least: That the Foundation is about One Brick thicker in some Places; and that it is in a very indifferent Condition:

That the Floor, in most Places, is Five Feet below the Surface of the Ground on the Outside: Thar the Ground in the Church-yard is raised by the Burial of Corpses, which makes the Church excessively damp and unwholsome.

And being asked, If it could not be repaired for £.500 he said. That the Building may be supported; and that £.500 would repair it, to make it Hand for 40 or5oYcars, but not to repair it effectually:

That the Church cannot be madefafeand wholfomefor the Inhabitants to assemble in, without railing the Floor; and that the Roof must be raffed in proportion to the Floor; and that the Walls are not capable of bearing & Superftrudure:

That it cannot be drained, without removing a great Number of Corpses;and that the Expence of these Repairs and Works will amount to jt. 4 or 5,000; and that the building of a new Church would cost about or £. 5,000.

And that it can never, by any Repair, be made safe and wholsome, and fit for People to fit in.

Mr. James Steer, Surveyor to the Hand in Hand Fire Office, and Saint Thomas's and Guy’s Hospitals, being examined, said, That he had surveyed this Church; and that it was not built in thatsubstantia) manner that Parish Churches usually are: That the Walls of many Houses are as thick: That it was built in the Year 1617: that the Pavement of the Church, in many Places, is or 5 Feet below the Surface of the Ground on the Outside; and that when the Pavement of the Church was dug up, found it 18 Inches deep in Water:

That the Church isTwo Feet below the Ditches at high Water Mark, and the Water cannot be drained from the Church: That the Water soaked against the Walls of the Church, and prejudices the Foundation:

That the Level of the Church-yard is higher than the Bottom of the Shore: That the Water in the Churchyard will not drain into the Shore, but will loak into the Graves:

That it is practicable to raise the Floor of the Church; but that the Galleries must be taken down, and raffed, and then there will not be room for People in the Galleries to stand upright:

But that he did not think it possible to raise the Floor of the Church above the Level of the Church-yard; and that the Foundation is too weak to raise aSuperftrufture upon.

And being asked. Whether, by some little Expence, it might not bealtered, to answer the Purpose of Rebuilding ? said. That it may be supported; but that he would not advise the Repair of it:

That it is impossible to repair it effectually; and that it will be continually in want of Repairs: That the Foundation is decayed, and hollow, and the Waterfoaking under.it makes it ftillworfe; and that it would cost as much to repair it, so as to remedy the Inconveniences, as to rebuild it; and that it would be a Cripple in a few Years, if it was repaired:

That if a Drain was to be made, a great Number of Corpses must be removed: That the Inhabitants would

Wapping Church, &c.

not suffer Corpses to be removed; and that no Method can be found to drain the Church and Church-yard, without removing the Corpses.

And being asked, What would be the Expence of draining the Church and Church-yard ? he said, About $ or £.600 in the best Method it could be done; but that he apprehends it is not possible to keep the Church dry by any Drain whatl'oever, as the Floor of the Church is Two Feet below the high Water Mark: and that if a Drain was to be made Three Feet above the Floor of the Church, it would not be practicable to keep the Church dry, as all the Water that falls on the Graves will loak under the Bottom of the Church: That if the Church was to be new-paved, it might, in fotne measure, remedy it; but that if an Area was to be made, a great number of Corplis must be removed.

Part of an Act made in the 5th and 6th Years of King William and Queen Mary., was read; whereby it appeared,'

That for repairing, or, if Occasion be, for rebuilding, enlarging, and adorning, of the said Parish Church of Saint John of Wapping, and for the making of the same more convenient for the Inhabitants thereof, a Rate was to be made,.to be allowed by Two Justices.

Mr Richard Clarke, Parishioner and Inhabitant of St. John of Wapp'ing being examined, laid. He had frequented the Church conftautly; but for Six or Seven Years past had not been there Ten Times, because he thought the Church damp and unwhollome: That going into the Church is as bad as going into a Vault: That it proceeds from the Water soaking out of the Church-yard into the Church: and that he has heard many other Inhabitants have been intimidated from attending divine Worship for that Reason.

And being asked, If any Drain had been made to drain the Water off from the Church ? said. He did not know; but that he knows the Bottom of the Church is lower than any Groundabout it, and thinks it inypoffible to drain the Water off.

Mr. Thomas Goodland, being examined, said, That he is a Parishioner, and has lived Three Years in the Parish, and has constantly attended divine Service till within this Quarter of a Year: and that he tat at one End of the Church, where the Graves in the Church-yard were over his Head; and that he ivas taken very ill in the Church, and was nut able to follow his Business fur a Fortnight: That when he went into the Church, he was in good Health: That he has often seen the Walls wet and damp, which he apprehends was owing to the Ground on the Outside being raised so high.

Mr. John Norris, being examined, laid, That he has

attended the Church, as Clerk, for 9 Years: That he has often found the Church cold and damp, and is now much damper than it uled to be, and, in many Places, has not been dry for a Week: That the Water lies within Two Foot of the Floor of the Church; and that when Graves have been dug, have been obliged to lade the Water out with Pails: That the Church-yard is so full of Corpses, that feme lay partly above Ground; and that he has found the Stench lo great, that he has not been able to go within Ten Feet of the Graves; and that the Church-yard has been dug up Five or Six times since he has been Clerk; and that they bury Five or Six Corps upon one another:

That there has been double Doors to the Church about Nine or Ten Years; and that it is not now sufficiently warm:

That lie has found the Church very cold in the Week Days, when there has not been Ten People at Church, except the Children: That he apprehends the Dampneis to proceed from the Ground on the Outside being raised so high above the Church; and that the Water cannot be carried off without removing Five or Sixhundred Corpses:

That the Floor of the Church is more than Two Feet below the high Water Mark, and Five Feet below the Surface of the Ground in the Church-yard; and that the latter is occalxoned by the many Burials there:

20

That if a Trench was to be made round the Church,-to carry the Water off, he apprehends above 50c Corpses must; be removed, several of which have been but lately buried; and that several Families have Vaults; and he believes they would not suffer the Corpses to be removed.

That the Church-yard, in its present Condition, is much too small; and if a Trench was made. Half the Church-yard would be taken away:

That if these Corpses were to be removed, they would be very offensive; and that he has heard People complain, in the Summertime, that they have not been able to bear their Windows open, the Stench has been so great.

And being asked, Whether the Fees that arile from Burials are not sufficient to provide a proper Burying Ground? said. They were not. That the Parish were at great Expences in burying People that are drowned; which the Tide leaves in the Parish, which obliged them to expend most of the Money arising by those Fees.

The reverend Mr. Griffith, being examined, laid. That he has performed divine Service in this Church for about Five Years; and he thinks it is not a proper Place for the Inhabitants to assemble in: That it is very damp and un-whollome: and that he knows many People keep away, who would come if it was made commodious and whol-some: That the Coffins in the Church-yard lie above Ground in many Places: That the Ground is so full that they can’t be put lower; and that the Church is very damp, owing to the Ground in the Church-yard being raised so high: That the Church-yard is much too small, in proportion to the Number of Burials: That his House adjoins to the Church-yard, and, in hot Weather, the Corpses are very offensive: That they bury about Three hundred Persons in a Year.

Mr. John IV ebber, being examined, said. That lie is Sexton of the Parish of St. John of trapping: That in digging the Graves in the Church-yard, he has always found Water at the Depth of about Four or Five Feet; and that the usual Depth of the Craws is about Five Feet; and that when he buried in the Church, he found Water at about the Depth of Two Feet: and that when a Grave has been opened in hot Weather, lie has not been . able to come near it, the Stench has been so great; and that the Church-yard is not sufficient to contain the Number of Corpses; and that several Houses have been pulled down, to enlarge the Church-yard.

Bolton Manwaring Esquire, Surveyor to the London Hospital, being examined, said, That lie had surveyed this Church, and should recommend the building a new Church: That the present Church is a very weak Building: That the Walls, in many Places, are decayed and hollow, and not able to bear any more Weight than they now bear: That the Walls above Ground are about Two Bricks or Two Bricks and a Half thick; and that the usual Thickness of the Walls of Churches is Four, Five, or Six Bricks thick; That he never knew the Walls of Churches less than Four Bricks thick:

That the Church is very damp, which cannot be remedied by any Means, but by raising the Floor of the Church to the Level of the Church-yard; and that if this was done, it would be necessary to raise the Roof in proportion to the Floor: That the Performance of all Works necessary for this Purpose would cost as much as it would to rebuild the Church; and that it would be continually in Want of Repairs, and the whole would be a Cripple; and that if it was his own Property, he would not repair it, nor for any Body else:

That if an Area was to be made round the Church, it would cause a great number of Corpses to be removed: That, from the Pavement of the Church to the Underside of the Planking that covers the Sewer, there is a Fall of Nineteen Inches: That the nearest Distance from the Church to the Sewer is 94 Feet; and that the Sewer is frequently choaked up; and it is impossible for any Water to get into it but from the Drains that run.into it: That the Sewer is frequently filled with Mud, and rhe

Vaster

29 Geo. II.

Water must reflow: That the Floor of the Church, upon a common Spring Tide, is about Three Feet lower than the high Water Mark: That the Tide frequently runs through a Butcher’s House right against the Church Gates.

And being asked, laid. He did not suppose that the Floor of the Church is lower than when it was built; and that he did not believe there was any Ground in the Fa* rish higher than the Level of the Church;and that there are no Means for making the Church as useful now as it was formerly, without rebuilding it: That the Church cannot well fall down, it is lo jammed in by the Ground round it; and that it is but about Ten Feet above Ground:

That the Church-yard, in moll Places, is higher than the Level of the Church *. and, that, round the Church in general, he_ thinks the Difference in the Heighth of the Ground, is not above Five or Six'Inches. '

And being asked, Whether lie did not know of any Church that the Ground on th» Outside was higher than the Level of the Church? he laid. He did not, so much as this: ’ ' ’ ’ '

That the Pavement of the Church is in a very bad Condition; and that the Church cannot be" drained, and made fife and wholfome1 for the inhabitants to assemble in.

Mr. Cotton, Vestry Clerk of the Parish of St. Joky of Wapping, being examined, said, That if there was a gopd Church, it would increaserhe Rents in that Parish: That if the Expence of the Repairs of the Church was to be defrayed by the Inhabitants only, many of them would be obliged to quit their Houses and that the Generality of the Inhabitants are poor People; many in the upper Part of the Parish are not able to pay the Scavengers Rates; and that the Rates made for the Relief of the Poor have increased within these Three Years:

And that if the Church was rebuilt, the Land Owners would reap lading Advantages:

And that new Churches have been built in the Parishes of Saint Olave and Saint Botolph where the Inha

bitants were better able to bear the Expence of building a Church than the Parish of of

Bolton Manwaring Esquire, being further examined, said, That there is a great Number of poor Persons in this Parish; and that no Parish is more burthened than this; and believes very few so much:

And that if the Church was to be rebuilt, and the Rates to be charged on the Inhabitants only, he thinks they would not be able to hear it:

And that the Church may be repaired, but can never be made safe and wholsome; and that if he was Owner of all the Land in the Parish, helhould think it necessary to rebuild the Church.

To prove the Allegations of the second-mentioned Petition,

Mr. Henry Keene Surveyor, being examined, laid, He liirveyed this Church on the 22d of January last: That it was built as substantial as was necessary for a Church of that Height; but if lie was to build a Church now, should build it thicker, because he should build it higher: That he had examined the Walls, and found them, from the Level of the Pavement up to the Bottom of the Windows, to be Three Bricks thick, and from thence to the Plate of the Roof, Two Bricks and an Half thick, common sized Bricks:

That he found no Part of the Building unfound: That all the Timber that is visible, and which is the material Part, is very found, not quite lo found as when put up, but will last many Years: That the Pews are very good and found, except here and there One a little torn by burying near the Walls; but that if proper Care was taken, they would last 40 or 50 Years:

And that the Floor of the Church is funk in many Places by Burials, and has settled in Holes all over the Church; and that it wants repairing:

And t hat the Ground in the Church-yard is from Three Vo l.27.

507

to Six Feet above the Floor of the Church, occasioned, as he apprehends, from the many Burials: That several Tombs lie now improperly; and that no Care has oeen taken to throw the Water off from the Walls: That there is no Means of carrying off the Water but by a dry Drain; but that will occasion the Removal of a great Number of Corpses; and thataTrench may be dug round the Church, about 18 Inches wide, which would prevent the Ground from lying immediately against the Walls of the Church; and that about Three Feet of Earth might be taken away all round the Church; and that such dry Drain, if made about Six Inches below the Paving of the present Church, would prevent the Water from coming against the Walls of the Church:

That he examined the Roof of the Church: That it appeared to him to be in a good Situation; the Rafters and Gutters lay very straight; but that there had been great Neglects in cleaning the Gutters; One of the Gut--terswas stopped up, there was near a Hog (head of Water; so that all the Water that fell on that Side of the Church must lodge there.

: And being asked, Whether the Tide would not break into this dry Drain ? he said, Some little might ouze through; but that he should take care to prevent it as much as poflrble:

That he makes no doubt but the Tide comes into the common Sewer: That the Level of the Church is Two Feet lower than high Water Mark: That the Tide at high Water would flow up the new Drain; but it might be prevented by a Valve or Flap: That the Water must be Hopped in the Drain during the coming in of the Tide:

And that he apprehends the Dampness proceeded from Water soaking through the Ground that lay against the Walls of the Church; and that the Church appeared to him to have been kept in proper Repair in every Re-ipeft, but that of carrying off the Water; and that if proper Care had been taken to carry off the Water, it would be safe for the Inhabitants to assemble in; and that, with the Alteration he proposed, it would be as whdllome as it had been for 40 or 50 Years past; That the Ground on the Outside has been as high as it is now ihefe^o Yeark.

And being asked, he said it was practicable to carry the Water from the Foundation of the Church to the common Sewer, but not without removing some Corpses; not such a Number as have been before mentioned.

And he confirmed the Evidence of Mr. Manwaring, with respect to the Level of the Church, compared with the common Sewer:

That he does not think it necessary to enter into such a Repair as has been mentioned, but acommon Repair, such astaifing the Floor, and other Necessaries, which he thinks might be done for about £. 500; but that he had made no particular Estimate; and this would make it as safe, and as wholsome, for the Inhabitants to assemble in, as it has been for40 Years past; which Repairs would make the Church last for 50 or 60 Years.

Mr. Matthew Fairless, Surveyor and Builder, being examined, said. He had surveyed this Church in the Beginning of December last; and that he thinks it was built in a very good manner: That he never saw so old a Building so upright: At every Corner there is a great Buttress, which appear to have been built with the original Building; at the North West and South West Corners, there are Two more considerable Buttresses than any of the rest: That he measured ’em, and found ’em to be Four Feet thick, and built in an Octagon Form ;the rest from 18 Inches to 2 or 3 Feet wide, and from 3 to Bricks thick; and that, in his Opinion, the Walls are strong, and will Hand as long as any modem Building: That the Church is 140 Years old:

And that, at the original Building of this Church, there did not appear any Intention of building Galleries; but that, in the Year 1722, on the South Side, there appears to have been a Gallery built; and that as there was no Preparation in the Design to prevent the Gallery coming

That if a little Money is laid out, it will make the Church safe and wholsome: That he has frequently gone to this Church for 40 Years past: That, at the South East Corner, there is a Tomb that raises the Ground Five or Six Feet:

That, to repair the Church, and remove the Things complained of, and make it drier, and to beautify it, would cost between fc.4 and 500. and make it more convenient than ever: That the Dampness may be removed, if the Gutters are taken care of: That he thinks the Ground lying against the Church will not damage it, if Care is taken to keep the Wet from it: That the Water may be easily carried off: That it would be dangerous to build a heavier Church, and thinks a new Church is not necessary; and that he would go to the old Church as soon as any other; and that, with moderate Repairs, it will last Three or Fourscore Years.

And being aiked, Whether he could take upon him to say, that the Walls are not periftied in any one Part ? be said, he could: That in all the Walls, except one Place at the West End under the Window where the Water had run down, becaul'e the Gutterswere flopped, he found no other Decay but the common Decay of Bricks:

And that a Hole was dug Two Feet and an Half deep in the Church, and he found Water, which, in about Half an Hour, role Six Inches; but did not rife any higher in Three Days.

And being aiked. Whether there was any such thing as draining the Church? he laid, There was no such thing as draining that Water, either there or anywhere else in the Parish:

That he don’t know how deep the Foundation lies below the Floor; but that it is usual to carry the Foundation more than Four Feet below, and thinks the Water will not perish the Foundation of this Church: That he does not think the Water lying so near the Floor of the Church makes the Church damp; and that if the Water is kept from the Ground on the Outside, the Church will not b* more damp than common:

That at the South West Corner, the Ground is Five or Six Feet higher than the Floor of the Church, in i’ome Parts Four Feet higher, and in others Three Feetdefcending down:

That Wafting Street is not above a Foot higher than the Floor of the Church; and that the Church does not want any Draining:

That there are Floors to the Pews, some of which are found, and some not; and that he believes there may be some little Damps that may hurt the Pews:

And that he would not advile the carrying the Water oft from under the Church, because the Tide might flow up the Mouth of the Drain.

Resolved, i. That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it would be advantageous not only to the City of London, but to many others of his Majesty’s Subjects, and to the Public in general, that another Bridge should be built cross the River Thames, from some Part of the City to the Surrey Side of the said ltiver.

Resolved, 3. That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the most convenient Place for erecting the said Bridge will be from B/ack Friars, in the said City, to the opposite Side in the County of Surrey.

Resolved, 4. That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Petitioners, divers Merchants, Tradesmen, Citizens, and Inhabitants, of the City of London and Borough of Southwark, and of the several Counties of Surrey, Kent, and Sujj'ex, have fully proved the Allegations of their Petition.

Resolved, 5. That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Passage over and through London Bridge is at prefint very dangerous and incommodious; and that it is absolutely necessary immediately to widen and enlarge the fame: That the widening and enlarging the said Bridge, and One or more of the Arches thereof, would be of public Utility, of great Benefit to Trade and Commerce, make the Navigation upon the said River more safe and secure, and greatly tend to the Preservation of the Lives of his Majesty’s Subjects passing over and through the said Bridge.

Appendix, N# 1.

An Estimate of the Expence in making the proposed Alteration of London Bridge.

To fill up all the Cavities or Voids of all the Arches throughout the whole Bridge with Portland Stone, One Foot Six Inches thick, so that every Arch may be uniform and intire, and to extend some of the Piers to the proper Length of the rest, in order to make the Breadth of the Bridge alike throughout, toereft all the Piers and Spandrels of the Arches in the East and West Fronts with Portland Athler; to make the Plinth of the Baluf-trade of Portland Block on both Sides One Foot Four Inches thick; to make the Dado of the said Balustrade of Portland Block, One Foot Two Inches thick; to make the Cap over the said Dado of Portland Block, One Foot in Height and Two Feet wide, wrought with a large Torus; to make all the Baluftres of Portland Block,

One Foot Square each Baluftre; to make all those Parts of the several Piers, which are in a Line, and level with the said Baluftres, of - Portland Block, One Foot Two Inches thick; to crown all the said Balustrade and Pierson both Sides of the Bridge with a proper Cap of Portland Stone, One Foot in Height, to turn all the Coves in those Piers, which are designed for Recedes, with Portland Stone, Eight Inches thick; to turn Arches over all the Cavities in the Piers, and ered Walls for the said Arches to spring from, in order to support the Paving above; to find and provide all Manner of Centering, to execute the aforesaid Works; to make a Foot Passage Six Feet wide on each Side, which shall be elevated One Step above the middle Part intended for Carriages, and the said Foot-ways to be bounded with Steps of Moor Stone, and the Parts within the said Steps to be paved with good found Purbeck Paving; to pave the middle Part with the best middle-sized Guernsey Pebbles; to ered Pods and Rails of good found Oak, in a handsome manner, with Openings at proper Distances, to defend Foot Passengers from being annoyed or interrupted by Cattle; to fix irons and Lamps, as described in the Design herewith exhibited; and to make a temporary Bridge of Timber, in order to iecurc a free Passage to all Carriages and Passengers, that the Trade and Commerce of the City may not be interrupted, during the Prosecution of the aforesaid Works: All which proposed Design will amount to £.30,000.

The House being informed. That One of the Sheriffs of the City of London attended at the Door;

A Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of London, in Common Council assembled.

And then he withdrew.

And the said Petition was brought up, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners have been informed, that a Bill hath been brought into this House, pursuant to the Resolution of the Third Day of this instant March, for granting to his Majesty certain Sums of Money, to be paid by every Person or Body Corporate having Thirty Ounces of Silver Plate, and upwards; and that the Petitioners humbly presume, by a most respectful Application to this House, to express their Concern, that the Burthen of inland Duties, already imposed on almost every Branch of Trade, however cheerfully borne, is feverelyfelt; and that the subjecting all Persons whatsoever, having Silver Plate in their private Houses, to the Information of their Servants, and dissolute Persons, and bringing them under the Laws of Excise, will be insupportable, and render the Liberty and Property of the Subject very precarious: And therefore praying, That so much of the said Bill, as tends to levying of Penalties under the Power of Commissioners of Excise, may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

House being uncovered; and is as followeth; viz. France

GEORGE ft.

Mis Majesty has received repeated Advices from different Places and Persons, that a Design has been formed by the French Court to make a Hostiic Invafton upon Great Britain or Ireland; and the great Preparations of Land Forces, Ships, Artillery, and warlike Stores, now notofiously making in the Ports of France, opposite to the British Coasts together with the Language held by the French Ministers in some foreign Courts, leave little Room to doubt of the Reality of such a Design; his Majesty has therefore judged it necessary to acquaint the House of Commons with Intelligence of such high Importance to the Safety and Well-being of these Nations; and at the same time to inform them, that, in pursuance of the Advice and Atuirances of Ins Parliament, he has augmented his Forces by Sea and Land, and taken proper Measures and Precautions for putting hi- Kingdoms in a Postureof -Deft mce against so unjult anddelperate an Kntcrprize, pro-jested in Revenge fur those just and necessary Measures which have been taken for maintaining the Rights and Possessi ons ol his Crown and Subjects in North America:

That in order further to strengthen himselff his Majesty has made a Requisition of a Body of Hejian Troops, pursuant to the Treaty lately made with the Landgrave of HeJJe CaJJel, to be forthwith brought over hither, for which Purpnie Transports are ordered: His Majesty, trulling in the Divine Protection, and in the gcod Afteft ions, Zeal, and Fidelity, of his People, which he has so often experienced, is determined to neglect no means of Defence, but to exert all the Force which God leas put into his 1 lands, to repel so daring an Attempt; and his Ma’ctly doubts not that he wilt be enabled and supported by Ins faithful Commons in taking all such Measurcs as may be conducive to an End so essential to the Honour of his Crown, the Preservation of the Protestant Religion, and the Laws and Liberties of thclc Kingdoms.

Mr. Oswald reported from the Committee, to whom HenW the Petition of the Royal Boroughs of Scotland, in Fishery. behalf of themselves, and many others of his Majesty’s industrious Subjects, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of Fast contained in the said Petition; and had directed him to report a State thereof to the House , and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Mr. John Cathrart, being examined, said, That the Fishers in general in the Western Parts of Scotland complain of great Oppressions and Exactions which are very prejudicial to them, and a great Discouragement to the carrying on their Trade: That many of the Proprietors of Lands and Blands, or their Agents, exact from the Fishers considerable Sums of Money for Liberty to fish

t

560 2° Apr His. 1756.

Herring in particular Parts >1 the Sea and the Lochs, and re drain Fifoery. them from fishing during the Second and Third Quarters of the Moon, and oblige them to pay One Night’s Fishing in the Week, under the Name of Saturday Night’s Filing; and, in many Places, very considerable Sums are exacted by such Proprietors or Agents under the Name of Foreland Dues and Protestien Money; and that they seize and take away the Fish, and otherways didress them, if these Demands are not complied with:

That he has been concerned in the Fishery, and has allowed for Four Years pad the Payments made by his Fishermen to said Proprietors or Agents; and he produced Two Receipts for Payments, in this Year, of Foreland Dues, Baillies Fees, and Watchmen’s Dues.

And he produced several Certificates of Persons who have been employed in the Fishery, which he said he law signed and atteded, and that the Persons who signed the same are now at Sea, which Certificates are annexed in the Appendix, N° 1; and it appears therein, that considerable Sums of Money have been demanded and taken, for and on the behalf of the said Proprietors, for Foreland Dues, Protection Money, and SaturJayNights Fishing; and that, when these Demands were not complied with, the Fish had been seized, and the Fishermen treated in a very cruel manner; and that they had been redrained from fishing in xMoon-light Nights, and at other times.

Mr. George Walker, being called, said, That in Shetland a Tax has been exacted of a Guinea for each Scotch Boat employed in Ling and Tulk fishing: That such Tax was not paid for the Dutch Ships or Boats; and that if the L:ng and Tulk Fishery was encouraged in Shetland, it would be of general Advantage: And Mr. Cathcart added upon this Head, That, to his certain Knowledge, Two Guineas ter Boat was demanded in Shetland lad Fishing Season: And the said,

Mr. Walker and Mr. Cathcart said. That the Fishery maintains many Thousand People: That they go out in all Weathers, and consequently become in time hardy Seamen.

And in order to prove what Consequence this Fishery is of to the Nation in regard to its Wealth, Mr. Cathcart produced a Certificate from the Custom-house at Campbell ‘town, of the Quantity of Fish that were exported from thence last Year; whereby it appeared, that the Value of the Fish exported from this Place only, in the last Year, amounted to^.15,985. os. 4

And he added, That a much greater Quantity were exported the same Year from other Ports in the Frith of Clyde.

Then an Act, made in in the Third Session of

the First: Parliament of Queen Anne, intituled, An Act for advancing and establishing the FishingTrade in and about this Kingdom, was read; which " authorizes the taking, " buying, and curing, of Herrings and White Fish in all " Seas, Channels, Bays, Fritlis, Lochs, Rivers, £5 of " her Majesty’s ancient Kingdom, and Islands thereto " belonging; and also allows the free Use of all Ports, " Harbours, Shores, Forelands, (Ac. for bringing in, pickling, drying, unloading, and loading, the fame, upon " Payment of the ordinary Dues where Harbours are " built; and discharges all other Exactions, such as a " Night’s Fishing in the Week, commonly called day's Fishing, Top-money, Stallage, and the like;" and cnafts, that the Barrels made use of by the Fishers shall lie of a certain Largcness and Quality; and that all Herrings and White Fish put into them shall be pined, cured, and packed, with foreign Salt; and recites several other Acts for encouraging the Fisheries; but the said Acts only declare a general Prohibition, and inflict no. Penalty on Persons acting against them.

Mr. Cathcart further said. That a Person at Lochbroom was l'ued at the Expence of the Royal Boroughs for illegal Exactions on Herring Fishers in that Loch; and after a long Suit first in the Admiralty Court, and then in the Court of Session, he was fined in £.50. Sterling, but the the Charge of prosecuting amounted to much more than 20

the Fine — That, generally speaking, the Fishermen are poor, and not able to prosecute; and all'o live a great Way from the Courts of Justice; and therefore are either obliged byNeceflity to pay these Exactions, orchufe to pay them, rather than be at the Expence and Trouble of a Law Suit.

And he thinks it absolutely necessary, for the Prclerva-tion and Extension of ihis valuable Branch of Trade, that those Acts should be explained, amended, and enforced.

Then in order to shew the Methods used to defraud the Government of the Bounty allowed upon the exporting of Fish in feme of the Western Ports of Scotland and Shetland,

Mr. Cathcart laid. That several Persons, not Inhabitants of Great Britain, made over a Part of their Fishing Boats to Persons in Shetland and the West of Scotland, who swear off the Fish to be exported, and call themselves Proprietors of the Boat and Fish; but he thinks that Fraud might be prevented by amending the Oath of the Exporter.

Then an Act, made in the Fifth Year of the Reign of Queen Anne, for the Union of the Two Kingdoms, was read, which enacts, u That, from and after the Union, " the Laws in Scotland for pining, curing, and packing, " Herrings, White Fish, and Salmon, for Exportation, " with foreign Salt only, without any Mixture of " or Irish Salt, shall be continued in Force in Scotland, " subject to such Alterations as shall be made by the " Parliament of Great Britain-, and that all Fish exported " from Scotland, which shall be lb cured, shall have the " same Eases, Premiums, and Drawbacks, as are or shall " be allowed on Exportation of the like Fish from " land."

Then an Act, made in the Fifth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, intituled, An Act for recovering the Credit of the Fishery in

foreign Parts; and for better securing the Duties on Salt, was read; whereby the English Curers of Fish were air lowed to use foreign and British Salt together or separately, in curing Fish for Exportation; and to import foreign Salt, or take from any Salt Work or Salt Pit any such Quantity of British Salt, where the same is allowed by Law, for the curing Fish for Exportation, as they shall think proper, for curing Fish for foreign Markets, without paying any Duty for the fame, except the Customs payable upon the Importation thereof, under the Regulations therein mentioned; and certain Bounties are thereby granted upon the Exportation of Fish.

Mr. Cathcart said, That British and foreign Salt mixed are the moll proper for curing Fish; and that if the Regulations made in England were extended to the Scotch Fishery, it would tend to the Improvement of that Fishery, and would encourage the making of Salt in Scotland:

That the importing of Scotch Fish into England for Home Consumption, under the same Duties as are now paid in England; and the exporting of such Fish from thence, under the same Allowances and Regulations as English cured Fish are now exported; would be of great Advantage to both Parts of the Kingdom; and enable the Merchants, and others in the South Part, to make up their Aflbrtments for the Mediterranean, and other Markets, which, as the Laws now Hand, they cannot do.

An Act, made in the Second and Third Year of the Reign of Queen Anne, intituled, An Act for the better securing and regulating the Duties upon Salt, was read; whereby it is declared, That no Herrings shall be brought into England, unless cured with Salt put on board iri some Part ot England, Wales, or Berwick upon Tweed.

And an Act, made in the Eighth Year of his late Majesty, intituled, An Act for taking off the Duty upon all Salt used in the curing and making of white Herrings, and, instead thereof, laying a proportional Duty upon all white Herrings consumed at home only, was also read; whereby white Herrings are allowed to be cured with foreign

29 Geo. II. 20 Ap561

reign or home-made Salt for home Consumptiott or Exportation; and the Curer is to pay Three Shillings and Four Pence per Barrel for all such as are entered for home Consumption. And,

Mr. Cathcart said, That if Scotch white Herrings were allowed to be cured with foreign or British Salt, or with both mixed, under the like Regulations as English Her- rings are allowed to be cured, and to be exported from any Port of Britain under the same Allowances and Regulations as English Herrings are now exported, and to be brought for home Consumption into Scotland, upon Payment of a Duty of One Shilling per Barrel, and into England upon Payment of Three Shillings and Four Pence per Barrel, it would greatly encourage and extend the said Fishery:

And that if Cod, Ling, Tu/k, Salmon, and all other white FiCh, which at present are not importable from Scotland into South Britain, for Exportation, if cured with foreign Salt, or for home Consumption, if cured with Scotch Salt, were allowed to be brought in here for home Consumption, cuted with Scotch made salt, upon paying the Difference of the Duty between English and Scotch Salt, in the same manner as white Herrings are now Brought in, it would also tend to the Extension of the Fishery, and the Benefit of the Revenue.

Thelai Mr. Walker and Mr. George Spence, and Mr. Hugh Cravfurd, said, That to cure a Barrel of wet Fish, containing Thirty-two Gallons, will not take more than One Bushel of homemade Salt; and that One Bushelof such Sait will cure Two hundred Weight of dried Fish.

At Campbell Town, the Fifth Day of September One thousand Seven hundred and Fifty-five Years, in Presence of William Finlay Esquire, Provost of Campbell Tozvn, and One of his Majesty’s Justices of the Peace for ArgyUshire, Mr. Ronald Campbell, Sheriff Substitute of ArgyUshire, for the District of Kintyre, and Mr. Archibald Campbell, Chamberlain of Kintyre, and One of his Majesty’s Justices of the Peace for ArgyUshire, compeared Mr. John Cathcart, Merchant in London, who requested, that the said Magistrates would take the Declarations of some Masters of Fishing VdTels, and others, that have been employed in the Herring Fishery in the Ifics, and on the North West Con ft of Scotland, in order to know with Certainty the Truth of the Hardships complained of by People who follow the Herring Fishing in these Parts: Which being agreed to by the said Magistrates, compeared as follows:

Thomas Thomson, Matter of a Fishing Vessel in Campbell Towny certifies, That, in the Year One thousand Seven bunched and Thirty-two, he failed as Matter of a Fishing Vessel to the North West Jfles of Scotland; and, loon after his Arrival at Lochjhaphaig in the Isle of Sky, and, as he best remembers, the first Night he lets his Nets, he caught Forty-eight Barrels of Herrings, which were all taken from him the next Morning by the Laird of Mac-kinnon s Son, in Name of Saturday's Fishing, though it was then the Middle of the Week; and when the said Thomas Thomson complained of having his Fish taken from him, he was severely threatened; and some of his Neighbours from Campbell Tozvn were actually beat in his View: That, tome Days after, a Dispute happening between some of the Campell Tozvn Fishers and the Natives of the Country, with respect to the Saturday\Fishing, he the said Thomas Thomson was kicked and beat, and many of his Companions were bound, and whipped with Ropes taken out of their own Vessels, after being stripped naked — And that there was Plenty of Fish in that Loch at the time when the Fishers from this Place were obliged to come home with about One-third of their Cargoes, being in Terror of Their Lives — And the said Thomas Thomson further certitics, That, some Years after, he was fishing at Lochorn and Lochnivas, in the Estate of Glcngerry, where, as well as at Lochjhaphaig, the Baillies of the Country constantly exacted one Night’s Fishing in the Week, with Three Shillings Sterling of Foreland Dues for each Last,

besides four Pence Sterling each Night, of Prote&km

Money:

That, in the Year Thirty-fiVe, as he best remembers, he was at the Herring Fishing in Lochbroom, where all the Campbell Town Fishers were obliged to pay at the Rate of Four Shillings the Last of Foreland Dues and Protection Money; and that, in all the above-mentioned Places, the Fishers from Campbell Town were discharged Fishing the Second and Third Quarters of the Moon; and if they had been allowed to fish with the Moon Light, they would frequently have made their Cargoes, when they were obliged to come home without them; and that the Baillies of the Country often commanded them to fish how and where they the Baillies pleased, though they knew little about Fishing.

Arch. Campbell, J. P. Tho. Thomson.

It appeared to your Committed, by the Evidence of Edward Wade Esquire, That the waste Grounds in the several Manors mentioned in the Petition, do contain a Tract of Land, confiding of many Thousand Acres, unfit for Tillage or Pasture, but capable of producing, great Numbers of different Kinds of Trees, if Power were given to make Inclosures to secure the Plantation thereof.

And it appeared to your Committee, by the Evidence of Mr. Philip Miller, Gardener to the Company of Apothecaries, and ajlo of the honourable Charles,

and of a Member of this House (which Two last mentioned Persons have planted, with Success, a great Quantity of Trees in a Soil like that mentioned in the Petition) That Scotch Firs and Beech may be raised for Timber, in such Soil, on the Tops of the Hills; and that Birch, Hazel, Oak, and Chelnut, may be well planted for Underwood on the Sides of such Hills, and Oak for Timber in the Bottoms: /

And that planting such Lands would be much more advantageous to the Proprietors thereof, and be attended wtth leis Expence, than any other Method of Cultivation; and that tins was proved by Experience, in the several Plantations of the Dukes of Bedford and Argyll-, the Truth of which was confirmed to your Committee by several Members pretent.

And it appeared to your Committee, by the Evidence of Mr. La nylon and Mr. Tohn Thorey, Two considerable Tanners, That Bark for Tanning is become scarce; the Kealon of which Scarcity, they said, was, that many Woods l ad been lately grubbed up, and none planted, except for Pleasure.

Mr. Bird, a Ship-builder, informed your Committee, That the Price of common Timber is risen considerably within 50 Years last past, and large Timber, as he be-Jieved, much more; and that great Quantities of Timber were imported from foreign Parts.

And the Decrease of Timber in the King’s Forests was proved by the Evidence of Slade Esquire, Sur-

veyor of his Majesty’s Navy; and the Decrease of Timber in the King’s Demesnes was proved by the Evidence of Zachary Chambers Esquire, Deputy to the Surveyor General of his Majesty’s Lands; and the Decrease of Timber in Copyhold Lands, in which the Timber belongs to the Lord, was proved by Mr Richardson-, and the general Decrease of l imber in England, especially on the Sides of navigable Rivers, and in the Wilds of Surrey, and Kent, which have been esteemed productive of the best Timber, was proved by Mr. Purveyor of

Timber for Woolwich Y..rd, Mr Griffiths Timber Merchant, and others; who added, that the Price of Timber was raised from Three Pounds to Four or Five Pounds per Load. — That there was a Necessity to use foreign Timber in his Majesty’s Navy; and that there will be a great Want of Timber in a few Years, if forne Provision be not made to prevent the further Scarcity thereof. And, John Sunderland Esquire, informed your Committee, That Wood for Fuel, for the Iron Works, and for the Use of Coopers, is become scarce and dear.

And by an Account, laid before your Committee by the proper Officer of his Majesty’s Customs, it appeared, that the Importation of foreign Timber had of late considerably increased; in which Account, the Quantity of Planks imported is not included, the Officer not having Time to inlert it in that Account.

And Part of the Statute, made at Merton, directing in what Cafes, and in what Manner, Lords may approve Part of the Wastes, Woods, and Pastures, belonging to their Manors, against the Tenants; and Part of the Statute of Weflmbjier the Second, ordaining that the Statute of Merton shall in like manner hold Place between the Lords of Wastes, Woods, and Pastures, and their Neighbours; were ievcrally read:

And an Act, made in the 35th Year of the Reign of King Henry the Eighth, was also read; reciting, That the great Decay of Timber and Woods universally within England to be then such, that, unless speedy Remedy in Vo l. 17.

that Behalf Was provided, there was great and mani- Planting fell Likelihood of Scarcity, as well of Timber for build-ing and maintaining Houses and Ships, as for Fuel and Fire-wood; by which Act, Provisions are made, which, appear to your Committee not to have been duly observed, for preserving Woods and Timber; by one Clause of which Act, it is declared in what manner a Fourth Part of the Woods and Underwoods, growing in any Ground or Soil wherein any Persons have Common of Pasture,

shall be secured and divided by the Afferit and Agreement of the Lord and Owner of th^ Soil, and of the Moor Part of the Common; or, in case of no such Agreement; by the Justices of the Peace of the Shire where the said Ground or Soil lies, in their open Quarter Sessions, upon Request and Suit made to them by the said Lord or Owner.

And an Act, made in the 20th Year of the Reign of King Charles the Second, for the Increase and Preserva-tion of Timber within the Forest of Dean, for inclosing and keeping in Severalty 11,000 Acres of t he waste Lands of the said Forest, the Whole containing by Estimation

23,000 Acres, upon a Recompense thereby given to the Persons having Right of Common or Herbage within the said Inclosure.

And an Act, made in the 9th and 10th of King William the Third, for the Increase and Preservation of Timber within the New Forest, for inclosing in Severalty 2,000 Acres of the said Forest, Part of 85,454 Acres, whereof the said Forest consists, discharged from all Manner of common Herbage and Pannage, for so long time as the same shall remain and continue inclosed, according to the Directions of the said Act, and for the Inclosure yearly of 200 Acres more for a Nursery for Timber, were also read.

And it appeared to your Committee, that either the Inclosures, so directed to be made, had not been made according to the Directions of the said Acts, or that the Provision for that Purpose had been rendered ineffectual, by not continuing or renewing the Fences of the said Inclosures.

Upon the whole Matter, your Committee came to the following Resolutions:

A Message, by the honourable Sir Henry Bellenden, Gentleman Ulher of die Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

Royal Assent The Lords, authorized by virtue of his Majesty’s to Bills. Commission for declaring his royal Assent to several Acts agreed upon by both Houses do desire the immediate Attendance of this honourable House in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

And, being returned;

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House, at the Desire of the Lords authorized by virtue of his Majesty’s Commission afore-mentioned, had been at the House of Peers: Where a Commission under the Great Seal was read, giving, declaring, and notifying, the Royal Assent to several public and private Bills therein mentioned; and also impowering his royal Highness the Duke of land, the Lord Archbishop of the Lord High

Chancellor, and several other Lords, to declare and notify the royal Assent to the said Bills; and that the Lord High Chancellor, the Lord Privy Seal, and other Lords named in the said Commission, did accordingly declare and notify the royal Assent to the said Bills j which Bills are as followeth; viz.

An Act for granting to his Majesty several Rates and Duties payable by all Persons, and Bodies Politic or Corporate, having certain Quantities of Silver Plate: An Act for granting to his Majesty a Duty upon Licences for retailing Beer, Ale, and other exciseable Liquors, and for establishing a Method of granting such Licences in Scotland; and for allowing such Licences to be granted at a Petty Session in England, in a certain same therein mentioned:

And the said Message was read by Mr. Speaker, all the Members of the House being uncovered; and is as followeth; viz.

GEORGE R.

His Majesty, being desirous to be prepared against all Attempts and Designs whatsoever, that may be formed by his Enemies in the present critical conjuncture; and considering that sudden Emergencies may arise, which may be of the utmost Importance, and be attended with the most pernicious Consequences, if proper Means should not be immediately applied to prevent or defeat them; his Majesty hopes that he shall be enabled, by his faithful Commons, to concert and take all such Measures as may be necessary to disappoinc or defeat any Enterprises or Designs of his Enemies, and as the Exigency of Affairs may require. '

His Majesty having concluded a Treaty with the King of Prussia, has ordered the fame, together with a Declaration, signed at the same time, to be laid before this House, that he may be enabled to make good the gagements he has thereby entered into.

C. R.

Ordered, Nemine Contradicente, That his Majesty’s said most gracious Message be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of the Supply granted to his Majesty.

Then the said Lift was read.

The said Copies are preserved amongst the other Papers of this Session; and the said Translations are -as followeth; viz.

Translation of a Treaty between his Majesty and the King of PrvJJta, signed at Westminster, the 16th of January 1756.

Whereas the Disputes which have arisen in between the King of Great Britain and the most Christian King, the Consequences whereof become more and more critical, give Hoorn to Apprehension for the public Tranquillity of Europe, his Majesty the King of Great Britain, Elector of Brunswick, Lunenburgh, &c.

and his Majesty the King of Priijia, Elector of Brandenburg, &c. being attentive to so interesting an Object, and equally desirous of preserving the general Peace of,

2qGeo. IL i i° Mail. 603

and that of Germany in particular, have been pleased to concert together the Measureswhich maymost effectually contribute to so desirable an lind; and, for that Purpose, they have authorized their respective Plenipotentiary Ministers: viz. In the Name and on the Part of his Dri-tannic Majesty, his Privy Counsellors Earl of

wicke, his Chancellor of Great Britain, John Earl Granville, President of his Council, Thomas Holies Duke of

Newcajt/e, First Commissioner of his Treat'ury, Robert Earl of Holdernejje, one of his principal Secretaries of

State, and Henry Fox, Esquire, another of his principal Secretaries of State; and in the Name, and on the Part, of his PruJJan Majesty, the Sieur Lewis his Mi-

nifter, charged with his Affairs at the Court of his Britannic Majesty; which, after having reciprocally communicated to each other their full Powers, have agreed upon the following Articles:

Art. 1.

There shall be between the said most Serene Kings a sincere Peace and a reciprocal Fiiendship, notwithstanding any Disturbances which may arise in Europe in consequence of the above-mentioned Disputes; in pursuance whereof, neither of the Contracting Parties shall attack or invade, directly or indirectly, the Territory of the other, but, on the contrary, they will on each Side use all their Endeavours to prevent their respective Allies from undertaking any thing against the said Territory, in any manner whatever.

Art. a.

In case that, contrary to Expcdation, and in Violation of the Tranquillity which the High Contracting Parties mean to maintain by this Treaty in any

foreign Power should caul'e Troops to march into the said Germany, under any Pretence whatever, the said High Contracting Parties shall unite their Forces, in order to oppose the Entrance or Passage of such foreign Troops, and such Violation of the Peace, and to preserve the Tranquillity in Germany, according to the Object of the prefen t Treaty.

Art. 3.

The High Contracting Parties do expressly renew all the Treaties of Alliance and Guaranty which actually fub-fist between them; and namely, the Treaty of defensive Alliance, and of reciprocal Guaranty, concluded at minster, between their Britannic and Prussian Majesties, the 18th of November 1742; the Convention made be-, tween their said Majesties at Hanover, the 26th of gust 1745; and his Prussian Majesty’s Ad of Acceptation of that of his Britannic Majesty’s Guaranty of the 13th of October 1746.

Art. 4.

The present Treaty shall be ratified by his Majesty the King of Great Britain and by his Majesty the King of Prussia-, and the Letters of Ratification, in due Form, shall be delivered on each Side within the Space of One Month, or sooner, if possible, to be reckoned from the Day of the Signature of the present Treaty.

In Witness whereof; we the Under-written, being furnished with the full Powers of their Majesties the Kings of Great Britain and of Prussia, have, in their Names signed the present Treaty, and have put the Seals of our Arms thereto.

Done at Westminster, the Sixteenth Day of January in the Year of our Lord 1756.

(L. S.) Hardwicke, C.

(L. S.) Granville, P.

(L. S.) Holies Newcastle.

(L. S.) Holdernesse.

(L. S.) H. Fox.

Translation of a Secret and Separate Article belonging to the Treaty between his Majesty and the King of

PruJJa, signed at Westminster, the 16 th of January

1756*

Whereas the Convention of Neutrality signed this Day by the Ministers of his Majesty the King of Great Britain and of his Majesty the King of PruJJa, furnished VOL. 27.

with the necessary full Powers for that Purpose, relates TrpartJffia",tIx only to Germany, it is not to be extended to the ru ja‘

Netherlands, and the Dependencies thereof, which are not to be understood as being comprehended in the present Convention of Neutrality, under any Pretence whatsoever; and the rather, as his Majesty the King of PruJJa has, by the Eighth Article of the Treaty of Peace of Dresden, guarantied to her Majesty the Empress Queen of Hungary and Bohemia such Dominions only as Ihe is possessed of in Germany.

This Secret and Separate Article shall have the same Force as if it was inferred Word for Word in the present Convention of Neutrality signed this Day, and the Rati-fications thereof shall be exchanged at the same time as those of the said Convention.

In Witness whereof, we the Under-written, being furnished with full Powers from their Majesties the Kings of Great Britain and of PruJJa, have, in their Names, signed the present Secret and Separate Article, and have put the Seals of our Arms thereto.

Done at Westminster, the Sixteenth Day of January

in the Year of our Lord 1756.

Translation of a Declaration signed by the Plenipotentiary Ministers of his Majesty and the King of PruJJa, the 16th of January 1756.

In order to put an End to the Disputes which may have arisen between their PruJJanand Britannic Majesties,

it is declared, That, upon his PruJJan Majesty’s taking off the Attachment put upon the Sileja Debt, and causing to be paid to his Britannic Majesty’s Subjects w'hat remains due to them thereon, according to the original Contract, as well Interest as Principal, his Britannic Majesty does promise and engage, on his Part, to cause to be paid to his Prussian Majesty the Sum of Twenty thousand Pounds Sterling, for extinguilliing all and every Claim from his said Majesty, or his Subjects, upon his Britannic Majesty, under any Pretence whatever.

Done at Westminster, the Sixteenth Day of January, in the Year of our Lord 1736.

(L. S.) Louis Michell.

A P P E N D I X, N* 1.

To the Committee of the Company of Merchants trading to Africa.

Gentlemen,

As 1 fend you the Far, tee Recognition by this Conveyance, it will be proper fot me to say something concerning it: The Diary will shew you how the Death of Intuffero first introduced the Proposition of a Law; how I found by conversing with the inland Cabboceers, that they were willing to recognize our Right.

How all this was brought about, your Book'; will discover. I was obliged to be very liberal: The Braffoe* the Curranteers, the Priests, and all the principal Men in the Country, had Prefenfs both before and after passing the Law: These Presents were g^e :ter than otherwise they would have been, on account of the secret Opposition of John Currantee and Cosse Tango, Cabboceers of Annama-hue, who get so much from the French, that they do not want to Ice the Corned between them and us at an End. I did my utmuPt to gain them; but finding all Endeavours ineffectual, I went oir, and concluded with the BraffuC, Curranieers* and Priests, and with all Fautee, Annamaboe excepted, as John declared he was bound by the Law, but durst not sign it rill he got his Son from France.

The Proportion of those who have sworn to observe the Law, is, to Annamaboe* as Twenty to One, according to the best Accounts 1 can procure, and in the Number i9 their Legislature.

The B rafjbe and Curranieers, by and with the Advice of their God, whefe Oracles they receive horn the Priests, are the FcvilceLegiflaturc: The and

never drank Feitck (their Manner 01 1 wearing) tooblerve any Treaty, before this: At first they refused it, to observe the Law, but, by the Steadinels of Abrah and the Priests, they were obliged to take it.

When I first set out upon this Business, I looked upon it as extremely problematical, both inrefpcdto procuring the Law, and to the Efficacy of it after it was made: The Law is ratified more solemniy than any thing of the Kind ever was in this Country, and Time must shew the Advantage of procuring it.

From the Recognition itself, you will perceive, that I . Vol. 27

had another Point in View, which I thought was worth the risking £. f,oooo Sterling upon it has Cost about that Sum), and that was, to acquire a Right wherewith to combat the Pretensions of the French.

Before the Law was passed and ratified, we had nothing to shew in Support of our Right to exclude the French: The Brajfoeand Curranteers hail a Note, which shall be

altered, whereby we oblige ourselves to pay Ground Rent for Annamaboe, Aggah, and Anni/Ieaa; but, by this Note, we were onlyTenants at Will; and though we could have deputed the Right of the French to let tie at these very Places, yet what Pretence had we to exclude them*from settling elsewhere on the FaCoaft ? Their settling any-where upon it would do us as much hurt nearly as if they fixed themselves at Annamaboe -, where-ever the greatest Price is given, the Trade will go.

In procuring the Recognition, I think there is aPoffi-bility of persuading the French by fair Means to delift from their Enterprizes upon this Coast, at least till we are fixed, and can talk in a higher Strain to the People of Annamaboe, at a less Expence than we are at now.

To oblige the French to give up such an Attempt by superior Force alone, is wounding them in the tendered Part: If it can be shewn them that they have no Right to settle here, they may possibly be glad of the Discovery, as it may serve to bring them out of a Scrape, and bea Salvo for the Honour of their Prince. I mention this as it was oneof my Motives in taking so much Pains as I havedone to get the Recognition; to enlarge upon it would be indecent when I know into whose Hands this Letter is to go. I told you before, that Time must discover the Efficacy of this Law with respect to the Fantees themselves; They are a fiithlels and arapacious People, aConfcicufness of this appeared when they drank Fetick: No foonerdid the Bra foe's Son and the Curranteers fee the Fetick Water than their Countenances altered,a sudden Tremor seized them; and such a Languor, that they had scarcely Spirits to pronounce the Words of the Oath, and put their Hands to the Paper. Next Morning the y told me. They found 1 would be at their Hearts: I had got at their Hearts now; it was over, and they were glad of it.

One of the Pawns given for the Observance of the Law has a Desire to fee England, and goes home with Captain Cockburne :As he is to be One of the chiefPriefts of,

a little Money laid out upon his Education will not be thrownaway: If he istaught to read and write, it may ten- der him more useful to us, and may enable us the betterto keep up ourConnedions with the inland Ftf»/m;besides,. his Father, who is a Man of great personal Authority, expects that his Son shall be taught; and, in my Opinion, he ought to be gratified, as he has been one of the principal Actors in procuring the Law. I know there are Objections to teaching the Negroes to read and write, but I believe they would not hold good in the prefen t Cafe.

I am,

Gentlemen,

Your most obedient humble Servant,

Signed, Thomas Melvil.

APPENDIX, N* 2.

Upon the 12th of July last Mr. Poirier, the Secretary of the Committee for the Direction and Management of the Affairs of the African Company, acquainted me, that they were ready to pass their Accounts, and desired I would appoint a Day for that Purpose.

I then afleed him if all the Committee Men had acted? he told me, They had. Upon which I replied. They ought all to attend, that each might be sworn to his particular Receipts and Disbursements.

I appointed the 25th of July for the Committee to attend, upon which Day there came only the Five following:

They signed the Account first; and, as there is no particular Form in the Act of Parliament with regard to the Oath to be administered by the Cursitor Baron to the Committee, I prepared the following.

" You, and 'each of you, thall swear. That you " will true Answer make to such Questions as I thall atkyou, by virtue of an Act of Parliament, made " in the 23d Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, " intituled, An Act for extending and improving the " Trade to Africa.

" So help you God."

And atked each of them, when I had so sworn them after this Form, Upon the Oath that you have severally taken, does this contain afull and true Account of all the Money received by you, or by your Order, as Committee Men, for the Management of the Affairs of the African Company, and likewise of the Application thereof by you, or by your Order, from the 3d of 1734 to the 3d of July 1755?

I then desired they would acquaint the other Four Committee Men, that I expected they would attend to be sworn, and to sign the Account; for, as Three of the Committee are chosen by the Majority of the Freemen in Bristol, and Three others of the Committee by the Majority of the Freemen of Liverpo, I told them I thought it necessary that the Committee of each Place should be sworn, that the Freemen of the several Places might have the fulled Satisfaction of the Trustees having done their Duty.

They did not seem to think it right or necessary', but promised to acquaint their Brethren with it.

I then desired the Committee Men present would order their Secretary to lay before me the Minute Book, Charter Parties, Bills of Sale, Bills of Loading or Invoice, Bank Book, or any other Books or Papers which related to the Affairs of the African Company.

They said, Wednesday was their Committee Day; and they would then consider of it: After the Five Committee Men were gone, I gave their Secretary, in Writing, a Lid of the Books and Papers I wanted, that he might shew it to the Committee at their next Board, for their Order: Accordingly,

On the 3id of July lad the other Four Committee came:

Samuel Turner,

Charles Pole,

Vincent Bifcoe,

Robert Scott.

They objected at first to being (worn; and said, That the whole Committee were never sworn before; and that by the Act of Parliament Five were the Committee.

I answered, That the words of the Act, in the particular Clause that relates to the Cursitor Baron, mention, that the Committee should lay before him their Account upon Oath, and not Five, or a Part only; but whatever might be the Sense of the Clause, as I was to judge of it in the bed manner I was capable, it appeared to me to be the Intention of the Legislature that the whole Committee should be sworn; and, as they have all acted, it is my Opinion they ought all to sign and be sworn, for One Committee Man cannot swear what Sum or Sums another may have received or disbursed.

They did then sign the Account, and were sworn in the same Form as the other Five were; but went away immediately, without mentioning any thing relating to the Books and Papers.

After the Four last mentioned Committee Men were gone, Mr. Poirier, their Secretary, acquainted me. That the Committee had given him Orders not to leave any of the Books and Papers I required, but that he was ready to examine the Vouchers with the Account, I then told him* They appeared to be so numerous, that I

could not think of doing it info cursory a manner: That the Act of Parliament had appointed the Cursitor Baron, Auditor of this Account; and therefore it was necessary that I should have all the Lights which were possible in this Affair; and that I should be extremely cautious in passing it, unless I had a full and proper Examination of the Whole; for, as a Copy of such annual Account was directed by the Act to be laid before the Parliament, so audited by me, I ought to be particularly careful not to incur their Censure in any thing I do.

At the same time 1 desired Mr. Poirier, the Secretary, to acquaint the Committee, That I thought it a verygreat Slight and Contempt that they shouldrcfuietointruftme with the Books and Papers; and that I did not chuse to examine them with the Secretary in the First place, because in an Affair of this Conll-quence, I should take the Advice and Assistance of Persons who are conversant in Accounts, and would go through the Whole with the Secretary afterwards, when I was fully prepared to examine him upoA the Articles or Particulais of the Account; and that I would give him proper Notice when I required his At. tendance.

W hen I mentioned to Mr. Poirier, that I proposed to be afffted by Persons of Skill and Knowledge in Accounts, he replied. The Committee would not fuller any Person to inspect their Books and Papers, but the Cursitor Baron only; and, on my rcfuling to proceed in the Account unless the Books and papers were let:, lie said, He was only a Servant to the Committee, and mult obey (heir Orders, and thereupon went away, and took back (hole Books and Papers, which, upon the 25th ct July I directed Mr. Poirier to acquaint the Committee, I expected should be brought and left for my Inlpcction and Examination.

August the 7th 1755, Mr. Poirier attended me again by my Orders; and, upon my aflting him if the Committee had consented to my keeping the Books and Papers relating to the Account, that I might inspect; and examine them at my Leisure; he told me, That he was directed by the Committee to bring the Vouchers I required, and to assist me in comparing them, but not to leave them: Whereupon I said, If the Committee did not think proper to trust the Vouchers in my Hands, I should endeavour, as the Timewas verynearexpiring, toexaminetheAccount io his Presence as well as I was able, since they would not give me an Opportunity of doing it so well as I could with.

Mr. Poirier did accordingly attend me; and after, swearinghim, I went carefully and regularly through the whole Account Item by Item, and compared each Particular with the Minute Book of Orders of the Committee, with the Charter Parties or Agreements for Freight with the several Masters or Captains of Vessels, with the Bills of Lading or Invoices; and also examined the Receipts of the Committee, as stated by the Account, with the Bank Book, and found they corresponded with each other, except the Sum of £.184. which was retained by the Merchants at Bristol of the African Company, in Part Payment of the Expences they were put to in procuring the Act: of Parliament.

August nth, 1753, Mr. Samuel Poirier, the Secretary, attended me again, and produced the proper Vouchers from Thomas MelvilEfcjuire, Governor in Chief of all the

Forts upon the Coast of Africa, and from John Esquire, principal Engineer of the Fort at Amamaboe, residing in Africa, whereby they acknowledge the Receipt of the respective Dills of Lading of the several Vess-ls called the Hanover Planter, the Band the Spencer Fri-

iate-

drew up a Report of what appeared to me on the Face of the Account, and upon the Examination of Mr.

rier; and, on the tyth of August lull, I annexed it to the Account of the Committee of the Company of Merchants trading to Africa for the Year 1754.

On the 20th of August I lent it to Mr. Poirier, wlro said he would fiiew it to the Committee; at winch time he told my Clerk, that he apprehended a Copy only of this Account, Io audited by me, would be laid before the

Mr. Speaker also reported, That his Majesty was af- Theling't terwards pleated to make a most gracious Speech from sP*fC '* the Throne to both Houses of Parliament, of which Mr.

Speaker laid he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy; which he read to the House, and is as followeth; viz.

My lairds and Gentlemen,

After so long and unwearied Application to the public Business, it is reasonable that I Ihculd give you feme Recess: I must at the same time return you my hearty Thanks for the vigorous and effectual Support you have given me, in maintaining that just and national Cause in which I am engaged.

The Injuries and Hostilities which have been for feme time committed by the French, again!! my Dominions and Subjects, are now followed by the actual Invasion of the Wand of Minorca, which (lands guarantied to me by all the great Powers of Europe, and in particular by the French King: I have therefore found myself obliged, in Vindication of the Honour of my Crown, and of the Rights of my People, to declare War in Form again!!

France: I rely on the Divine Protection, and the vigorous Assistance of my faithful Subjects, in so just a Caule.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I return you my hearty Thanks for the lieadiness and Dispatch with which you have granted me such large Supplies; you may depend on their being strictly applied to the good Purposes for which they were given.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

Nothing has given me more inward Satisfaction than the Confidence which you repose in me: It is the most acceptable Return you could make to me, and you may be allured shall be made use of only for your Good: The Preservation of your Religion, Liberties, and Independency, is, and always shall be, my great Aim, and I trust you will not be wanting to yourselves.

And that, afterwards, the Lord Chancellor signified Adjournment, his Majesty’s Pleasure, that both Houses of Parliament should severally adjourn themselves until Friday the 18th Day of June next.

And the House accordingly adjourned till Friday the 18th Day of June next, Nine of the Clock in the Morning.
