A MESSAGE from his Majesty, by the honourable Sir Henry BeUenden, Gentleman L'lherof the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The King commands this honourable House to attend his Majesty, immediately, in the House ot Peers.

Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to attend his Majesty.

And being returned;

Several Members present took the Oaths, and made and subscribed the Declaration, and took and subscribvd the Oath of Abjuration, according to the Laws made for those Purposes.

A Bill for the more effectual preventing clandestine Outlawries, was read the Full time.

ReJ'ched, That the Bill be read a Second time.

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House had attended his Majesty, in the House of Peers: Where his Majesty was picafed to make a most gracious Speech from the rrhrone to both Houses of Parliament; of which, Mr. Sneaker said, lie had, to pi event Mistakes, obtained a Copy: Which lie read to the House; and is as followed]; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I have called you together in a Conjuncture, which "highly requires the Deliberation, Advice, and AfMarice, of Parliament; and I trust that (under the Guidance of Divine Providence) Union and Tirmness in my affectionate People will carry me with Honour through all Difficulties, and finally vindicate the Dignity of my Crown, and its indubitable Rights, against the antient Enemy of these Kingdoms.

The Succour and Preservation of America cannot but constitute a main Object of my Attention and Solicitude; and the growing Dangers, to which our Colonies may stanc! exnoled from our late Loftes in those Parts, demand Resolutions of Vigour and Dispatch.

An adequate and firm Defence at home mufl have the chief Place in my Thoughts; and, in this great View, I have nothing so much at heart as that no Ground of Dil-latistadlion may remain in my People.

To this End a national Militia, planned and regulated with equal Regard to the just Rights ot my Crown and People, may, in time, become one good Resource, in case of general Danger; and I recommend the framing of such a Militia to the Care and Diligence of my Parliament.

Vol. 27.

The unnatural Union of Councils abroad, the Calamities which, in consequence of this unhappy Conjunction* may, by Irruptions of foreign Armies into the Empire* shake its Constitution, overturn itsSyftem, and threaten Opprdfion to the Protestant Interest there, are Events which mud ienfibly acted the Minds of this Nation, and have fixed the Eyes of Europe on this new and dangerous Crisis.

The Body of my Electoral Troops, which I ordered hither at the Desire of my Parliament, I have directed to return'to my Dominions in Germany; relying, with Plea-lure, on the Spirit and Zeal of my People in Defence of my Person and Realm.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I wall order the proper Estimates to be laid in due time befote you; and I rely on your Wisdom, that you will prefer more vigorous Efforts (though attended with large Expence) to a less effectual, and therefore less frugal, Plan of War.

1 have placed before you the Dangers and Necessities of the Public; it will be your Care to lay in such a manner the Burthens you may judge unavoidable, as will lead distress and exhaust my People.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I pan not here be unmindful of the Sufferings of the poorer Sort from the present high Price of Corn, and the Disturbances which have arisen therefrom; and I recommend to you to consider of proper Provisions for preventing the like Mischiefs hereafter.

Unprolperous Events of War in the Mediterranean have drawn from my Subjects signal Proofs how dearly they tender my Honour, and that of my Crown; and they cannot, on mv Part, fail to meet with juit Returns of unwearied Cares, and unceasing Endeavours, for the Glory, Prosperity, and Happiness, of my People.

Resolved, That no Peer of this Realm hath any Right Ordered, That no Footman be permitted to be with* to give his Vote in the Election of any Member to serve in the Lobby of the House, or upon the Stairs leading in Parliament. thereto.

Refolded, That where the House shall judge any Petition touching Elections to be frivolous and vexatious, the House will order Satisfaction to be made to the Person petitioned against.

Resolved, That if it shall appear that any Person hath procured himself to be elected or returned a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt Practices, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Person.

Resolved, That if it shall appear that any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof, or directly or indirectly hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing or giving Evidence, the same is declared to be a high Crime and Misdemeanor, and this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That if it shall appear that any Person hath given false Evidence in any same before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That it is a high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain, for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from time to time, take into his Custody any Stranger or Strangers that he shall see, or be informed of to be, in the House or Gallery, while the House, or any Committee of the whole House, is fitting; and that no Person, so taken into Custody, be discharged out of Custody without the special Order of the House.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take care that there be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in the Room appointed for the Footmen attending the Members of this House to wait in.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take into his Custody such Footmen as shall presume to diibbcy the Orders of the House; and that no such Footmen be discharged out of Custody, but by the special Order of the House*

Ordered, That, to prevent the intercepting or losing of Letters directed to Members of this lioui'e, the Person appointed to bring Letters from the General Post Office to this House, or some other Person to be appointed by the Postmaster General, do, for the future, every Day* during the Session of Parliament, Sundays excepted, coo-stantly attend from Ten of the Clock in the Morning till One in the Afternoon, and for Two Hours at the least immediately after the Riling of the House; and also on every Monday, tVedneJ'day, and Friday, from Five of the Clock in the Afternoon till Seven, at the Place appointed for the Delivery of the said Letters; and take care, during his Stay there, to deliver the same to the several Members to whom they shall be directed, or to their known Servant or Servants, or others, bringing Notes under the Hands of the Members (ending for the fame.

Ordered, That the said Officer do, upon his going away, lock up such Letters as shall remain undelivered; and that no Letter be delivered but within the Hours aforesaid.

Ordered, That the said Orders be sent to the Post-nufter General.

Ordered, That when any Letter or Packet, directed to this House, shall come to Mr. Speaker, he do open the fame, and acquaint the House, at their next Sirring, with the Contents thereof, if proper to be communicated, to the House.

L

Ordered, That the Back Door of the Speaker’s Chamber be locked up every Morning at the Sitting of the House, and the Key delivered to the Clerk, to be locked upby him; and that he do not presume to deliver the same to any Person whatsoever, without Order of the House; and that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take care to clear the Speaker’s Chamber every Day before the Door is locked up.

Ordered, That no Member of this House do presume to bring any Stranger or Strangers into the House, or Gallery thereof, while the House is fitting.

Ordered, That the Constables and other Officers of Middlesex and Westminster do take care, that from Eleven ot' the Clock in the Morning to One in the Afternoon, and from Four till Six in the Afternoon, during the Sef-' fion of Parliament, the Passages through the Streets between Ten/ple Bar and Westminster Hall shall be kept free and open; and that no Obstruction be made by Cars, Drays, Carts, or otherwise, to hinder the Passage of the Members to and from this House; and that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do give Notice of this Order ro the Officers aforesaid.

Ordered, That the Constables in Waiting do take care that there be no Gaming or other Disorders in Westminster Hail, or the Passages leading to the House, during the Sitting of Parliament; and that there be no Annoyance by Chairmen, Footmen, or otherwise, therein or thereabouts.

Ordered, That the said Orders be font to the High Bailiff of Westminster; and that he do fee the same put in Execution.

Ordered, That the Votes of this House be printed, being first perused by Mr. Speaker; and that he do appoint the Printing thereof: And that no Person, but such as he shall appoint, do presume to print the fame.

Resolved, That this House will receive no Petitions for private Bills, after the 12th Day of February next.

Mr. 1'ownjhend reported from the Committee, appointed Yesterday to draw up an Address to be presented to his Majesty, That the Committee had drawn up an Address accordingly; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz Most gracious Sovereign,

We, your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled, beg Leave to return your Majesty our humble Thanks for your most gracious Speech from the Throne.

Your faithful Commons, excited by Duty, and warm with Gratitude, do, from our Hearts, acknowledge-the paternal Care and royal Condcfcension of your Majesty, in pointing out from the Throne such a Plan of Force for our Defence as may belt tend to the Satisfidlion of your People, and, in particular,a well modelled national Militia, as One proper Security for your Majesty’s Person and Realm.

In this present arduousCbnjun£ture, your faithful Commons, next after Divine Providence, rely on your Majesty’s WifJoni and Magnanimity, remembering Efforts in times puft, under Princes whose (irft Glory was to found, hke your Majesty, the Strength of their Government in the Contentment and Harmony of their Subjects.

Thus united, and thus animated, this House will chcatfu'ly lunport your Majesty through all Difficulties, and vindicate, to theutmoli, the Dignity of your Crown, and its indubitable Rights, against the ancient Enemy of these Kingdoms.

Wc trust, your Majesty. strengat home, will find yourself revered abroad, and in a Condition to support that Weight and Consideration in Europe which belong to a King of Great Britain, notwithstanding the unnatural and unhappy Union of Councils which have formed on the Continent lo new and dangerous a Crisis.

Th is House thinks with Pain on the fad Events of War in the Mediterranean and in America ,\they will take tiiefe affecting Matters into their most serious Consideration, not imputing Blame to any unheard; and will, with ail Confidence, Alacrity, and Dispatch, second your Majesty’s royal Care for the Speedy Succour and Preservation of America, under the growing Dangers to which those invaluable Possessions stand exposed.

We beg Leave to act ire your Majesty, That your faithful Commons will co.ifider of proper Provisions lor the Relief of the poorer Sort from the pufent high Price of Corn, and for preventing the like Mischiefs hereafter, according to the royal and compassionate Recommendation of your Majesty.

Vice Admiral Bofcazven, from the Commissioners for executing the Office of Lord High Admiral of Great Britain, acquainted the House, That the King and the Board of Admiralty having been dissatisfied with the Conduct of Admiral Byng, in a late Action with the French Fleet in the Mediterranean, and for the Appearance of his not having acted agreeably to his Instructions, for the Relief of Minorca, he is now in Custody of the Marshal of the Admiralty, in order to be tried by a Court Martial. Although this is no more than what is usual in like Cafes, yet as Admiral Byng is now a Member of this House, and as his Confinement may keep him some time from his Duty here,' the Board of Admiralty think it a Respect due to the House, to inform them of this Commitment, and of the Reasons thereof.

A Petition of the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Burgesses, of the Borough of NewcnJUeunder Lyne, in the County of Staf-

ford, was presented to the House, and read; representing to the House the Mileries and Hardships to which the poorer Sort are reduced by the present high Price of Provisions; and alleging, that the present Dearnels of Corn is not, as the Petitioners apprehend", occasioned by a real Scarcity of that Article in their Neighbourhood or County, but by an artificial Scarcity, created by the Millers and Badgers, to whom it has, for tome time part, been almost a general Practice, in the said County, for the Farmers to lell their Corn at their own Houses, instead of bringing it to Market: Tha,t the Millers grind theirs into Flour, which they fell out wholesale, mixing it with pernicious Ingredients of a lower Value; That the Badgers bring their Corn to Market, but by confederating among!? themselves to expose to Sale but small Quantities at a time, by buying up what little the Farmers yet bring to Market, before those, that want it for their own life, can supply themselves; and, by many other Contrivances, have brought it up to the exorbitant Price it now bears, which the Poor are obliged to p3y, as they cannot pofii-bly be supplied from any other Persons: That, if these Practices are suffered to continue, the Petitioners believe that all Kinds of Grain will soon be at a much higher Price than they are even at present; and further representing to the House, that when Farmers brought their Corn, and other Produce of their Farms, to Market, and there fold them to the Consumer, all such Commodities were at a reasonable Price; and that it is undoubtedly the Interestof a trading Nation to take care that the useful and industrious Manufacturer may be furnished with a Subsistence, for himself and his Family, upon moderate Terms; by which means the Price of Labour will be kept down, and the Petitioners shall be able to underfed their Rivals at foreign Markets: And therefore hoping that the House will take the Premises into their moll lerious Considera-

A Petition of the Lords of the Manor of Barton Stacy, in the Parish of Barton Stacy, in the County of ampton, and others, on behalf of themselves, and the other Freeltolders and Proprietors of Lands within the said Manor, was pretented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, by Articles bearing date the lft of August 1755, the said Proprietors entered into an Agreement for dividing and inclosing the common Fields, common. Downs, Meadows, and Pastures, within the said Manor, in such manner as should be ordered and appointed by Edward Goddard Esquire, James Poore, and 'Thomas Blandy, by their Award under their Hands and

Seals before the First of May then nepct enduing.; and that, in pursuance thereof, the said Edward Goddard, James Poore, and Thomas Blandy, made their Award, dated the Twenty-sixth April 1756, whereby they divided, set out, and apportioned, to every of the said Proprietors, their several Shares of the said common Fields, common Downs, Meadows, and Pastures, and appointed the several Inclosures and Fences to be made by the Persons to whom such Shares are fespectively set out; and also directed such Exchanges to be made, as will be necessary to enable the several Proprietors of the Lands so divided to hold their respective Shares in Severalty; but although such Divisions, Exchanges, and Inclosures, w'ill be of great Advantage to the Teveral Proprietors, and of public Utility, yet the same cannot be rendered effectual without the Authority of Parliament: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to confirm and establish the said Articles of Agreement and Award, in such manner as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Mr. Bankes and Mr. Fellowes do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

And then the House adjourned till Monday Morning, Nine of the Clock.

Sir John Philipps reported from the Committee, who were appointed to consider of proper Provisions for preventing the high Price of Corn and Bread for the future; and to report the fame, with all convenient speed, to the House; That the Committee had made some Progrefe in the Matter to them referred; and had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table; Where the feme were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it Is the Opinion of this Committee, That the taking off the Duty upon foreign Corn, to be imported into this Kingdom, for a limited Time, wilf-be a proper and speedy Means of reducing the present high Price of Corn and Bread.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the permitting such foreign Meal, Bread, and Biscuit, as hath been, or shall be, taken from the Enemy, to be landed and expended in this Kingdom, Duty-free, for a limited time, will be another proper and speedy Remedy of reducing the present high Price of Corn and Bread.

Mr. Ridley reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Sheriff, and the rest of the Common Council, of the Town of upon Tyne, in Common Council assembled, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same as it appeared to them, together with the Resolution of the Committee thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followed } viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition.

Mr. Alderman Stephenson of London, and Mr. William

Aynjley, being severally examined, laid. That great Quantities of Butter are made in the Counties adjacent to castle, viz. Northumberland, Durham, Cumberland, and West more land; great Part of which are carried to

castle, to be expended and otherwise disposed of: That Butter is a principal Article at; great Quanti-

ties whereof are sent to London: That they have frequently heard the Factors complain of a Deficiency of Weight in the Butter at Newcastle, they being obliged to make up 56 lb.in each Ftrkin, though they do not receive so much from the Maker.

That, for Time out of mind, there has been a free Market for Butter at the Cale Cross in Newcastle: That there is no Statute for the just Weighing of Butter there, nor has the Corporation any Power to punish for felling short Weight; and thar it would be of great Advantage in general, if Power was given to ascertain the Goodneis, Weight, and fair Packing, of Butter brought to the said Town to be sold.

Mr. Henry Cooling, Cheesemonger in London, being examined, laid, That he has bought Butter from castle, which does not bear so good a Character, as to Weight and Quality, as Butter from does; there being generally Three or Four Shillings a Firkin Difference: That Cheesemongers, who have Butter sent from Newcastle, are obliged to trull to the Factors to fend them what they think proper; That it would be of great Advantage to the Public, if a proper Officer was appointed to weigh and mark Butter at Newcastle; for then Masters of Vessels could not cut out any of the Firkins without being detedled;

That, instead of having the Calk xo Weight, they frequently make them 14 or 1 Weight; and there is no Penalty on not tareing the Calk; and that if a Searcher was appointed at Newcastle, the Cheesemongers would not be fond of fending for Butter to other Places.

Upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolutions -,viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Petitioners have fully proved the Allegations to their Petition.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the House be moved. That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to prevent Frauds in the Weight, Quality, and Packing, of Butter, in the Town of Newcastle upon Tyne, in the County of the Town of Newcastle upon Tyne.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to prevent Frauds in the Weight, Quality, and Packing, of Butter, in the Town of Newcastle upon Tyne, in the County of the Town of Newcastle upon Tyne: And that Mr. Ridley and Sir Thomas Clavering do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of the Mayor and Burgesses of the Borough of Stafford, in the County of Stafford, in Common Council assembled, was presented to the House and read; taking Notice of the distress'ed State of the poorer Sort of People in the said Town and Neighbourhood, by theex-ceflive high Price of Corn and other Provisions, occasioned, as the Petitioners believe, by the almost general Practice which hath, for some time past, prevailed in that and the neighbouring Counties, for the Farmers to fell their Corn at their own Houses to the Millers, who manufacture the same into Flour, and to the Badgers, who buy Com to fell again in that private and collusive manner, that it is very difficult, if not impossible, by the Laws now in Force against Forestallers, Engrossers, and lle-grators, to remedy this so great and much-complained-of Grievance: and, it being doubtful, whether there is any Law now inbeing, which can hinder the Farmers from felling Corn at their own Houses, representing to the House, that if the Laws now in being against Forestallers, Engrossers, and Begrators, wereclearly explained and amended, and all Millers, and others, buying Corn to manufacture into Flour, to fell, all Bakers, and others, making Bread to fell, and all Badgers, Laders, Kidders, Carriers, Buyers, and Transporters, of Corn or Grain, licensed, and to be licensed, were obliged to buy their Corn in open Market, and not by Sample, otherwise or elsewhere, and making the Method of convicting the Offenders more easy and concise, it would abate the present excessive high Price of Corn, and prevent the like for the future: And therefore expressing the Hope of the Petitioners, that the House, the Premises considered, will provide such Remedy or Remedies, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, who are appointed to consider of proper Provisions for preventing the high Price of Corn and Bread for the future.

That, in pursuance of the said Act, a Workhouse was set up in the said City, and now continues; and that the Poor thereof have been, and are, employed and maintained there, and several considerable Sums of Money have been given to the Corporation for the Uses aforesaid; but that the Revenues of the said Corporation, and the Monies thereby impowered to be by them raised, afterfome Y'ears, became insufficient for the Maintenance of the Poor; and also reciting several Parts of an Act, made in the 13th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, for repealing Part, and making more effectuul the Residue of, the aforesaid Act; and alto setting forth, that, in pursuance of t he said last mentioned Act, the Poor of the Hamlets of Sr. Michael, St. , and St.

In Support of the Allegations of the said Petition,

Mr. John Simpson, being examined, said, That he is acquainted with the Parish of Saint Luke, and that it is a very large and populous Parish, and adjoins, on the South Part thereof, to the Liberties of the City of , and contains upwards of Three thousand Houses, and that not above One Third of the Inhabitants pay to the Rates made for die Relief of the Poor.

And that the present Rates are Four Shillings in the Pound, and that they raise at this time about 1,500; and that die Proportion charged upon the Stock, is now Seven Shillings and Six Pence for every One hundred Pounds: That he has paid for Stock himself many Years, and that he apprehends they have no Power to aifefs the Rates by the Laws in being.

Mr. IVillnm Spencer confirmed the Evidence of Mr. Simpson; and added, that if the Landlords, who lett Houses in Tenements ready fumished, were obliged to pay to the Rates for the Relief of the Poor, it would be a great lv.ue to the Parish in general:

the South Side of a Street, Way, or Passage, called Jage into Spring Garden, and the North Side of certain Houses, Buildings, and Walls, belonging to his Majesty’s Office of Admiralty; and that the Petitioners ordered an Estimate of the Value of the said several Premises to be made} whereby it appears, that, on a moderate Computation, the total Value thereof amounts to 25,344; and that the Petitioners finding the said Estimate amount to lb large a Sum, they directed an Estimate to be made of the Expence of purchasing so much only of the said Premises as would be absolutely necessary for opening and widening the said Street leading from Charing Cross, so as to make the narrow Part thereof of an equal Breadth with the present Breadth of Parliament Street, and to leave Ground besides sufficient for erecting a Row of Front Houses next to the said Street leading from Charing Cross; distinguishing, in that Estimate, how much such Expence would amount to, exclusive of leaving Ground for erecting the said Row of Front Houses; the Whole of which Estimate amounts to 18,634; and that deducting the reout the Value of Ground for erecting the said Row of Front Houses, will reduce the feme to £. 11,402: And alleging, that in case all the above-mentioned Premises, estimated at 25,344, were to be purchased, the Petitioners would be thereby enabled to use lb much thereof as (ltould be necessary to open and widen the said Street leading from Charing Cross in a commodious and handsome manner; and the remaining Ground, which would be proper for building Houses thereon, /night be fold, or lett on Building Leases, for such public Ule as to the House shall seem meet; but if it should be deemed more proper for the Purposes aforesaid, to purchase only so much of the said Premises as are comprised in One of the said Idler Estimates of £. 18,634, or £. 11,402, the Petitioners apprehend, that either of those x7

Purchases would be diladvantageous to the Public; and the remaining Premises, unpurchaled by the Petitioners, would in all Probability be incapable of being made into a uniform Range of Buildings: And further letting forth, that it would be proper to open and widen the public Way near Whitehall, by pulling down a Brick Messuage which adjoins to the East Side of the old Gate-way near the House Guards, the Purchase of which Messuage, the Petitioners are informed, will cost about £.1,137; an<^ that, besides the Sums necessary to make such of the Purchases above mentioned as shall be deemed proper to be made, further Monies will also be requisite, to enable the Petitioners to defray several other incidental Expences which will unavoidably attend their executing the Powers and Trufis reposed in them by the said Act; and as the Sum of £ 10,000 granted to the Petitioners by that Act, fells greatly short, as they apprehend, of carrying the Purposes of the said Act into Execution, they have not as yet applied for the Payment of any Part thereof: And therefore praying the Hou'e to grant the Petitioners such Sums of Money, and such other Aid, to enable them effectually to execute the several Powers and Tiufts reposed in them by the said Act of the'last Session, as to the House shall l’eem meet.

Sir Cordel Firebrace reported from the Committee, to

whom the Petition of several Trustees for putting in Execution an Act, made in the 20th Year of his present Majesty's Reign, for opening, cleansing, repairing, and improving, the Haven of Southwold, in the County of Suffolk, and of several other Persons, Inhabitants of the Towns of South wold, HulcJ'jcorth, and other Towns and Places in the said County of Suffolk, whose Names are thereunto lub* feribed, Was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Tabic: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

The said Act was read; whereby several Rates and Duties were granted, and several Powers given, for the Purpose of opening, deanfing, repairing, and improving, the said Haven. Then,

Mr. John Poole was examined; who laid. That the Trustees to the said Act have not been able, under the Provisions thereof, effectually to perform the Works thereby directed to be done: That they have been obliged to employ the whole Money arising from the Rates and Duties in Support of the Piers only, which has not been sufficient even for that single Purpose: That if the said Haven was thoroughly repaired, it would be of general Advantage; for which Purpose it is absolutely necessary that the Terms of the said Act should be enlarged, and ibme Alterations and Additions made thereto.

Mr. Thomas Knight, being examined, said, That the

River Blyth in Suffolk is capable of being made navigable from the said Haven to Ha Bridge in the said County; and that if the Navigation of the said River was opened, and effectual Provision made for maintaining the lame, it would be of great Benefit and Convenience to the Inhabitants of the said County, and to the Public in general.

Mr. Thomas Manning, Engineer, laid, That he apprehends the said River Blyth may ealily be made navigable.

Ordered, That I-cave be given to bring in a Bill for making the River Blyth navigable from,

in the County of Suffolk, into the Haven of Soutlnvold; and alia for enlarging the Term, and amending and alter-Von. 27.

Upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolutions:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That John Mitton having, on the 19th Day of this instant January, delivered to Sir Nicholas Baily Baronet, a Member of this House, a Copy of a Writ fakement against him in an Action of Trespass, with an Intention to serve Notice of such Action on the said Sir Nicholas Baily, is thereby guilty of a Breach of the Privilege of this House.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That William Williams, Attorney at Law, having caused the said Copy of a W rit, in an Action of Trespass, to be delivered to Sir Nicholas Baily Baronet, a Member of this

House, with an Intention to serve Notice of such Action on the said Sir Nicholas Baily, is thereby guilty of a Breach of the Privilege of this House.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Thomas Gooch, having directed the said Writ, in an Action of Trespass, to be served on Sir Nicholas Rally Baronet, a Member of this House, is thereby guilty of a Breach of the Privilege of this House.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the QuelUon severally put thereupon, agreed to by*the House.

A Petition of the Matter, Wardens, Assistants, and Commonalty, of the Society of Merchants Adventurers of Iron, within the City of Bristol, under their common Seal, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, That great Quantities of Bar Iron are imported into this Kingdom from Sweden, Russia, and other Parts, which are chiefly paid for in Specie; feme of1 which lion is exported again to Africa, and other Places, slndthe rest is wrought up by the Manufacturers and alleging, that Bar Iron brought from North America would answer the same Purposes; and the Importation of it would tend not only to the great Advantage of this Kingdom, by increasing its Shipping and Navigation, but also to that of the Colonies; and that by an Act, passed in the 23d Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, the Importation of Bar Iron from America into the Port of London, Duty-free, was permitted, but prohibited from being carried Coastwise, or further by Land than Ten Miles Distance; by means whereof, several very considerab'e manufacturing Towns are deprived of the Use of American Iron, and the Out-ports are prevented from employing it in their Export Trade;

And therefore praying, That Bar Iron may be imported from North America into Great Britain, Duty-free, by alt his Majesty’s Subjects.

A Petition of the Commissioners appointed by virtue of the Acts of Parliament for restoring the Harbour of Rye, in the County of Sussex, to its ancient Goodness, was presented to the House, and read; representing the Ulefulness and Convenience of the said Harbour: And alleging, that the Commissioners appointed to execute the Powers given by the said Acts have proceeded with the utmost Integrity and Diligence, as salt as the Income of the Fund granted, and the Money which could be borrowed thereon, would allew; and that the moil difficult and expensive Parts of the Works are done; but the Commissioners could not carry on the remaining Works till they had paid, from the Produce of the Fund, the Money which had been borrowed thereupon; and that the Petitioners would now proceed with the utmost Diligence to complete the said remaining Works, if they were enabled thereunto by having the Term and Powers granted by the former Acts for those Purposes further continued, or by such other Means as this House shall think proper: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to do therein what to them shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Merchants* Maltsters, and Farmers, Distillatioti in Ipswich, and Places adjacent, whose Names are there- from Com. unto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and many others, was presented to the House, and read; taking Notice,

That Provision is to be made to restrain the distilling Barley, Malt, and all other Grain, for a limited Time; and representing, that very large Quantities of Wheat and Barley arc so ordinary and damaged as to be rendered unfit for ar.y other Use than distilling; and alleging, that very considerable Quantities of Malt are made in that'

Country, which are not fit for the Brewers; and that in case the Distillers are restrained from the Use of Barley,

Malt, and all other Grain, the Petitioners apprehend it will put a Stop to a great Part of the Malting Trade, and leave the ordinary Barley upon the Farmers Hands:

And therefore praying the House to take into Consideration the great Inconveniences and Hardships the Petitioners and many others must inevitably suffer by restraining the Distillers from using Bailey, Malt, and all other Grain, and to make such Provision for their Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the several Farmers and Occupiers of Ditto. Lind in the County of Norfolk was also presented to the House, and read; taking Notice, That a Bill is now depending to restrain the distilling of Barley, Malt, and all Grain whatsoever, for a limited Time; and alleging, that if the same pass into a Law, it will be very hurtful to the Petitioners, who have great Quantities of Barley now in their Barns, of so ordinary a Quality, that the same is deemed fit for no other Use than to be converted into Malt for the Use of Distillers, who can use such ordinary Malt as cannot be used by Brewers: And therefore praying, That the Distillers may not be restrained from using ordinary Barley malted.

Ordered, That the said Petitions be referred to the said Committee of the whole House.

Then the House resolved itself into the said Committee.

Mr. Thomas Coale, Clerk to the Guardians of the Poor of the Town of Plymouth, being examined, said, That he had seen the Rates made for the Relief of the Poor, from the Year 1715 to 1748, and that they all amounted to the Sum of £. 672. i$s. 3d. and that the yearly Rate or Aflertment of £.672. i :s. zd. hath been annually raised pursuant to the Directions of the said Act; but that the said Sum has been found insufficient to answerthe Purposes intended by the said Act; and that several Sums' of Money have been borrowed at interest, amounting, in the Whole, to the Sum of£.1,200:

And that the Poor of the said Town and Parishes of Plymouth arc become very numerous, and burdensome to the said Town:

That the Expences of relieving and passing Vagrants were formerly allowed and reimbursed out of the County Rates, but that the same hath been discontinued for about Twenty-two Years !act pail:

That he was lent to the Sessions in MiJsummer 1749, to move the Sessions to be allowed the Money out of the County Rates, for passing of Vagrants; and that the Jutbces laid they had no Power to relieve them, as the Town of Plymouth had refused to pay their Quota of the Charge of support ng and maintaining the public Gaols and Holpitnls of the County of Devon.

Mr. Abraham Pyke, being examined, laid, That many of his Majesty’s S! ups of War are built, repaired, harboured, Rationed, and fitted out, and do rendezvous, in the Bay and Port of Plymouth; and that great Numbers of the Wives of Seamen who serve on board, or belong to, the said Ships, do daily resort to their Husbands in the said Port, from divers Parts of Great Britain and Ireland; and that great Numbers of Soldiers, sent to serve in his Majesty’s Army and Garrisons abroad, do frequently come to the said Town, in order to embark from thence to the respective Places of their Destination; and, upon their Departure, many of their Wives and Children remain and are left in the said Town in great Distreis, and are forced to beg lor their Suilenance, and do frequently commit Acts of Vagrancy, and are relieved and main- tained, and sent away by Vagrant Pafies, in order to be

Part of an Act passed in the First Year of the Reign of King James the First, for the Explanation of the Statute made in the Fifth Year of the Reign of Queen Elizabeth, concerning Labourers, was read; whereby it appeared, that the Powers in the said Act were extended to rate the Wages of any Labourers, Weavers, Spinsters, >7

A. 1757.

Workmen, or Workwomen, whatsoever, either working by the Day, Week, Month, Year, or taking any Work at any Person or Persons Hands whatsoever, to be done in Great, or otherwise.

Part of another Act, passed in the 29th Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, for preventing Disputes among the Persons concerned in the Woollen Manufactures, was allb read; whereby it appeared. That, from and after the 24th Day of June 1756, it should be lawful for the Justices of the Peace, assembled at arty of their General or Quarter Sessions held next after Michaelmas, yearly, to make Rates for the Payment of Wages to Weavers, and others employed in the Woollen Manufactures, according to the Number of Yards that the Chains are laid upon the Warping Bars, and not otherwise.

Mr. William Vallaway, being examined, said, That he is a Clothier at Stroudivater, and manufactures great Quantities of Broad Cloths:

That he never heard of any Rate for Wages being made by the Justices of the Peace, before the First Year of his present Majesty, when a Rate was made, of which he has l'een an attested Copy; but that it was a very different Rate from that made by the Justices at the last Michaelmas Sessions: That the said former Rate was never complied with, that he has heard of:

And being asked why r he said, The Trade could not be carried on under it.

He further laid, That a Petition was preferred by the Weavers to the Justices for GlonceflerJiiire, at their last Michaelmas Quarter Sessions, held the 5th of October, praying, That they would proceed to make a Rate in pursuance of the Authority given them by the Statute of the 29th of his present Majesty: That a Counter Petition, or Memorial, was prefen ted to the Justices by the Clothiers; and the Merits of both Petitions were fully entered into, and Evidence examined on both Sides; after which the Justices gave it as their Opinions, that no equitable Rate could be made by the Hundred, or the Yard:

That the immediate Consequence of this was, that the Weavers appeared in a tumultuous manner, even before some of the Clothiers left Ghuc as they did in several other Parishes, viz. Stroud, Hampton, Bifley, and many other Places: That they committed great Outrages, and interrupted many of the Weavers that were desirous to work: That several of the Witnesses Weavers complained to him, that they were forced from their Looms by the Mob:

That these Disorders were a very great Impediment to Trade, and continued from first to last for Six or Seven Weeks; and verily believes, the Loss to the Country* from these Disturbances, was from £. 15 to f. 20,600.

That, at an Adjournment 01 the said Miihaeimas Quarter Sessions, which was held at Gloucester on the Sixth of November last, a Rate was made; which Rate was produced, and is hereunto annexed. Appendix, N° 1, but that the same is so formed as not to be complied with, without Prejudice to Trade in general:

And being asked his Reasons, he laid. That, by the Hundred and Yard, it was not possible to ascertain the true Value of Weaving; for many other Considerations were to be taken in; viz the Weight as well as the Number of Threads in the Chain or Warp, the Breadth that islet in the Loom, the Colour, the Fineness of the Abb, which is the Shoot that is wove into the Piece, the Size of the Threads, feme being as large again as others, according to the different Purposes for which the doth is intended; also the Colour, as well as the Quantity, of the Abb. These were his general Objections to the Rate: That he had particular Objections to the Rate; some of which were as follows:

That, under the Article of 1,200Threads to the Chain, he makes Four different Sorts of Cloth; each Piece containing the same Number of Yards; for which he uled to pay \-js.6d. lot. zis.and 22 6 per Piece, for

Weaving: That Three of the Sorts he makes in common, the other occasiooally: That this Rate obliges the

Clothiers

a 40 Februariu

30 Geo. II. 24 0 Februa731

Clothiers to pay zis. 6d. Piece for all Articles of

1,200 Threads to the Chain, without Distinction: That, in the Prices he used to pay, he believes as good Wages were earned at the lowed as the highed Price: That the highed Sort is what he makes the lead of; and the Length of these Goods is 30 Ells apiece.

Being asked, whence this Difference of Wages arose ? he said, From the different Sorts and Qualities of the Goods, and the different Purposes for which they were intended; some being Six Quarters, some Seven, and feme Eight, Quarters in Breadth: That if he is obliged to pay 22 j. 6 d.for that which he used to pay 17*. 6 it would be impossible for him to follow this Part of his Bud nets: That he had paid 17J. 6 per Piece for that particular Sort, for Two or Three Years: And being asked, whether the same Sort was made in his Neighbourhood ? he said. Very probably it was:

That he had carried on Business Ten Years, and had never varied in his Prices.

Being asked, by whom this Rate was settled? he said. He believed by some Clothiers and some Weavers.

He further Taid, That he made Goods confiding of 1,600 Threads in the Chain: That the Difference between the Price settled by this Rate for weaving a Piece of Goods of this Number of Threads in the Chain, and what he formerly paid, is 7 s. 6d.per Piece, or £.23 per Cent, to his Prejudice:

That, by the Cudom of the Country, every Hundred of the Chain confids of One hundred and NinetyThreads; and that a Bear is One-fifth of >90 Threads, or One hundred of the Chain: That for a Piece of Cloth of Eleven hundred and Two Bears (or Two-fifths of a Hundred) in the Chain, 45 Yards in Length, which, when milled, is to be Seven Quarters in Breadth, he is to pay, by this Kate, 18$. 9 d.for the Weaving: If he was to make a Cloth of the same Sort, and the same Length, Eight Quarters wide, there ought to be an Addition of One-seventh in the Price of Weaving, which would make it 5 per Piece; but, according to this Rate, an Addition of One-seventh Part of the Chain will bring it under the Article of’1,300 in the Chain; for which, by the Rate, he mud pay 25 3d. per Piece for the Weaving; which ought to be, according to the foregoing Proportion, but 21 5

And that if he should make a Cloth of the same Sort and Length, for Nine Quarters wide, which is a Cloth now greatly in Demand, that would be 1,400, and Three Bears, in the Chain; for which, according to the above Proportion (viz.adding Two-sevenths to the Price of weaving a Cloth of Seven Quarters wide), he ought to pay £. 1. 4J. id; whereas, by this Rate, he is obliged to pay

£. 1. 11 s 1 o' d. or thereabouts:

That, in some Sorts of Cloth, if he was to pay his Weavers according to the Letters of this Rate, he should pay them from £.20 to £.30 per Cent, and above, less than what he usually has paid, and does now pay, them for those Sort of Goods; in one Indance, particularly, he pays them £.\. is. id. per Piece weaving, which, accord-

ing to the Rates, comes only to 1 id. per Piece.

Being asked the Question, he said. He made from superfine to very low-priced Cloths; and that a Cloth of the same Hundred in the Chain may be worth One-fourth more in the Labour of Weaving than another: That he believes it impossible to form a Rate to get over thel'e Difficulties:

That one Workman will make the same Cloth much more valuable than another with the same Materials, by the Difference of his Work:

That a good indudrious Weaver, with his Wife and one Child, with full Employ, can earn from 13*. to i8r. per Week, with one Loom:

That he thinks it impossible to make an equal Rate by the Breadth of the Cloth:

That he never heard of any Rate being made for the Wages of Workmen in the Woollen Manufacture, in any other County of England:

That the Peace of the County was redored soon after the making of the Rate; but that the Soldiers were then V01. 27.

quartered there; and believes, if they were gone* the like Outrages will be renewed:

That these Disputes affect every Branch of the Manufacture.

Mr. 'Thomas Powell,a Broad Cloth Weaver, being examined, laid, That he employs Two Looms, One for Mr. Onifephorus Paul, and the other for Mr. Thomas Roberts's Work:

That he can earn at one Loom, with an Apprentice, from i6j. to 18 j. a Week: That if the Apprentice has wove for Five or Six Years, can earn with one Loom Three Shillings in 13 or 16 Hours; and that, in general Weavers, if they are not idle and unskilful, may earn a comfortable Livelihood.

And being asked the Question, said, That he did not think the Rate an equitable One, as the Weavers cannot earn so much by 6 d.a Day upon some Sort of Work a’s on others of the same Hundred Threads in the Chain.

And he apprehends, that if it was left open fot Clothiers and Weavers to make their own Bargains, it would be more advantageous for the Trade in general; and if the Clothiers were to make their own Rate, and abide by it, it would make very well for the Weavers Trade.

And being asked the Question, fa id, He thought ho equitable Rate could be made, on account of the Difference of the Breadth of Cloth, and the Allowance that mud be made for the Difference in the Weight of the Thread:

That he works upon the middling Sort of Work for Mr. Roberts: That the Weavers are, in general, better paid by this Rate; but, for some Work in the Trade, are worle paid than before: That he has worked for the above Gentlemen about 20 Years, and always had the same Prices for his Work:

That if a Rate should be made agreeable to the Weavers, it would certainly transfer the Work to other Counties:

That the Persons he works for employ a great many Weavers, and pay them the same Prices for the same Kind of Work; and that it is usual to make Agreements with the Maders.

Lazarus Brown, a Broad Cloth Weaver, being examine ed, said, That he works for Mr. Nathanael , and employs one Loom; and that, with a Boy, he can earn from 16s. to 18/.per Week.

Being asked the Question, he said, That a Journeyman Weaver, if he has Work, may earn 1 in a Day of 14 Hours, including Meals, which he thinks Money enough; and that the Mai ter Weavers allow thenvPrivilege, which is small Beer, Lodging and Firing, which is reckoned at One Shilling a Week more.

Samuel Hopkins, a Journeyman Broad Cloth Weaver, being examined, laid, He works upon Mr. Roberts's Work; and that he can earn, if he is condantly employed. One Shilling a Day of 14 or 13 Hours; and that they have Privilege over and above, which is worth One Shilling a Week more:

And that if lie works close, can earn One Penny per Hour: That any Journeyman, who is a good Workman, can earn at that Rate.

Michael Harmer, a Journeyman Broad Cloth Weaver, being examined, laid, He works for Mr. Peach, and has been a Journey mat) Weaver for 30 Years: That he can earn 6j. a Week, working 14 Hours a Day; and has, over and above that, final! Beer and Lodging, which is worth is. per Week more; and that he has always, during the 30 Years lie has been Journeyman, been paid the same Wages.

Whereupon the Committee came to the following Resolutions:

A Petition of the Mayor, and several of the Aldermen and Members of the Common Council, and other principal Inhabitants, of the City of , was presented

to the House, and read; talcing Notice, That Application hath been made to the House by the Governor and Guardians of the Poor of the said City, for a further Power to levy and raise much larger Sums of Money upon the Inhabitants of the fev ral Parishes and Precincts within the said City, than they have hitherto done, for the Support and Maintenance of the Work house, and Poor thereto belonging, and for discharging certain Debts already con-trafted by the said Governor and Guardians, and forraifing a proper Fund to provide Lamps for the better lighting the Streets of the said City; and alleging, that the Petitioners upon a strict and thorough Examination and Inquiry into the State and Accounts of the said Workhouse, are persuaded that the Application of the said Governor and Guardians is just and reasonable; as it plainly appears, that the Levies now raised by the said Governor and Guardians upon the said Inhabitants, together with the additional Incomeof their several Estates, and all other Be-nefactions whatsoever, are not sufficient to answer the Expence of the said House and Poor; and that this hath actually been the same for many Years; by which means, as well as by providing and Lighting Lamps for the whole City for Twenty eight Years, without any particular Allowance for that Purpose, they first began to be in Debt, and so continue; and that the said Governor and Guardians have long laboured under great Difficulties in procuring and causing the said Levies to be col left ed and paid by the respective Parish Officers of the said City to the Treasurer of the said Workhouse, by reason of a Defect in the former Acts of Parliament made for that Purpose; and being fully convinced that the Poor of the said City are, and may be, better maintained, and at less Expence, within the said House than without, and having no just Cause to allege any thing against the Management and Proceedings of the said Governor and Guardians, or to complain of any Neglect of the Poor whatsoever, who, on the contrary, are now as well provided for as ever: And being delirous, for the general Good and Benefit of the whole City, that Lamps should be erected; therefore praying, That the said Governor and Guardians may be enabled to raise such an additional limited Sum of Money upon the Inhabitants of the said City, for the Purposes of the said Workhouse and Poor, and for discharging, by Degrees, the necessary and unavoidable Debts they have contrafted, as to the House shall seem meet; and also may have Power to enforce the collecting and paying the Levies made upon the said Inhabitants, by the respective Parish Officers, for the Use of the said House, within a reasonable time to be allotted for that Purpose; and that no Parish or Precinct whatsoever, within the said City, may be exempt from paying thereto, as they are all mutually benefited by it; and that Lamps may be erected and set up in the moll commodious manner, for lighting the Streets and Lancs of the said City, agreeable to the Practice, and under the Rules and Regulations, of other Cities and Corporations; and that the Management of them be left to the respective Parishes to which they shall several ]y belong.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Governor and Guardians of the Poor of the City of G/ou-cester, is referred: And that they do examine the Mat-

ter of this Petition; and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

GEORGER. '

His Majesty, agreeably to his royal Word, for the lake of justice, and of Example to the Discipline of the Navy, and for the Safety and Honour of the Nation, was determined to have let the Law take its course, with relation to Admiral Byng, as upon next; and re-

filled all Solicitations to the contrary.

But being informed, that a Member of the House of Commons, who was a Member of the Court Martial, which tried the said Admiral, has, in his Place, applied to the House, in behalf of himself, and several other Members of the said Court, praying the Aid of Parliament to be released from the Oath of Secrecy imposed on Courts Martial, in order to disclose the Grounds whereon Sentence of Death passed on the said Admiral; the Result of which Discovery may shew the Sentence to be improper; his Majesty has thought fit to respite the Execution of the lame, in order that there may bean Opportunity ofknowing, by the separate Examination of the Members of the said Court, upon Oath, what Ground there is for the above Suggestion.

His Majesty is determined still to let this Sentence be carried into Execution, unless it shall appear, from the said Examination, that Admiral Byng was unjustly condemned.

R.

A Petition of the several poor and distressed Broad Cloth Weavers of the Parishes of Stroud, Hamp-

ton, Bifley, and other adjacent Parishes and Places, in the County of Gloucefltr, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and many Thousand more of their distressed Brethren, was presented to the House, and read; reciting. That by an Act, passed in the 49th Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, the Justices of the Peace for the said County, at their Michaelmas Sessions yearly, were impoweted to settle or make a Rate for the Wages of Broad Cloth Weavers; and alleging, that the Petitioners applied to the said Session, pursuant to the said Act, to have their Wages settled and adjusted, when the Clothiers opposed the fame, declaring, by a Memorial then presented to the said Court, that the said Act was inconsistent and unrealizable, or to that tiffed, and ought not to be carried into Execution; and that the said Justices made no Order for the Purposes aforesaid, but adjourned the said Court to the Sixth of November following: That, afterwards, some of the Clothiers aforesaid, for the Peace of the said County, and Relief of the poor Petitioners, drew up a Plan or Rate for Payment of their Wages, which was produced at the said adjourned Sessions; and the Justices made a peremptory and final Vol. 27.

Order for the ascertaining and settling the said Wages; and further alleging, that several of the said Clothiers absolutely refuse to pay Obedience to the said Orders, and infill the Adjournment of the Sessions was not legally made, and, as the Petitioners arc informed, have applied to the House to have the Ad above mentioned repealed, and all other Acts relating to the settling of the Petitioners Wages, or at lead so much thereof as impowers the said Justices to settle the fame, and to subject the Petitioners to such Agreement as the said Clothiers shall think fit to make with them, in respect of such Wages; and that in calc the said Clothiers should prevail in their said Petition, the Petitioners would be in a worse Situation than before the Law was made, as aforesaid, in their behalf: And therefore praying, That no such Act may pass as prayed by the said Petition; or if the House should think fit to amend or explain the Acts aforesaid, there may be some Power lodged in the said Justices of the Peace, or else-where, as to the House shall seem meet, to ascertain and settle the said Wages that the Petitioners may notbefub-jed to the arbitrary Will and Power of the said Clothiers; and that the Petitioners, if Occasion be, may be heard, by their Counsel, or otherwise, against the Palling of such Bill as prayed for by the Clothiers aforesaid in their laid Petition, several of the Suggcftions therein being, as the Petitioners doubt not but to prove, false and untrue.

Sir John Philipps reported from the Committee, to whom the Report was re-committed, which was made from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Society of the Free Briiijk Fishery, was referied; and who were directed to inquire into, and report to the House, the State of the said Fishery in general; That t he Committee had reconsidered the said Report, and had inquired into the State of the said Fishery in general; and had directed him to report a State thereof to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the feme was read; and is as followeth; vi

It appeared by the Acts of the 23d and 28th Years of his present Majesty’s Reign, that the said Society were incorporated, and had several Encouragements given to them for carrying on the White Herring Fishery:

And, by the Accounts of the said Society, it appeared that they have employed the Sum of £. 130,305. 8j.

together with the whole Produce of the Fish, and the Bounties allowed on the Tonnage of their Shipping, in carrying on this Undertaking:

And it appeared by the Evidence of Mr. Thomas Collett, and also by the said Accounts, that, notwithstanding the Produce of the Fish and Bounties, the Society have sustained great Loss every Year, which has never been less than £.3,000; and, in one Year, amounted to £, 14,000 and upwards, occasioned by unavoidable Accidents, and great Expences incurred, in carrying on the said Fishery; and that they find their Capital so much reduced, that it will be impossible to prosecute their Design with any Prospect of Success, without the Assistance of Parliament:

That these extraordinary Expences were occasioned by their Want of Experience in the Beginning, and by the Society’s being obliged, by the first-mentioned Act, to expend the Sum of £. ioo.coo within Eighteen Months,

to entitle them to the Bounty of Three per Cent. This led them into great and hasty Contracts; and Persons

1757-

knowing the Obligations they lay under, took Advantage of their Necessity:

That they built too many Bufles, and have not been able to employ above One-half, or Two-thirds of them: That the Number of Bufles occasioned a great Expence in Nets and Storehouses:

That the Expence of bringing over Danes, to instruct the Fdhermen, amounted to £. 10,000; and that the Dutch reduced the Price of Fish in Germany from 465. to 18s. a Barrel, with an Intent, as the Evidence apprehends, to ruin this Fishery in its Infancy:

And he produced an Inventory of /. /. d.

the Value of the present dead Stock, amounting to ----- 41,858 3 if

Exclusive of the Calli, which is - 6,400 — —

Amounting in the Whole to - £. 48,253 3 if

And it appeared by the Evidence ot Mr. John Yeakky, Superintendent of the Fishery, that the Nets, which the Society are obliged to use, are too heavy and cumbersome, being Thirty Yards long and Seven Fathom deep: That they arc desirous of having them made thorter; but are willing to carry the same Quantity.of Netting.

Mr. Collett further informed your Committee, that the capital Stock of the Society, and the Price of Fish in Germans, bei.-ior so much reduced, it will be impossible to carry on the Fishery, without au Inc real e of the Bounty.

It appeared by the Act of the 28th Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, that the Society’ LSiock 4s unalienable, from the Date of their Charter, for the ip ace of Twelve Years; of which near Six are yet unexpired.

And it appeared, upon the further Examination of Mr. Collett, that the present Adventurers are unwilling to advance any mere Money* but he apprehends, if the Stock was made transferable, other Adventurers would come in, as they might purchase at 30 or 35, what cod the present Proprietors 63 per Cent.

And that it they bad Liberty to employ their Bufles during the Intervals of the Fi filing Season, in some other Business, it would be a great Advantage to the Society; but they had taken the Advice of Counsel, who Were of Opinion they could not employ them any Way but in the Fishery.

The Lord Mayor of London reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Lord Mayor, Alder-

men, and Commons, of the City of in Common

Council assembled, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

It appeared by a Charter granted by King the

First, in the 3d Year of his Reign, and by the Evidence of Mr. Dobson, That the Office of Bailiff'and Conserva-for of the River of ‘Thames, and Waters of Medway, hath been Time out of Mind in the Mayor and Commonalty, and Citizens, of the City of London.

And it appeared. That by an Act, made in the 9th Year of the Reign of Queen Anneintituled, An Act for the better Preservation and Improvement of the Fisherv within the lliver of Thames, and for regulating and governing the Company of Fishermen of the said River, a Court of Assistants of the Company of Fishermen was appointed for regulating and reforming Abuses in the said Fishery: Then,

Mr. Dobson gave Evidence, That the said Company continued (though not without several Intermilfions) till the Year 1727, since which Year the said Company have ceased toad; which Evidence was confirmed by,

Mr. Isaac Peverfen, formerly one of the said Court of

Assistants: Who added, That the Quarterage and Privilege of the said Court was so small that no one would aft: That the Body of Fishermen are now under no Regulation: That any one may fish that will, and that no Times or Seasons are kept for fishing.

Mr. Matthew Dwyre, being examined, proved to your Committee, by producing several small Filli which he had bought in the Streets, and several Pieces of Fishing Nets which he said he took from some Fishermen, that Fish are taken of too small a Size; and that new Methods of unlawful Fiffiing are practised, whereby the Destruction of the Fry of Fish is increased: That he attended on the Water BailiffTen Years, and has seized Twenty Pounds worth of unlawful Nets in a Season, and has frequently been insulted and abused in his Office.

Mr. John Selby, being examined, also said, That he has been with the Water Bailiff at the seizing of unlawful Nets, and has been greatly abused by the Fishermen.

Roger Griffiths Esquire, late Water Bailiff, being examined, said, That in general there has been a constant Practice, whereby the Fishery in the River Thames has been injured :. That he has very frequently been obstructed in his Office: That he has been thrown out of his Boat by the Fishermen, and otherwise greatly abused, though he had a Right to ftize all unlawful Nets: That the Price of Fish is grown excessive, and that the Abuses committed in the Fishery cannot be prevented without the Aid of Parliament.

Ordered, That-Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the more effectual Preservation and Improvement of the Fry and Spawn of Fish in the River of Thames, and Waters of Medway, and for the better regulating the

Fishery thereof: And that the Lord Mayor of London,

Mr. Recorder of London, Sir Robert , Sir John

Philipps, and Sir William Calvert, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

In Support of the Allegations of the said Petitions,

Mr. Richard Serjeant, being examined, said, That the present Communication between several Parts of London and Westminster with the great Roads into Essex,

Norfolk, and other Counties, is very inconvenient:

That if a new Road was made from Brook house at Clapton, in the Parish of Hackney, over certain Lands and Grounds there, down to the lliver Lea, at or near Jeremy's Ferry, and a Bridge built over the same at or near the said Ferry, and a new Road made from thence to Mark house Lane, cross Waltha Mead or Marsh, and over certain Lands lying between the said Marsh and Markhouse Lane, and cross the Road on the East Side of the said Lane leading to the North East Corner of Knot's Green, in the Parishes of W and Low/ayton, and from thence into the great Road near the Eagle at Snarejbrooke, in the County of Essex, was repaired and widened, it would open a much more commodious and convenient Communication between several Parts of l.ondon and Westminster with the great Roads into

Suffolk, Norfolk, and other Counties, and between all the great Roads on the West, North, and East, Parts of London and Westminster. ....

Mr. Thomas Marshconfirmed the above Evidence; and

added, That he had l'urveyed the said Read, and the Ground intended for such new Road; and that the Distance from the West End of the Lane opposite Brookhouse at Clapton, to the proposed Bridge within Fifty Yards of the l orry, is Half a Mile and Fifty-five Yards; and from thence acrot's the Marsh to the First Meadow is One Quarter of a Mile and 147 Y ards, and from thence alohg tiic Meads to the V\ eft End ot a Lane leading to Butter-fold Lane is One Quarter of a Mile and 191 Yards, and from thence akng the said Lane, through M

Lane, cross Knot's Green and Lipping Forest, to the at Snaresbrooke, is Two Miles and a Half and 190

Yards; and that the whole Distance from Clapton to the Eagle at Snaresbrooke is Three Miles Three Quarters and 143 Yards.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for building a Bridge over the River Lea, at or near a Place called Jeremy's Ferry; and for making, repairing, and widening, Roads from thence into the great Roads at Snaresbrooke, in the County of Essex, and at Clapton, in the County of Middlesex: And that. and also the several Rents or yearly Sums of /. 1,838. 12s. 6d. and /. 612. 171. 6d. due and payable, and to be due and payable, to his said late Majesty, his Heirs and Successors, on several former Demises of the' said Duty, to hold and enjoy the same to the 1’aid Charles Duke of Richmond and Lenox, and the Heirs of his Body, lawfully begotten or to be begotten; subject, neverthe-lcls, to the Payment of the Yearly Sum of/. 500 to Sir Thomas Claries Knight, his Heirs and Assigns, according to a Grant made to him thereof; yielding and paying the refore to Ids Majesty, his Heirs and Successors, the yearly Rent of/. 1. 6r. 8<A; and also reciting, that, by virtue of the said Letters Patent, the Petitioner, upon the Death of his Father, became feiled of thelaid Coal l3uty, to him and the Heirs of his Body; and alleging, that the same will go to the Petitioner’s Daughters, in calc hefbould die leaving Daughters only; and in default of tuch lfluc to the lleirs of the Body of Charles Duke of Richmond and Lenox, his Grandfather, instead of the present Limitations thereof by the said Grant; and further alleging, that a Treaty of Marriage having been had and lately concluded between the Petitioner and the honourable Lady Mary Bruce, Daughter of the right honourable Charles late Rail ofyf/Ay^/n^sdeceased, the Petitioner hath proposed, in Consideration of the said intended Marriage, and of the Portion of the said Lady Mary Bruce, to make a Grant of /. 3,000 a Year to the said Lady Mary Bruce, to issue and be payable out of the said Coal Duty, to her and her Af-ligns, during her Life, as a Jointure, in case she shall survive the Petitioner *, and that the said Lady Mary, and her Trustees and Guardians, are willing to accept thereof, in lieu and bar of the Dower and Thirds of the Petitioner’s Estate, to which the said Lady Mary Bruce might otherwise be intitled; but, by reason of the Minority of the said Lady Mary Bruce, the said Proposal cannot be carried into Execution, nor can the Limitations in the said Grant be varied without the Aid and Authority of Parliament; Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Sum of Seven hundred thousand Pounds be granted to his Majesty, to enable his Majesty to discharge the like Sum raised in pursuance of an Act made in the last Session of Parliament, and charged upon the First Aids or Supplies to be granted in this Session of Parliament.:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum not exceeding Fifteen thousand Three hundred Eighty-one Pounds Four Shillings, be granted to his Majesty, upon Account, for defraying the Charges incurred by supporting and maintaining the Settlement of his Majesty’s Colony of Nova Scotia in the Year 1755, and not provided for by Parliament.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Three thousand Pounds, be granted to his Majesty, for repairing and finishing a Road proper for the Passage of Troops and Carriages from the City of Car lijle to the Town of Tyne-,

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Forty-seven thousand Eight hundred and Sixty-nine Pounds Two Shillings and Four Pence, be granted to his Majesty, for defraying the Remainder of the Exceedings of the Office of Ordnance for Land Service, for the Year 1756, not provided for by Parliament.

A Petition of the Bailiff, Burgesses, and Commonalty, Regrator# of the Borough of Tewkesbury, in the County of Glou- porc^cr8 cester, was presented to the House, and read; alleging, That the Petitioners believe, that the Miseries and Hardships to which the poor and laborious People in the said Borough and Neighourhood are reduced, and the present Price and Scarcity of Corn, are occasioned by the Badgers of Corn and Millers, who, for several Years pafl, have constantly travelled round the Country to buy Corn at the Farmers Houses, or by Samples, which prevents the same being exposed to Sale in public Markets, so that the Poor have no Opportunity of buying it there; and more especially so, as many of those Badgers are Millers, who convert the same into Flour, which they fell out Wholesale; and that if the Provisions made in several Acts of Parliament, in relation to Badgers of Corn, were explained, and further Restrictions laid on Badgers, and a more easy and shorter Method prescribed for conviding Persons offending against the said Acts, the same would in a great measur prevent the pernicious Practice of engrossing Com, and greatly tend to the reducing, and for the future prevent, the excessive Price of Corn in that Borough and Country; and that by reason of the present Irregularity of Measuresufed in different Markets it is importable for Magistrates to fix an equal and just Assize of Bread: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to give such Relief therein as to them shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Sir John Turner reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Owners of Marsh and Fen Lands and low Grounds lying in the Parish of Wiggenhall Saint Mary Magdalene, in the County of Norfolk, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read: and is as followeth viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Mr. Langley Edwards said. That he knows the said Fen Lands and low Grounds, which contain about Four thousand Acres: That upwards of Three thousand of them have been for several Years and still are, frequently overflowed with Water, through the Defect of their Out-falls..to the Sea, and, in their presentState, produce little or no Profit: That if the said Lands were effectually drained, it would be of public Utility, and of great Profit to the Owners thereof, as they would then be worth Seven Shillings an Acre, one with another.

John Spilman, Esquire, being examined, confirmed the Evidence given by Mr. Edwards.

A Petition of the Free Brit Fishery Chamber of Whitehaven, in the County of , was presented

to the House, and read; alleging. That, as the Law now stands, the Petitioners go to, and return from, Shetland, at a great Expence and Loss of Time; and, while the War continues, dare not (lay there to fish; besides, they are to go to, and return from, Shetland without Convoy, by which they run a great Rifle of losing their BuiTes; and that ever since the Institution of the present Fishery, Experience has fully shewn, that the Fishery at Shetland has not proved worth following; and that the Petitioners have thereby loft Two Months, or more, of a much better Fishery in St. George's Channel, within a Day’s Sail of Whitehaven; and taking notice, that the Free British Fishery have applied to the House for further Assistance and Relief: And therefore praying. That Campbeltown may be appointed the Place of Rendezvous for the BuiTes belonging to Whitehaven, for the Summer Fishery, as well as for the Winter Fishery, in order that they may be enabled to fish with greater Advantage; or such other Relief in the Premises as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.
