w*y» Refohed, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

Means. That, towards railing the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Surplus of the Duties on Licences for retailing spirituous Liquors, be granted to his Majesty, from and after the ioth Day or October 1756.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, an additional Stamp Duty of One Shilling be charged upon every Piece of Vellum, Parchment, or Paper, on which shall be ingrafted or written any Indenture, Lease, Bond, or other Deed, for which a Stamp Duty of Six Pence is payable by virtue of an Act made in the 12th Year of her late Majesty Queen Anne.

Resolvetd, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, an additional Stamp Duty of Five Pounds be charged upon every Piece of Vellum or Parchment, or Sheet or Piece of Paper, on which shall be ingrafted or written any Licence for retailing of Wine, to be granted to any Person who shall not take out either a Licence for retailing of spirituous Liquors, or a Licence for retailing of Beer, Ale, or other excii'eable Liquors.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, an additional Stamp Duty of Four Pounds be charged upon every Piece of Vellum or Parchment, or Sheet or Piece of Paper, on which shall be ingrafted or written any Licence for retailing of Wine, to be granted to any Person who shall take out a Licence for retailing of Beer, Ale, and other exciseable Liquors, but shall not take out a Licence for retailing of spirituous Liquors.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, an additional Stamp Duty of Forty Shillings be charged upon every Piece of Vellum or Parchment, or Sheet or Piece of Paper, on which shall be ingrafted or written any Licence for retailing of Wine, to be granted to any Person who shall also take out a Licence for retailing of spirituous Liquors.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, all Persons retailing of Wine shall be obliged to take out Licences annually, to be granted by the Commissioners appointed lor managing the Duties arising by Stamps upon Vellum, Parchment, and Paper.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made 12 Car. 2. intituled, An Act for the better ordering the felling of Wines by Retail, and for preventing Abuses in the mingling, corrupting, and vitiating, of Wines, and for setting and limiting the Prices of the fame, except so much thereof as relates to the preventing Abuses in the mingling, corrupting, and vitiating, of Wines, and for setting and limiting the Prices ' of the fame, shall, from and after the 5th Day of July 1757, be repealed.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, from and after the 5th Day of July 1757, the Commission whereby Agents and Commissioners are appointed, by virtue of the said Act, for granting Licences for retailing of Wine, shall cease and determine.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, out of the several Duties before mentioned, his Majesty be empowered to grant, during Pleasure, to the several Agents or Commissioners for managing the Duties on Wine Licences granted by the said Act, and their Officers, or such of the said Agents or Officers as his Majesty shall think proper, such yearly Allowances as his Majesty shall think fit; so as no such Allowance to any Agent or Commissioner shall exceed Five hundred Pounds a Year, and so as no such Allowance toany other such Officer shall exceed the pretent annual Amount of the Salaries and Wages due and payable to such Officers relatively.

Refohed, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, Thar, after the Determination of the said Duties upon Wine Licences granted by the said Act, in lieu thereof

there shall be set apart and paid to his Majesty, out of the several Duties before mentioned, the yearly Sum of Seven thousand and Two Pounds Fourteen Shillings and Three Pence, which appears to have been the net annual Produce of the former Duties on Wine Licences, upon a Medium of Six Years, ending the 5th Day of January 17S7-

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, towards raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, an additional Duty of One Half penny be laid upon every Paper not exceeding One whole Sheet, containing public News, Intelligence, or Occurrences, printed in Great Britain, to be dispersed and made public.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, towards raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, an additional Duty of One Shilling be charged upon every Advertisement contained in the London Gazette, or any other printed Paper, to be dispersed or made public weekly, or oftener.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, a Duty of Two Shillings be charged upon every Advertisement contained in, or published with, any printed Paper or printed Pamphlet whatsoever, to be dispersed or made public yearly, monthly, or at any other Interval of Time, exceeding One Week.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, towards raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, an additional Duty of One Penny be charged upon every Almanack or Calendar for any one particular Yeir, or for any time less than a Year, printed on one Side only of One Sheet or Piece of Paper.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, towards raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, an additional Duty of Two Pence be charged upon every other Almanack or Calendar for anyone particular Year.

Resolved \That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, towards raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, for every Almanack or Calendar made to serve for several Years, the said several additional Duties be charged for every such Year, not exceeding Three Years.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, towards raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, an additional Duty of Four Shillings be paid for every Chaldron of Coals, Newcastle Measure, which shall be shipped for Exportation to any Part beyond the Seas, except to Ireland, the Isle of Man, or his Majesty’s Plantations, and after the same Rate for any greater or lesser Quantities.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Annuities payable pursuant to the Resolution of this House, of the 14th Day of this instant March, be charged upon the said several Rates and Duties before-mentioned.

Mr. Charles Gore reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of several Gentlemen, Clergy, Merchants, Traders, and other Inhabitants, of the Counties of Bedford, and Hertford, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had di-rested him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as fol'oweth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the Agent for the Petitioners called,

Mr. Langley Edwards,a Surveyor: Who infofmed your Committee, That he had surveyed the River Ivel, from the River Ouze, in the Parish of in the County of Bedford to Broad Mead in the Parish of in

the said County, and from thence up the Three several Branches thereof, one to a Place called Port Mill in the Town of Hitchin, in the County of Hertfordanother to the Black Horse Mill in the Parish of Bygrave, in the liid County; and the other to the South and North Bridges in the Town of Shefford, in the County of Bedford:

That he was employed to take the said Survey in February iaft, and finds, that the intended Navigation is very practicable in all the Branches.

Being asked, Whether he had ever been concerned in making Rivers navigable f he said. He was employed in making the River Nene navigable, pursuant to a late Act of Parliament; and that he had been concerned in several Works of the like Nature in the Fens:

That the Distance from the River Ouze to the Baldock Branch is about 12 Miles, in which space the Water falls near 50 Feet; and that the Depth of Water required for the Navigation will be Three Feet, which will carry a Barge of 20 Tons Burthen.

Being aflced, Whether, when the Navigation should be completed, it would not deprive the several Mills of Water ? he laid. That the Method proposed for the Navigation was, not to raise the Surface of the Water, but to deepen the River by taking away the Shoals; and that by making Locks and Penns the Mills will be preferred: That it was proposed to lay a Duty of $d. for every Barg? paflfing through a Lock, to be paid to the Occupiers of the Milk, as a Recompense for the Loss of Water; That he had proposed this to the Millers, at a Meeting which was held for that Pumofe; and that Mr. Blower, a Mailer of the Mills at agreed it

would be a sufficient Recompence, and none of the others made any Objection to it; but that Mr. s Mill

at Hitchin will receive more Prejudice than any of the relt: That there will be no Necessity for a Gang of Barges to pats above Once a Week, and therefore the loss of W rat?r will be bat small; and the River must be en-

7.3

larged, by which a greater Body of Water will be preserved for the Use of the Mills; and that some of the Mills will not receive any Prejudice at all from the’Navigation, nor will any of the Mills be prevented from working, except Mr. Bogdanie's Mill at Hitchin aforesaid:

That the Lands on each Side of the River are for the most Part a dead Flat; and that the Height of the Locks are proposed to be the same with the present Heads of the Mills; and that he thinks there will be no Fear of the Country suffering for want of their Corn being ground, for that there will be a constant Supply of Water in Summer, since the River will be made narrower and dequer.

Mr. Thomas Yeomans, Surveyor, being examined, said, That be had surveyed that Part of the River which lies between Langford and Hitchin, and between Langford and Baldock, both which Branches he thinks capable of being made navigable.

And he confirmed the Evidence of Mr. Langley with regard to the Mills upon the several Streams; and added, That the gd. a Barge will be more than a sufficient Re-compenfe for the Loss of Water; for that the Rain Water will be better retained by the opening of the River; and that in a Head of Water of Six Feet it will take more than Six Lockfuls to grind a Sack of Corn;

That the making the River navigable will be a great Advantage to the Lands on each Side, and will be a Means of furnishing the Country with Fuel cheaper;

And that there is no Danger of overflowing the Lands, for the Locks will be of Service to drain them, because they will throw open their Gates in Times of Flood, which will draw off the Water much sooner than the present Stream.

Mr. Edward Rudd, Maltster at Biggleswade, said, Teat the present Price of I and Carriage for Coals from Temps -ford to Bigglcfwade is 6 s.a Chalder Lynn Measure; and that there are 1,000 Cnalder in a Year consumeJ at Big-glefwade, and about 1,100 Tons in the Neighbourhood:

That the Difference of Expence between Wood and Coal Fires is very great; and that it is the general Opinion of the Country, that the opening of the Navigation would be of great and public Utility.

Being asked, if it would not be a Detriment to the Persons employed in the Land Carriage of those Coals ? he said. That nobody was employed in the Carriage of Coals but poor Farmers, who, for the fake of the ready Money, spend their Time in carrying Coals; which would answer much better if employed in the Cultivation of their Lands; for that the rich Farmers will not undertake it, because they can employ their Time better.

Mr. Richard Triflram, an Inhabitant of Hitchin, being examined, laid. That the Price of Land Carriage for Coals, from Tempsford to Hitchin, is 12 s. per Chalder Lynn Measure; and that it is the general Opinion of the Gentlemen and other Inhabitants of Hitchin, and the neighbouring Places, that the Navigation would be cf great Use to that Part of the Country, as it would be the Means of furnishing them not only with Coals, but several other Commodities, at a cheaper Rate.

Mr. Thomas Love, who lives at , and is Sur-

veyor of the Turnpike Road between Bigglefivade and Stevenage, informed Yrour Committee, That die piefent Price of Land Carriage for Coals, from Tempsford to Baldock, is 9 s.a Chalder small Measure, which is something more than One Fourth short of Lynn Measure; That according to a Calculation he had made, the Coals consumed in the Town of Baldock amount to near 1,000 Chalder, and there is more consumed in the Neighbourhood than in the Town:

That the Coal Carriages use the Roads at all times of the Year, and all of them (except One Carriage) use narrow Wheels; and that they do more Harm to the Road from Tempsford to Stevenage, than the Tolls paid for their Passage will make good.

With respect to what relates to the paving of the said Streets,

By the Evidence of several Persons wdiom the Committee called bdore them, your Committee find. That many Parts of the Pavements of the public Streets within the said City and Liberty, and Precinct of the Savoyf and that Part <,f the Duchy of Lancaster adjoining thereto, are at present in a ruinous Condition, occasioned by the said Streets in general being paved in an improper 2 6

Manner, and by the respective Companies who furnish Water to the Inhabitants being permitted to take up the Pavements by their own Paviours, who are not imerested in repaving the same in a proper and effectual manner, and also by the great Number of heavy Carriages which pass over the said Pavements, having their Wheels (hod with Iron; and that if the Pavements of the said Streets were properly regulated, it would be a very great Convenience to the Inhabitants in general, and a!lb a great Advantage to those who keep Carriages.

Your Committee are now proceeding upon the other Matter referred to their Consideration; but thought it necessary in the mean time to inform the House, that the Committee have come to the following Resolutions:

Major General Cornwallis reported from the Committee, to whom the Report was re-committed, which" was made from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Commissioners for building a Bridge cross the River Thames, from the City of Wefmto the opposite Shore in the County of Surrey, was referred; and who were empowered to receive Proposals from Persons who would undertake, by Contract, to widen the Street leading from Charing Cross towards Whitehall-, That the Committee had received Proposals accordingly; and had directed him to report a State of the Matter of Fact contained in the said Petition, together with the said Proposals annexed, to the House; and he read the Report and Propokds in his Place; and afterwards delivered them in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read.

The said Proposals, and also several Plans thereunto annexed, are preserved amongst the other Papers of th is Session; and the said Report is as followeth; viz.

A State of the Fasts contained in the said Petition is

as follows:

By an Act passed in the last Session of Parliament, the Commissioners for building Westminster Bridge were empowered to open and widen, in such Manner as they should think proper, all the Ways, Streets, Avenues, and Paffagrs leading from Charing Cross to the Two Houses of Parliament, Westminster Haand the Courts of Justice

there, and Westminster Bridge; and that out of all or any

of the Supplies granted to his Majesty for the Service of the Year 17.56, there should be paid to the said Commit-(loners the Sum of Ten thousand Pounds, to be applied towards purchasing Houses and Grounds for widening the said Ways, and making more laic’and commodious the Street', Avenues, anJ Passages, aforesaid, and the Payment cf other Incidental Charges and Expences attending

Vol. tj.

the Execution of the several Trusts reposed in them by that and former Acts.

Then the Minute Book of the said Commissioners was produced, and several Parts thereof were read; whereby it appeared, That the said Commissioners had met, and considered what Methods would be the properest for carrying the said Act into Execution;, and were of Opinion, that it would be proper, in the First place, to open and widen Part of the Street leading immediately from Charing Cross towards Whitehall; and that they therefore caul’ed a Plan of the said Street to be made; and, after inspecting and perusing the fame, were further of Opinion, that it would be necessary to purchase, and become possessed of, the Freehold and Inheritance, of all the Buildings, Houses, Grounds, and Estates, situate between the Wdt Side of the said Street leading from Charing Cross and the East Side of another Street called Spring Garden, and between the South Side of a Street Way or Passage called Passage into Spring Garden and the North Side of certain Houses, Buildings, and Walls, belonging to his Majesty’s Office of Admiralty; and that the said Commissioners thereupon ordered their Surveyor to make an Estimate of the Value of the several Premises to be purchased by them as aforesaid; and that such Estimate was made accordingly; whereby it appears, that, on a moderate Computation, the total Value ct all these Premises amount to the Sum of£.25,344:

That the said Commissioners, finding the said Estimate amount to so large aSum, they then dire died another Estimate to be made of the Expence of purchasing (b much only of the said Premises as would beablbl utely necessary for opening and widening the said Street leading (eomC/iaring Cross, so as to make the narrow Part thereof of an equal Breadth with Parliament Street, and to leave Ground besides sufficient for erecting a Row of Front Houses next to the said Street leading from Charing Cross, distinguishing in that Estimate how much such Expence would amount to, exclusive of leaving Ground for erecting the said Row of Front Houses; and that such Second Estimate having been made, it thereby appeared, that the Expence of purchasing only so much of the said Premises as would be sufficient to open and widen the said Street, and to leave Ground for the said Row of Front Houses, is computed at £. 18,634; and that deducting the reout the Value of Ground for erecting the said llow of Front Houses will reduce the same to £.11,402.

And the said Commissioners observed.That in case all the above-mentioned Premises, estimated at £.25,344, were t,o be purchased, they would be thereby enabled to use so much thereof as should be necessary to open and widen the said Street in a commodious and handlome manner; and the remaining Ground, which would be proper for building handsome new Houses thereon, might be fold, or let on Building Leases; but if it should be deemed more proper to purchase only so much of the said Premises as are comprised in one of the said lesser Estimates of£.18,634 or £.11,402, the said Commissioners apprehend, that either of those Purchases would be Disadvantageous to the Public, and the remaining Premises unpurchased would in all Probability be incapable of being made into an uniform Range of Building.

Mr. John Simpson, Surveyor to the Commissioners of

Westminster Bridge, being examined, confirmed the Observations made by the said Commissioners; and added.

exclusive of the Rooms which Mr. Ramsden has over the old Gateway.

A Petition of several Persons under the Denomination Attaining of Pawnbrokers, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, Goods i»y in behalf of themselves, and several others within the Fraud. Cities of London and Westminster, and the Bills of Mortality, following that Business, and no other, was presented to the House, and read; alleging, That the Petitioners having perused a Bill depending in the House for preventing, among other Things, the unlawful Pawning of Goods, and for the easy Redemption of Goods pawned, are apprehensive, if that Part of the Bill which relates to the Petitioners Business should pass into a Law, it would subject them to so many Frauds, Impositions, and Inconveniences, as would render it totally impracticable for them to carry on their Business: That the Petitioners, being themselves intire Strangers to the Practices intended to be prevented by the said Bill, imagine they mu ft a rife from Persons that keep Chandlers Shops, and follow other such-like Businesses, lending Money upon Pledges, and assuming the Name of Pawnbrokers; and that the Petitioners humbly conceive, if the Business of Pawnbroking was properly regulated, and such Persons only were permitted to follow it as should appear to be of Character and Reputation, that those Mischiefs would . not only be removed, but that great Good would likewise result from it to the industrious Poor: And therefore praying, That the Petitioners may be heard, by their Counsel, against such Part of the said Bill as affects them in their Business; and likewise permitted humbly to submit such FaTs as may enable the House to put the Business under such Regulation as may best promote the Security of the Public, and render the Petitioners able to carry on their fiid Business with Safety and Reputation.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Bill for the more effectual Punishment of Persons who shall attain, or attempt to attain, Possession of Goods or Money by false or untrue Pretences; for preventing the unlawful Pawning of Goods; for the easy Redemption of Goods pawned; and for preventing Gaming in Public Houses by Journeymen, Labourers, Servants, and Apprentices; is committed: And that the Petitioners be heard, by their Counsel, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

AN ir.grofitd Bill from the Lords, intituled, An Act for Sale of Part of the settled Ellrate of Wi. Yhomfon Esquire, in the County of , to raise Money towards discharging several Mortgage Debts and Incumbrances affecting other Parts of his settled Estates in the same County, was read the First time.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a Second time.

Mr. Hammond reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of Edward Cox, of the Parish of,

Lambeth, in the County of Su, Barge Builder, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, together with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Mr. Richard Cox, being examined, said, That his Father Edward Cox has, with great Labour and Application, and at the Expence of Two hundred Pounds, invented, and brought to Perfection, an Engine or Machine, for the unlivering Ships loaded with Coals.

Mr. James Hickfon,a Coal Factor, being examined, said, That he has seen the said Machine worked, and believes it will be of more Utility, and will unload Coal Ships with more Dispatch, than the Method now prac-tiled — That when a considerable Number of these Ships are in the River Thames, there is often a great Want of Coal-heavers, and the Price of Labour has been thereby raised from 14 d.to 35. each Man, for unloading a Score or Twenty Chalders of Coals — That the advanced Price of Labour sometimes raises the Price of Coals — That when there are mostShips in the River, Labour is at the highest Price; and "that Ships are often delayed several Days, by reason Labourers cannot lie procured.

Mr John Gibjon, a Coal Factor, being examined, said,

That lie has seen the said Machine worked; and if there were a sufficient Number of them to supply Ships as they are wanted, any Number of Ships might be unloaded at the same time — That when a great Number of Ships are in the River, Labourers are fearce — That there are great Delays in unloading Ships, occasioned by the Coal-heavers entering into Combinations — That Ships may be unloaded quicker, and at a cheaper Rate by this Machine than by the present Method:

That from 15 to 17 Coal-heavers are employed in Unloading a Ship; and if a Man who works between Decks, or in some other Parts of the Ship, is taken ill, a whole Gang may stand still a considerable time, before a Person can be procured to supply his Place — That this Machine will require 14 or 15 Men; but they will work cheaper, as the Labour is not so great: and any Sort of Labourers may work at it, except the Vatmen, who will require some Experience.

Mr Middlemarsh, being examined, said. That he has

known a Ship of 400 Chalders of Coals delivered in Four Days; and that he believes this Machine will not be more expeditious than the present Method; but that he has known when a Coal-heaver, who works on the middle Deck, has been taken ill, the whole Gang has (food still — That Coal-heavers will frequently raise Six Pence Score more in their Price than they have agreed for; and that he never law a Machine of this kind before.

Mr. Jonathan Sh&kefpear, a Lighterman, being examined, laid. That he has seen the said Machine worked; and in Times of Want of Men, which often happens, it will be of great Utility, as it requires little or no Art in Working it, and may be worked by any Sort of Persons: That he has bought a Ship of Coals, and has been de-Voi. 27.

Aprilis. 859

layed Ten Days in delivering It, for want of Hands---

That there are often great Delays by Coal-heavers getting drunk; and the Absence of one Man flops a whole Gang — That there are a great many Instances of Corn-binations amongst the Coal-heavers to raise their Price, when a Number of Ships arrive together; and that they will, in this Cafe, often raise the Price they have before agreed for — That, by means of these Combinations, the Price of Coals is often enhanced; and that there is more Art in Coal-heaving than is generally imagined.

Being aiked, Whether if a great Number of Ships were to come into the Pool at one and the same time, there would be more Dispatch by this Machine than the present Method ? he said, he thought there would be more Expedition by Coal-heavers; but that if they had all the Coal-heavers and these Machines, they could work more Ships at the same time — That Coal-heaving is confined to a certain Number of Men — That there has been frequently more Ships to unload than they could get Labourers for, which might have been delivered by these Machines.

James Don, being examined, laid, That he has been a Coal-heaver almost Ten Years, and has worked at this Machine; and that it will be of great Utility — That it will clear 80 or 100 Chalders of Coals in a Day, when the Men have got the Method of working it — That feme strong Gangs of Coal-heavers will unload about the same Quantity; but that the usual Quantity is not above Sixty Chalders per diem — That Coal-heavers must be strong Men, and used to the Business; and that Men are unwilling to engage in the Business of Coal-heaving, the Labour being so very hard; and that few of them continue in their Prime more than Six or Seven Years; but that any common Labourers may work this Machine, which will be a great Saving of Labour; and therefore Hands may be much easier procured; and that the Coals will not be so liable to be broke by this as by the present Method.

William Bridon, being examined, laid. That he has, practised the Business of Coal-heaving Fifteen Years; and that it is very hard Labour — 'That Ships are often delayed for want of Labourers — That he has seen this Machine worked, whereby Ships may be unloaded with more DIB patch and less Labour than by the present Method — That it will not require such strong Men as Coal-heaving; and if it meets with no Stops, it will unload 100 Chalders a Day, or 90 one Day with another — That some Gangs of Coal-heavers will deliver 100 Chalders a Day, if they meet with no Obstruction; others cannot unload above Sixty; and that he never few a Machine of this Sort used on board Ships before. '

Captain William Coates, Master of a Collier, being examined, said. That he has seen the said Machine worked; and that it may be of Ul'e in delivering small Ships, when Labourers are scarce — That he has known Delays in unloading Ships, for want of labourers — That he has given from One Shilling to Two Shillings and Six Pence each Labourer per Score, London Measure, for unloading Ships — That any Persons may be employed in working the said Machine — That the principal Art is the mea-furing tire Coals — That he has been used to the Coal Trade all his Life, and never fawany thing like the said Machine on board any Ships before — That the present Method, when Coal-heavers are scarce, is to unload with Baskets; -but that, by means of this Machine, Ships may be delivered sooner than with Baskets, with a proper Number of Hands, and the Coals not so liable to be broke — That if a proper Number of Men are employed with this Machine, they will unload sooner than Coal-heavers in a large Ship; and believes it will be a greac Saving in the Expence of unloading Ships — That the Ships employed in this Trade are from 100 Tons Burthen to near 700 Tons; but that the common Sizes are from 200 to 500 Tons; and that if there were a proper Number of these Machines, and one put on board each Ship, as they come into the River, they would be delivered sooner than by the present Method; and they would not be liable to wait for Hands, as they now are.

Thus the Price of Labour to Coal-heavers is sometimes at One Shilling per Score each Man, and sometimes at 2j. id. or is. yd.-, and that when a Number of Ships arrive, Labourers are scarce, and Ships have been detained Three or Four Days, for the Want of Hands to unload them; and has known (last Summer) Three Shillings per Score paid to each Labourer; and the lowest Price within thele Twelve Months part was one Shilling.

William Hcrfelcy Esquire, produced to your Committee, an Account of the Prices of Labour in unloading of Coal Ships in the Pool at different Periods, extracted from the Books of Messieurs Biggins and Ward Coal Factors, CrutchedFryars, for the Year 1756; by which it

Upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Uesolutions:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Edward Cox hath invented a Machine for unloading Coal Ships different from any thing of the Sort heretofore used in this Kingdom.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,. That the said Machine may prove more useful for the I’urpose of unloading Coal Ships than any other Method heretofore practised.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the House be moved for Leave to bring in a Bill for vesting the fble Property of the said Machine in the said Edward Cox, his Heirs, Executors, Administrators, and Assigns, for such Term of Years as to the House shall feeni meet.

Mr. Cox proposes that the present Medium shall be his highest Price, and the present 3)0)550,41)3 lowest Price his Medium; and it appearing that the Number of Chalders imported in

18,347 the Year 1756, was 550,413; and that the Difference between the Medium and

highest Price is Eight Pence per Chalder, that there will be therefore saved to the Public, as per Margin, £. 18,347 annually.

And as it amounts to the same thing in the proportionate Value, whether the Price be adjusted by the Score, or by the Chalder, yet as feme Disputes may hereafter arise on that Head between the Inventor and Masters of Ships, on account of the Number of Men casually employed, it is humbly proposed, that the Price of Unlading be fixed by the Chalder only.

A Petition of the several Inhabitants of Charing Cross, and Parts adjacent, whoseHands are thereunto subscribed, being offered to be presented to the House;

The Lord Bateman, by his Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That his Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; taking Notice, That a Petition of the Corr.missioners for building of Westminster Bridge has been presented to the House, reciting an Act passed the last Session of Parliament, to enable them to purchase Houses and Grounds, and to widen the Ways, and make more l'afe and commodious the Streets, Avenues, and Passages, leading from Charing Cross to the Two Houses of Parliament, minster Hall, and the Courts of Justice there, and

minster Bridge-, and praying the House to grant such Sums of Money as would enable the said Commissioners to execute the Powers and Trails reposed in them by the said Act; and alleging, that there is a Way leading from his Majesty’s Metus at Charing Cross, and other Parts, into Spring Garden, at the North End thereof, and from thence into Saint James's Park, which is much used by Persons going to and from both Houses of Parliament, Westminster Hall, and the Courts of Justice there; but, by reason of the Narrowness of the said Way, it is very inconvenient and unlafc; and that it would be of very great public Utility to have the same opened and widened; which, as the Petitioners conceive, may be done at a moderate Expence, by taking down fotne Buildings on the South Side thereof, which are old and decayed: And therefore praying, That the said Commissionersmay be enabled to open and widen the said Way leading into Garden, at the North End thereof, in such manner as to the House shall seem meet.

The House was moved, That the Title of an. Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, An Act to enable the Commissioners for building a Bridge cross the River of Thames, frony the City of Westminster to the opposite Shore in the County of Surrey, to purchase Houses and Grounds, and to widen the Ways, and make more safe and commodious the Streets, Avenues, and Passages, leading from Charing Cross to the Two Houses of Parliament, Westminster Hall, and the Courts of Justice there, and Westminster Bridge; and to enable a less Number of Commissioners to execute the several Acts relating to the said Bridge than at present are required by Law; and for Relief of George and James King, with regard to a Lease taken by their late Father from the said Commissioners; might be read.

And the same was read accordingly.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

GEORGE R.

His Majesty, being desirous that his faithful Subjects in his Provinces of North and South Carolina and Virginia, in America, should receive a proper Recompence for such Services as, with the Approbation of the Commander in Chief of his Forces in America, they respectively shall have performed, or shall perform, either by putting the find Provinces in a State of Defence, or by acting with Vigour against the Enemy, recommends it to this House to take the same into their Consideration, and to enable his Majesty to give them a proper Recompence for such Services: His Majesty also acquaints this House, That a Battalion of his Forces, which has been employed in the Settlements of the United Company of Merchants of England trading to the East Indies, is by his Order withdrawn from those Settlements; and therefore recommends it to this House to enable his Majesty to assist the Lid Company in defraying the Expence of a military Force in the East Indies, to be maintained by them in lieu of the said Battalion.

House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Petitioners be at Liberty to make use of such Nets in the White Herring Fisheries as they shall find best adapted to the said Fisheries; provided that each Buss do carry to Sea, in the whole, the like Quantity of Netting as they are now bound to carry.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,' That the Bounty of Thirty Shillings per Ton, payable on the Vessels employed in the Lid Fisheries, be increased to Fifty Shillings per Ton, and made payable for inch Term of Years as the said Bounty ol Thirty Shillings is now payable.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Petitioners be at Liberty, during the Intervals of the Fishing Seasons, to employ their Vefills used in the said Fisheries in any other Btifiness not prohibited by Law; provided such Vessels shall have been employed in the Herring Fisheries during each of the Fishing Seasons.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Petitioners beat Liberty to make use of such Barrels, with respect to the Thickness of the Staves, for the packing of their Fish, as they now have in Use, or may hereafter find best adapted to that Purpose.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion o! this Committee, That the Petitioners have Liberty to make use of any Waste or uncultivated Land, One hundred Yards at the least above the highest Water Mark, for the Purpose of drying their Nets.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Campbeltown would be the most proper and convenient Place for the Rendezvous for the Busies belonging to the Free British Fishery Chamber of Whitehaven, for the Summer Fishery as well as for the Winter Fiftierv.

Then the lit id Petition was brought up, and read; Petting forth, "1 hat the Port of Milford, in the County of Pembroke, is a lafe and commodious Harbour, capable of

Vol. 27.

receiving at all times the whole royll Navy and Trade of Great Britain-, and is most conveniently situated for the Resort and Security of Merchant Ships, when they cannot easily enter the English Channel, and for the fending

out and relieving of Cruizers, from time to time, upon proper Stations in the Ocean; and for the immediate repairing and refitting such Cruizers, in case of Damage: That Ships may proceed from the said Harbour into the Ocean, and return from thence with almost any Wind, by taking a proper Advantage of the strong Currents, and in a gr*at deal less time than isusually employed in failing with the most favourable Wind from to the

Land's End: That the said Harbour may in a very short time, at a moderate Expence, be rendered defensible and secure against any Attack: That a Dock Yard may be established there, and any Number of Ships, and of any Rate, rebuilt, careened, repaired, and fitted for Sea, with the greatest Convenience and Expedition; and that Plenty of proper Materials for the Construction of Ships abound in the adjacent Counties: And therefore praying the House to take this Matter into Consideration, and to make such Provision'relative thereto, as its Nature and Importance may appear to require.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding One million, be granted to his Majesty, upon Account, to enable his Majesty to defray any extraordinary Expences of the War incurred, or to be incurred, for the Service of the Year 1757; and to take all such Measures as may be necessary to disappoint or defeat any Enterprises or Designs of his Enemies, and as the Exigency of Affairs may require.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding Fifty thousand Pounds, be granted to his Majesty, upon Account, to be paid to such Per ions, and in such Manner, and by such Proportions, as his Majesty, shall direct, for the Uie and Relief of his Majesty’s Subjects in his several Provinces of North and South Carolina and Virginia, in America, in Recom* pence for such Services as, with the Approbation of the Commander in Chief of his Majesty’s Forces in America, they respectively shall have performed, or shall perform, either by putting the said Provinces in a State of Defence^ or by acting with Vigour against the Enemy.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding Twenty thousand Pounds, be granted to his Majesty, upon Account, to be paid to the United Company of Merchants of England trading to the East Indies, towards enabling them to defray the Expence of a military Force in their Settlements, to be maintained by them in lieu of the Battalion of his Majesty’s Forces withdrawn from those Settlements.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding Ten thousand Pounds, be granted to his Majesty, to be employed in maintaining and supporting the British Forts and Settlements upon the Coast of Africa.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding Two thousand Five hundred Pounds, be granted to his Majesty, to enable the Commissioners for building Westminster Bridge, and for widening the Avenues leading from Charing Cross to both Houses of Parliament, to widen the Street or Passage leading from Ccckfpur Street to the Passage in Spring Garden leading to Saint James's Park.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Claim, in the said Resolution, of a Right in the Assembly to appoint such Person or Persons for the receiving and issuing of public Money, as the said Assembly shall think proper, is illegal, unconllitutional, and derogatory of the Rights of the Crown of Great Britain.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Six last Resolutions of the Assembly of Jj-mai.a, of the 29th Day of October 1753, proceed upon a manifest Misapprehension of his Majesty’s Instruction to his Governor, requiring him not to give his Afient to any Bill of an unusual or extraordinary Nature and Importance, wherein his Majesty’s Prerogative, or Property of his Subjects, may be prejudiced, or the Trade or Shipping of this Kingdom any-ways affected, unless there be a Clause inserted, suspending the Execution of such Bill, until his Majesty’s Pleasure shall be known; and that such Instruction is just and necessary, and no Alteration of the Constitution of that Island, nor any-ways derogatory to the Rights of his Subjects there.

The Commons disagree to the next Amendment, made by your Lordships, Press 8, Line 13; which is to leave out the Word " Four," and inlert " Two:"

Because however this Amendment may seem to be founded upon that other Amendment, by which your Lordships pt opose to reduce the Number of Men in each Company, yet it is, in fad, not correspondent with it; in-afinuch as by confining the Number of Serjeants to Two, your Lordships take away that very Latitude of forming Companies of more than Forty Men; which your Lordships, it is presumed, intended to give, when you directed that the Companies should consist of Forty Men at the lead.

The Commons disagree to the 2d Amendment in the 7th Line of the 10th Press, which is to leave out from " the" to "County," in the nth Line of the same Prels:

Because the Provisions made by this Bill, for establishing a more useful Militia, are at lead as necessary for the Tower Hamlets as for the rest of the Kingdom; and the leaving them as proposed by your Lordships Amendments, under the Regulation of the Act of King Charles the 2d, would subject them to pecu'iar Hardship9.

The Commons decline, at this time, offering any other Reasons; believing these may be l'ufficient to prevail with your Lordships not to inlist upon the said Amendment, that a Bill so necessary may not be loft.

The Commons disagree to the next Amendment, Prels H, 1 Jne 21; which is to leave out " One of them, together with any Three Commissioners of the Land " Tax," and, instead thereof, to insert " Tiitee or more " Deputy Lieutenants; or in calc Three Deputy Lieutenants shall not meet, then any Two Deputy Lieute-'

" nants, together with any One Justice of the Peace for " such County, Riding, or Place, or any One Deputy Lieutenant, together with Two such Justices of the Peace:"

Because they apprehend that it would be scarce possible, in many Counties, for the Justices of the Peace to execute the several Powers veiled by the Bill in the Commissioners of the Land Tax, upon account of the Paucity of their Numbers; whereas the Commissioners of the Land Tax are not only much more numerous, and more conllantly resident in the several Counties in which they are required by Law to have their Qualifications situated, but are also actually intruded with the Execution of Powers bearing the nearest Resemblance to those which are the Subject of this Amendment, in all the late Acts for recruiting his Majesty’s Forces; in which Acts it hath been found necessary to add the Commissioners of the Land Tax, upon the Experience of the Impossibility of their being carried into Execution by the Justices of the Peace.

The House proceeded to take into Consideration the Report made of tire Conference with the Lords upon Friday the 27th Day of Maylaft; and the Reasons given by the Lords for inlisting upon several of the Amendments made by their Lordships to the Bill, intituled, An Act for the better ordering of the Militia Forces in the fevvral Counties of that Part of Great Britain called Env-

u

land, to which this House had difigreed, were read; and are as followeth; viz.

The Lords agree to the Amendments made by the Commons to Clause B, added by their Lordships to the Bill, intituled, An Act for the better ordering of the Militia Forces in the several Counties of that Part of Great Britain called England.

The Lords infill on their Amendment made to the said Bill, in Press 8. Line 13. which is, to leave out the Word " Four," and insert " Two," to which the Commons di I agree:

Because it appears to the Lords, That as the Number of Men is reduced One Half fom the original Plan, which the Commons do agree to, it kcms luperfluous to demand more Serjeants from his Majesty’s other Forces than will be luificient to discipline the Number of Militia Forces allotted by this Bill, which, as they are reduced to One Half of their former Number, will consequently not require above Half the Number of Serjeants, who will be able to instruct others in the Duty of Serjeants; and

VOL. 27.

i>rJ?

thereby obviate the Objection made by the Commons, of the not leaving a Latitude of forming Companies of more than Forty Men; and the Lords do farther consider, that the reducing the Number of Serjeants, by One Half, to be taken out of his Majesty’s other Forces, will greatly obviate any Objection of weakening the Army.

The Lords do not insist on their 2d Amendment, in Press 10. Line 7. which is, to leave out from " the" to " County," in the 11 th Line of the same Press, to which the Commons disagree.

The Lords agree to the Amendment made by the Commons to their Lordships Amendment, in Press 10. Line 12.

The Lords do also agree to the Amendment made by the Commons to their Lordships Amendment in Press 11. Line 34.

The Lords insist on their Amendment made to the said Bill, in Press 14. Lines 21 and 22, which is, to leave out " One of them, together with any Three Commissioners " of the Land Taxand, instead thereof, to insert " Three or more Deputy Lieutenants, or in case Three " Deputy Lieutenants shall not meet, then any Two " Deputy Lieutenants, together with any One Justice " of the Peace for such County, Riding, or Place; or " any One Deputy Lieutenant, together with any Two " such Justices of the Peace to which the Commons disagree:

Because the Lords conceive, that such Acts of Magi-stracy should not be vested by Act of Parliament in any Set of Men, this being the executive Part of Government, and undoubtedly, by the Constitution, a peculiar and natural Right of the Crown, which thisPradice has doubtless intrenched upon; and the Lords cannot agree on this Occasion to countenance another Precedent of that Sort; Neither do the Lords admit the Reasoning used by the Commons, that the Justices of the Peace, by reason of the Paucity of their Number, will not be able to carry, in Conjunction with the Deputy Lieutenants, this Bill into Execution, as the additional Trouble occasioned by this Bill to those Magistrates will not be great, nor more than what is laid in almost every Session of Parliament, by new Acts, upon them; the Lords do therefore hope the Commons will not, upon this Expofi-tion of their Reasons, any longer disagree to this Amendment, which their Lordships think it incumbent on them to adhere to.

The Lords do also insist on the Seven Amendments immediately following, made by their Lordships to the said Bill, to which the Commons disagree, for the same Reasons for which their Lordships insist on their laid Amendment, Press 14. Lines 21 and 22.

The Lords do likewise insist on their Amendment in Press 18. Lines 39 and 40, and the Four following Amendments, to which the Commons disagree, for the same Reasons for which their Lordships insist on their Amendment, Press 14. Lines 21 and 22.

The Lords do insist on Clause C, added by their Lordships to the said Bill, to which the Commons disagree:

Because the Lords think there cannot be a more proper Encouragement to those who are to bear the Burthen of the military Service directed by this Bill, than the Liberty given them by it to set up and exercise any Trade they are apt and able for, in the manner set forth in the said Clause, which the Lords esteem a full and adequate Compensation; and though the Commons object to the thus incidentally repealing the Act of Elizabeth, in a Bill which undoubtedly cannot justly be deemed one ot Police or Commerce, yet they think themselves well founded in this Amendment, as well on account of the Keasonable-ness of the Objcd proposed, as on the Precedent of what has been enacted by a former Parliament.

The Lords insist on their Amendment in Press 21, Lines 27, 28, and 29, and the Two following Amendments, to which the Commons disagree, for the same Reasons for which their Lordships infill on their Amendment, Preis 14. Lines 21 and 22.

The House proceeded to take into Consideration the Report from the Committee, to whom the Petition of several Merchants of London, in behalf of themselves, and all others concerned in the Trade and Commerce of this Kingdom, was referred.

And the said Report was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Barrington Esquire informed your Committee, That he had lived many Years in Devand had frequently heard of Ships being taken in or near the Channel: That, during the lall War, a Month never passed without Accounts of Ships being taken, which he apprehends would have been in a great measure, if not totally, prevented, had the Haven at Milford been used as one of his Majesty’s Harbours, and a Place of Rendezvous for Ships of War.

Mr. John Hutchinson, an Insurance Broker, produced

to your Committee an Account of Ships taken during the present War (extracted from the Books kept at Lloyd's Coflee-house) by which it appeared, that 198 had been taken in Latitude 49 Degrees, or to the Northward of it.

Captain Fairy, who has commanded a Ship 20 Years in different Branches of Trade, informed your Committee, That Cruizers and Merchant Ships are frequently detained in the British Channel by North Well and Well Winds, and that they cannot clear this Channel with the Wind at South: That Milford I laven is more conveniently situated for lending out Cruizers than any other Harbour: That Ships may go into it with Winds that will not carry them into the British Channel: That it is the fined Harbour in

England, and the whole royal Navy and Trade of Great Britain may ride there at cne time with Safety.

Captain Lyon, who has commanded Ships in the Coading and Irish Trade for 15 Years, said, That he is well acquainted with Milford Haven: That it is a safe VOL. ij.

Harbour, and convenient for the Reception of Ships from the West Indies, when they cannot get into the Channel: That if they are detained by Eaderly Winds-at the Chops of that Channel, they may go into Milford when they cannot get into any other Port in Great Britain: That frequently in Winter Time, when they a e.' notable to make an Observafion, they fail to the Northward of Solly, and get into Bristol Channel, and are in great Danger before they are sensible of their Midakej and are then obliged to put for Milford Haven, as that is the most proper Place for Shelter:

That a Ship may go out of this Harbour with any Wind that will carry Ships out of the British Channel,' and with some that will not: That in moderate Weather a Ship may get into, or out of, this Harbour, by the Strength of the Tide, with the Wind full against her: That one Tide will fling her out of the Harbour, and then Ihe may proceed on her Voyage either through St. George's Channel, or the open Sea, according as the Wind shall happen to be to the North or South of the Wed:

That Ships may go from Brest and Rochfort with Winds that will not carry Ships out of the British Chan--nel; but that Ships may go from Milford with any Winds that will carry Ships from those Ports, and with fume that will not; and that if the Fleet now under the Command of Admiral Holbortie had been at Milford, they might have failed with a N. W. Wind, which detained them at Spithead.

Being aiked, Whether Ships making {oxMilfordHaven-could keep a Reckoning? he said, They may, provided, they know the Tides: That he had lain Eleven Days together about the Islands, and the Chops of the Channel,* under reefed Courses, and never was at a Loss about his Reckoning.

And being asked, How far from the Harbour’s Mouth the Currents would have any Effect on Vessels? — He said, Several Leagues} but that, properly speaking, they are not Currents, but Tides which run regularly Six Hours one Way and Six Hours the other.

This was confirmed by Captain Vyner, Matter of a Ship for 20 Years, mostly in the Coatting Trade, who also confirmed the Evidence given by Captain and Captain Farry, as to the Capacioufness and Safety of the Harbour, and the Facility with which Ships may go in and out; and also that Part of Captain Lyons Evidence which relates to the failing of Ships from Brest,

and the British Channel.

And Captain Vyner also informed your Committee, That a convenient Dock Yard may be made at Milford Haven, as it abounds with Rivulets and Creeks, which will save Expence in digging: That Conveniences may be made for building 1,000 Ships at one time; and that thelargest Ships might be docked there, without waiting for a Spring Tide, as the Water riles 24 or 25 Feet on a Neap Tide, and 35 or 36 Feet on a Spring Tide; and this Part of his Evidence was confirmed by Captain Farry.

Mr. Gardner, who deals in Timber, and lives at cester, said. That he is well acquainted with the Rivers Severn, Wye, and Avon: That great Quantities of Oak grow near thcle Rivers, which is deemed the bed Timber in England: That Shropshire Oak in particular is much esteemed, and bought by Contractors, and others, for Ship-building: That the Forest of Dean adjoins to the River Severn, and great Quantities of Timber are carried by his Majesty’s Hoys from Gatcomb to Plymouth, for the Use of the royal Navy: That thele Vessels pass by Milford in their Way, and are frequently obliged to wait for Convoys to go round the Land's End; but that open Trows would be able to carry this Timber to Milford at much less Expence, and with greater Expedition:

That the Freight of a Load of Timber from the Forest of Dean to Plymouth is about 4c s. but the Evidence would be glad to contract to carry it to Milford for 20; and that there is now a large Quant ity of Timber to be sold at Neath in Swancey, and also in several other Parts . of W cUswhjch lie still nearer to Milford.

Lieutenant Colonel TVatfon produced to your Committee a Survey of the Haven, taken by him in the Year 1756; and said, that it is so excellent and commodious a Harbour for Trade and Navigation, that Vessels are in and out in an Hour’s Time into the open Seas, and in a fair Way betwixt Lanets End and Ireland, and are, in 8 or 10 Hours after leaving Milford, round the Land's End into the English Channel, or upon the Irish Coast: That

they can likewise get much looner to the Westward from' this Harbour than from any Port in the Channel,

such as Plymouth, Foy, Falmouth, &c. and that the Haven comprehends the whole Space betwixt the Harbour’s Mouth and Haverfordwest, which is about 23 Miles, and

navigable to that Town:

That SpringTides rife in this Harbour betwixt 30 and 34 Feet, and Neap Tides between 20 and 24; and the Bottom being soft deep Ouze, Ships may be safely laid ashore in ally Place:

That the Entrance into the Haven betwixt Block-house on the East, and Dale Block-house on the West, is One Mile and an Half over, with deep Water almost close to the Cliff*, which generally rife about 130 Feet above the Level of the Water:

That Huhberjlon Road on the North Side is the largest

2nd belt Anchoring Place in the whole Harbour, where Vessels of any Burthen may ride fafein Water from 3 to 12 Fathom deep, free from every Accident of Weather, unlei's it blows hard at W.N. W. which, coming over the harrow Neck of Land West of Dale, blows up the Reach to Peterchurch, and occasions a great Swell:

That in the Mouth of NailandPill, on the North Side, Vessels anchor in 9 or 10 Fathom Water, or lie dry within the PHI at Ebb Tide:

That Nature seems to have formed this Haven for the particular Benefit and Advantage of that Part of the Island lying on the North-West Side of the which

abounds with so many Rivers, which are navigable into the Rrjfo/Channel: That nothing would more effectually contribute to the general Improvement of the Country, than the establishing a Port in a commodious Part of the Haven, which mult soon raise a Spirit of Industry, and produce the usual good Effects which attend Commerce; and that nothing can be of more Consequence than this Harbour to the Trade of Great Britain and Ireland; but that, unless some Forts and Batteries are erected, there can be no Security to the great Number of Vessels continually obliged to put into this Haven, either from StrefV of Weather, or to wait for a fair Wind; which Number of Shipping will be greatly increased in Time of War; and, without something is done, may be destroyed: That too Ships were there, when he made his Survey, which might have been burnt by a Privateer of Six Guns:

And being examined as to the proper Method of fortifying this Harbour, he delivered to your Committee the following Proposals; viz.

Proposals for protecting Huhberston Road and Nailand Pill, in Milford Haven.

First Method.

If thought proper to erect Batteries for the Protection of the Trade that continually resort to this Harbour, the most proper Situations for that Purpose appear to be Great Cajlk, or Bickton Point, and Thorn island, near IVift

Handle Point.

Bickton Point is a narrow Neck of Land fronting the Entrance; the Cliffs round this Point rife irregularly, and are from 4.0 to 80 Feet above the Level of the Water: Thorn Island is about 200 Feet long, and 150 Feet broad; the Cliffs on the West Side rife about 100 Feet above the Level of the Water, and Hope to the East, where they are about 40 Feet. This Istand is separated from IVft Nangle Point by a narrow Channel, about 400 Feet broad.

If the above Istand was cut to a proper Height, it is the most convenient Ground to assist a Battery on Bickton Point, and command the Entrance of the Harbour; but if it should bethought too expensive to make use of Thorn

1757-'

Island, it would be necessary to erect a Battery on the most convenient Part of West Nangle Point.

Second Method.

Within the above-mentioned Points is a high Rock, called the Stack. This Rock is 60 Feet long, and 30 Feet broad at Top, and rises about 50 Feet above high Water Mark. The Stone seems to be of a red Tandy Nature, and flopes in shelving Beds towards the South.

Close to the East and West Ends of the Stack runs Two narrow Ledges of Rock, which are mostly covered at high Water. The East Ledge projects about 250 Feet, and the West Ledge 150 Feet, from the Stack. The Whole forms at low Water a Sort of Island, about 450 Feet long, and 200 broad.

In order to bring the whole Area of this Rock upon an equal Level, the Stack to be put down to 20 Feet above high Water Mark, and the Rubble Stone to be employed, as far as it will go, in raising the projecting Points to the feme Level with the Rock, which would afford sufficient Area for proper Batteries, and necessary Cover.

The Di fiance from the Sta to the South Shore is 1,366 Yards, where it would be necessary to erect a Batter)' opposite to the Stack Rock; which Two Batteries would be a very good Security to lload.

But as the preparing Thorn island, or Stack Rock, to receive proper Batteries, will be not only expensive, but attended with several Inconveniences (such as continually supplying the Garrisons with Provisions and Water, and the Accidents they nuift be exposed to in blowing Weather from the Spray of the Sea); and as the Scheme of a Hulk or floating Battery would likewise be not only very expensive, but subject to Variety of Accidents, I imagine the frugaleft Method would be to erect a Battery on PVeft Nangle Point, and another opposite to it on Bickton Point, of 16 Guns each, and Cover for 150 Men, in each Place, without attempting any thing on the Islands, or having a Hulk.

Ifproposed to establish aPort at the Mouth Pill, no Part of the Haven can be more convenient for that Purpose. This Port would be very easily and effectually secured by Two Batteries, one on Peterchurch Point, the other on the West Part of Nailand Point, each of Six Guns, and Cover for 50 Men at each.

This is only meant as a Protection and Security to Nailand Pill, because any Vessels that are forced into Milford by Stress of Weather or contrary Winds, can have no better anchoring Ground than Hubberston Road; above which Road no Ship waiting, for a Wind would chuse to go.

And being examined as to the Expence of each Pro-pofel, he said. That Two Batteries, and Cover for 30 Men at each, may be built at Nailand Pill, for about z or ^.3000, if Labour and Materials are cheap:

That the erecting Two Batteries, of 16 Guns each, one at West Nangle Point, and the other at Bickton Point, and Cover for 150 Men at each, would ’ cost about £.16,000: That the Guns should not be Jess than Twenty-four-Pounders; and he thought f UefeTwo Batteries would be sufficient for defending the Ships in the Harbour:

That the cutting down and fortifying Thorn island would be very expensive, and may cost £.20,000, before the Works are begun to be ere died.

Vice Admiral Knowles and Colonel PVatfon informed your Committee, That as the said Works cannot be completed in less than Two Years, it will be proper to station a Hulk of 40 Guns near the Stack island, for the Defence of the Harbour, until the Works are finished.

Mr. Whitaker, being examined, said. That he has been concerned in Buildings in this Haven: That the Price of Labour, as well as Materials, is very low: That there are Two Sorts of Lime there; viz. the Aberdaw, which will cement under Water, and the common Sort, which are both very reasonable; and that Stone is very plentiful, there being Quarries all over the Haven.

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of his Majesty’s Commission, desire the immediate Attendance of this honourable House, in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read:

Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers: Where the Commission was read, for the further proroguing of the Parliament until Thursday the First Day of December next: And the Parliament was accordingly prorogued until Thursday the First Day of December next.
